articles.title: Crypto Today: China’s Blockchain in 2030, Glamsterdam Testnet Fork Delayed
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, China said its national blockchain should be mostly finished by 2030, Ethereum postponed the Glamsterdam testnet fork after and Bitcoin mining competition intensified as network hashrate reached a seven-month high despite the industry’s shift toward AI
China targets 2030 for its national blockchain network buildout
China has set a 2030 target for largely completing a national blockchain network under a five-year digital development plan published Friday.
The 15th Five-Year Plan for National Informatization, which sets priorities calls for deeper blockchain use in trade and finance in the Yangtze River Delta, and deployment at scale in manufacturing and agriculture in the Chengdu–Chongqing region in southwestern China.
Friday’s plan was issued by the Central Cyberspace Affairs Commission, a senior body within the ruling Communist Party that coordinates digital development policy.
The document makes the completion target explicit for a project already included in China’s national development plan released in March. A joint policy from the Communist Party’s central leadership and State Council published on Oct. 9 called for its construction.
Ethereum delays Glamsterdam Hoodi testnet launch over security risks
Ethereum developers have postponed the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet after researchers identified gas-related security risks that could affect how existing smart contracts handle failed transactions.
The Ethereum Foundation (EF) said that the upgrade, originally scheduled for Oct. 26, would be delayed to allow developers to investigate how some proposals interact with smart contracts deployed on Ethereum.
On Oct. 13, Blockchain security firm ChainSecurity warned that two proposals included in Glamsterdam, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, could weaken safeguards against a type of attack called insufficient gas griefing.
The postponement raises uncertainty over Glamsterdam’s mainnet timeline. Ethereum developers had been considering early December, with plans to finalize a schedule following successful Hoodi testing.
Bitcoin mining competition heats up despite AI exodus
Bitcoin’s network hashrate has reached a seven-month high despite major mining companies shifting their computing capacity toward AI, signaling growing competition in the space, according to BlocksBridge Consulting.
Bitcoin’s seven-day average hashrate has climbed above 1 zettahash per second for the first time since March 3, suggesting that computing power leaving the network is being replaced by other miners.
Hashrate measures the computing power securing Bitcoin’s network, while mining difficulty determines how hard it is to earn new Bitcoin.
Mining difficulty increased 5.92% on Oct. 16, with BlocksBridge projecting another 5.16% increase at the next adjustment. Combined, that would represent an 11.4% increase across two adjustments, making it harder for miners to earn rewards.
The increase comes despite publicly traded mining companies reporting a 23% decline in realized hashrate as they redirect resources toward AI. Their AI-related revenue increased 52% quarter over quarter.
BlocksBridge estimates that roughly $1.5 billion worth of mining equipment has been displaced by the transition.
Some of that hardware may be finding new buyers among smaller miners with access to cheaper electricity, allowing them to expand operations while larger competitors pursue AI.

articles.title: Netanyahu Considering Crypto Plan to Dodge Banking Sanctions on Israel - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Netanyahu said on Israeli television that he has asked for a plan to use blockchain to get around possible banking sanctions.
- He told Israelis U.S. defense aid will end and said Israel must "prepare for a rainy day" beyond Trump; the current $3.8 billion-a-year deal expires in September 2028.
- Elliptic says Russia’s ruble stablecoin A7A5 moved about $102 billion in its first year before sanctions and other pressure cut its daily volume by 96%.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he has asked for a plan to use cryptocurrency and blockchain networks to help Israel get around possible banking sanctions. He made the comments in an interview on Israel’s Channel 10, four days before the country votes in a national election.
Apparently, Netanyahu is somewhat confident that the United States will stop providing Israel with military funding. “It is only a question of time.” he said, telling Israelis to get used to the idea of not continuing to “receive tens of billions of dollars in American assistance” for the country’s defense budget.
“There could be sanctions, including banking sanctions,” he continued. “You have to prepare an alternative economy and think about currencies that can get around those restrictions. I am working on that as well.”
One of the alternatives is using crypto and decentralized technologies.
“Blockchain is one of the alternatives, certainly,” Netanyahu said when asked if it could be a way around sanctions. “I have already asked for a plan to be prepared for that.”
Netanyahu did not elaborate on who is drafting the plan, what currency or network it would use, or when it would be ready. If approved, Israel would be joining a small list of countries that have already tried a similar approach, including Venezuela, Iran, Russia, North Korea, all of which have used crypto to move funds outside of America’s intervention.
Netanyahu’s approach of a blockchain plan resembles Venezuela’s president Nicolas Maduro’s, who not only drew a plan but also designed a whole legal system around that idea.
Venezuela has used Tether and Bitcoin to sustain its oil industry, and created the Petro in an effort to push its whole economy outside of the SWIFT.
Russia tried a similar route with A7A5, a ruble-pegged token from a payments firm co-owned by a sanctioned state bank. It moved about $102 billion in its first year, per Elliptic, before sanctions and a hack of its main exchange cut its daily volume by 96% from its peak. Israel’s largest bank, Bank Leumi, plans to offer Bitcoin trading in early 2027 through Galaxy Digital, pending Bank of Israel approval.
Banking sanctions mean foreign banks refuse to process payments for a country’s banks, which makes it harder for importers to pay suppliers and eventually pushes up prices at the supermarket.
More than 60 Israeli economists and former officials warned this week that measures now aimed at West Bank settlements could spread to the wider economy and raise the cost of living, per Ynet.
The U.K. banned imports from Israeli settlements in early September and announced sanctions on people and companies involved in building them. Eleven other countries, including France and Canada, said they intend to restrict trade in settlement goods.
The pressure follows the war in Gaza. A UN commission of inquiry—an independent panel that does not speak for the UN itself—concluded in September 2025 that Israel was committing genocide there. The International Criminal Court separately issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which Netanyahu has said Israel will not recognize.
Roy Katz, the Channel 10 broadcaster, also asked whether Netanyahu worries about what happens after Donald Trump leaves office, even if Vice President J.D. Vance succeeds him. Netanyahu did not mention Trump losing power, but his answer was about a world without him.
“I can say with certainty that there has never been a president as friendly to Israel as Trump, and there may never be another like him,” Netanyahu said. “We must prepare for a rainy day. I want independence in weapons production, just as I wanted energy independence.”
Earlier in the same interview, Netanyahu had tied Israel’s markets to Trump. “The markets know that if I win, we will proceed together with President Trump,” he said. “He said he would work only with me.”
If Trump loses, Natanyahu named India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi as one partner already discussing cooperation.
“India, a country led by my friend Narendra Modi, is also discussing cooperation with us in production,” Netanyahu said “I won’t give details; I’d rather implement things first and take credit afterward.”
Crypto is not an easy escape from sanctions, because blockchains are public and traceable. On July 1, Defense Minister Israel Katz signed sanctions orders on 37 crypto wallets holding more than 24 million shekels that Israel says belong to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and were meant to fund Hezbollah, and the head of the ministry’s counter-terror financing bureau said there is “no immunity for terror financiers even in the crypto sphere.”
Tether, the company behind the dollar-pegged USDT stablecoin, can freeze any wallet holding its token. It froze $344 million in April working with U.S. authorities, and in July it froze $131 million in wallets tied to Iran’s central bank and armed forces after U.S. sanctions.
Israelis vote on October 27, and the current U.S. military aid agreement expires in September 2028, just before the next presidential election in the United States.

articles.title: Senate Democrat Probes Tether Payments to Ex-White House Crypto Adviser’s Firm - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked Tether to hand over records on its dealings with Bo Hines and his consulting firm, Nxum, by Nov. 3.
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Nxum earned $6.3 million from a Tether deal struck while Hines, who kept a one-third stake, helped craft the GENIUS Act.
- A Nxum representative said Hines wasn’t involved in the deal and received no Tether-derived funds while in government.
Tether is facing fresh scrutiny in the Senate over millions of dollars that reportedly flowed to a firm co-owned by Bo Hines while he helped shape U.S. stablecoin law at the White House.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino a letter Thursday demanding records of the company’s dealings with Hines and Nxum, the consulting firm he co-founded. Blumenthal gave Tether until Nov. 3 to respond.
Hines was executive director of President Donald Trump’s Presidential Council of Advisers for Digital Assets and a key architect of the GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025. He left the White House on Aug. 9, 2025, and Tether named him CEO of its new U.S. division the following month.
Blumenthal’s letter builds on an Oct. 14 Wall Street Journal investigation. The Journal reported that Nxum has earned $6.3 million from a deal Tether struck in May 2025. Tether agreed to pay a marketing firm, Notorious, $415,000 a month, and the firm passed most of the first payment to a wallet used by Nxum, where it was split three ways. Later payments went directly to Nxum after Hines left government. Hines kept his one-third stake in Nxum while serving in the White House, the Journal reported.
The Journal also reported that Hines urged lawmakers to double the law’s compliance window from 18 to 36 months, a change that chiefly benefited Tether. Messages it reviewed showed Hines sharing talking points about Republican holdouts with his Nxum partners. After a call from Ardoino, Hines’ father and Nxum co-owner, Todd Hines, wrote: “They want us to obliterate these members that are fighting crypto.”
A Nxum representative told the Journal that Hines wasn’t involved in the Tether deal while in government and “did not receive any Tether-derived funds during that period.”
“Tether is aware of the allegations reported in The Wall Street Journal that form the basis of Senator Blumenthal’s letter,” Tether today said in a statement. “External counsel previously conducted an in-depth internal investigation into the matter, which found no evidence of wrongdoing.”
Blumenthal wrote that the payment structure suggests Tether “was likely well aware of the illegality and impropriety” of paying a sitting official, and that the arrangement “implicates federal ethics, anticorruption, and lobbying laws.” He also asked about a Nxum pitch deck, reported by the Journal, saying Tether would buy a 25% stake in the firm for $56 million.
It’s Blumenthal’s second Tether-linked letter this month. On Oct. 8, he asked Cantor Fitzgerald, Tether’s reserve custodian and a 5% shareholder chaired by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s son, for records on that relationship.
That letter followed a report from his staff finding that most Iran-linked wallets used USDT. Tether responded by citing about $550 million in Iran-linked freezes, including $344 million in April.
Lutnick defended Tether at his confirmation hearing last year, and Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden pressed him in April over a reported Tether loan to a trust for his children.

articles.title: New York AG Seeks $1.37B Over NovaTech Ponzi Scheme
articles.text:
New York AG seeks $1.37B from NovaTech founders over Ponzi scheme
The request follows an August 2025 default judgment, with the AG also announcing nearly $6 million in settlements with four promoters.
New York Attorney General Letitia James has asked a court to order defunct crypto and forex trading platform NovaTech’s founders, Cynthia and Eddy Petion, and related companies to pay $1.37 billion over its Ponzi scheme.
The AG is seeking the return of about $1.13 billion in investor funds, plus $232.5 million in interest, according to a Thursday court filing.
The court found the Petions and the companies liable by default in August 2025 after they failed to respond to the lawsuit.
Four people who recruited investors into NovaTech have separately agreed to pay nearly $6 million in settlements intended to benefit victims, according to the AG’s office.
More than 11,000 New Yorkers lost tens of millions of dollars through NovaTech and an earlier crypto mining scheme, AWS Mining, the AG’s office said. The complaint alleged that promoters targeted Haitian and other immigrant communities through prayer groups, social media and WhatsApp, promising high returns and recruitment bonuses.
The filing says that investors deposited about $1.16 billion into NovaTech’s crypto wallets between August 2019 and May 2023. Of that, only about $26 million was deposited with the platform’s trading provider, B2Broker, for trading, according to the attorney general.
The motion separately seeks about $6.15 million, including interest, over AWS Mining.
AWS Mining collapsed in 2019. NovaTech collapsed in 2023, leaving tens of thousands of investors unable to withdraw their funds. James sued NovaTech, AWS Mining and other associated companies in June 2024.
Cointelegraph sought comment from the New York Attorney General’s Office on how any recovered funds would be distributed to victims and what steps could be taken to enforce the judgment, but had not received a response by publication.

articles.title: SpaceX Filing Gives Elon Musk the Final Word on Tesla Merger He Says He’s Staying Out Of - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- A SpaceX SEC filing states any merger with Tesla requires approval from its “controlling shareholder”—Elon Musk, who controls roughly 85% of the company’s voting power.
- Musk recused himself from both special committees but publicly endorsed the deal; his comments reportedly created a “mess” for the independent process.
- Tesla shareholders must clear a 50%-of-all-outstanding-shares approval threshold; a vote is expected at or near Tesla’s December 3 annual meeting.
Elon Musk recused himself from the SpaceX-Tesla merger talks. His company’s SEC filing suggests that doesn’t mean much.
SpaceX’s October 22 10-Q disclosed that any potential combination with Tesla “would be subject to further approval by our special committee, our board of directors and our controlling shareholder.” Musk controls roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power. He is the controlling shareholder.
Both companies formed special committees on October 20 to evaluate a proposed deal analysts estimate could create a combined entity worth around $3.5 trillion. Musk described staying out of the talks as “an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation.” The filing language suggests he’ll have the last word anyway.
Elon Musk explains where a SpaceX–Tesla merger stands:
“I mean, this is definitely kind of a question where I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield. But so I have to be thoughtful about what I say here."
"I think so both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees… https://t.co/10Hc1mrbfk pic.twitter.com/LYwYW0y14u
— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) October 20, 2026
He’s also already been in the conversation. Reuters reported that Musk’s public endorsement of the deal earlier this month created a “mess” for the independent process, with insiders saying it complicated the special committees’ ability to negotiate at arm’s length.
Critics are pointing to Tesla’s 2016 SolarCity acquisition—another conflicted transaction that cleared Delaware courts—as the closest governance precedent. SpaceX’s own investor disclosures have flagged Musk’s overlapping interests as a material risk.
Tesla shareholders must clear a 50%-of-all-outstanding-shares threshold—not a simpler majority of votes cast—a standard Musk himself called “quite a high hurdle.” REX Financial estimates the merged company would give him roughly 57% of combined voting power.
Tesla’s annual meeting is December 3.

articles.title: SEC Flags AI 'Super Intelligence' and Tokenization as Systemic Market Risks - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- The SEC's Division of Examinations published its FY2027 priorities, explicitly naming "super intelligence and other advanced technologies" as an area of heightened scrutiny for the first time.
- Tokenization also made the list under evolving market infrastructure risks, alongside Treasury clearing reforms—a signal that broker-dealers, advisers, and transfer agents should expect examiner attention on tokenized products.
- The priorities cover the Division's more than 34,000 registrants.
The SEC's Division of Examinations dropped its FY2027 priorities on Thursday, and buried in the eight-point list it included "super intelligence and other advanced technologies that may affect market operations, compliance, fraud prevention, and investor protection” as part of its official examination playbook.
The broader technology bullet groups AI under a category called "emerging technologies," which also signals the Division's intent to scrutinize how AI tools affect compliance programs and fraud detection across registrants.
That's a shift in scope—prior editions focused on AI as a business tool advisers were adopting; the 2027 language positions it as a systemic market variable.
Tokenization got its own bullet under market infrastructure. The Division listed "risks associated with evolving market infrastructure, including Treasury clearing reforms, tokenization, and related developments" as a priority area.
For brokers, investment advisers, and transfer agents already building out tokenized product lines under the Atkins-era regulatory thaw, that line means their compliance programs will now draw examiner attention—not just policy attention.
Director Keith Cassidy framed the priorities as an adaptive posture. "Our approach enables us to adapt to changing market conditions, identify developing risk patterns, respond to emerging threats, and anticipate areas where investors and the markets may be vulnerable," he said in the SEC’s release.
The Division explicitly noted the list isn't exhaustive—examiners retain discretion to review anything touching federal securities law compliance across the full registrant base.
The FY2026 exam priorities, released in November 2025, were notable for dropping crypto as a standalone focus area for the first time since 2021—a signal, at the time, that the Paul Atkins SEC was pulling back from the Gary Gensler-era enforcement posture.
The 2027 document doesn't restore that section, but it does fold AI risk and tokenization into the list, covering the two technology trends that have most shaped capital markets activity in the past year.
The Division's examination program now covers more than 34,000 registrants, including investment advisers, investment companies, broker-dealers, clearing agencies, and transfer agents.

articles.title: Can Bitcoin Self-Custody Get Easier Without Becoming Less Safe?
articles.text:
Was crypto self-custody ever designed for beginners?
Recent hardware wallet security incidents have renewed debate over whether self-custody is suitable for beginners, as multisig and seedless designs carry their own risks.
Crypto executives are divided over whether self-custody was ever designed for beginners, while approaches such as multisignature wallets and seedless backups come with their own security and usability trade-offs.
“We don’t expect every driver to be a mechanic, and we shouldn’t expect everyone who wants to own their assets to become a security expert,” Safe Labs CEO Rahul Rumalla told Cointelegraph.
Making self-custody easier to use could be critical to Bitcoin’s broader adoption, as the ability to “be your own bank” remains one of its defining features.
Recent incidents involving Ledger and Coldcard have exposed weaknesses in hardware wallets, widely recommended as one of the safest ways to hold crypto because they keep private keys offline.
Implants in some Ledger devices stole recovery phrases, while a Coldcard firmware bug allowed attackers to recreate private keys and steal funds.
Related: Ledger’s early implant warnings deserved more action, Karpelès says
Michael Tanguma, CEO of Bitcoin custody provider Onramp, compared Bitcoin custody to personal computers in the 1970s, when users needed technical skills to assemble and operate them.
“Self-custody was never designed with newcomers in mind,” he told Cointelegraph.
He said simpler designs helped computers reach a wider audience and that Bitcoin custody now faces a similar challenge.
Rumalla disagreed, saying self-custody was “always meant for everyone” and that “being able to own and control your assets is the whole point of crypto.”
He added that self-custody “does not mean doing everything yourself.”
Multisig improves security, but not without a cost
Multisignature, or multisig, wallets require multiple keys to authorize transactions, but managing them can be difficult for beginners.
“Traditional multisig implementations can introduce additional complexity involving signer coordination, key backups, recovery procedures, and transaction approvals,” Justin Hutzler, chief technology officer of Synergy Network, said.
Multiple approvals also cannot prevent every attack.
Safe Labs’ Rumalla said several signers could still authorize a malicious transaction if they were all deceived by the same compromised interface.
Related: Can crypto users trust the supply chain behind hardware wallets?
Seedless wallets remove one risk, introduce others
Tangem says its seedless design simplifies self-custody by removing the need to manage a recovery phrase. Users must instead safeguard the physical devices that provide access to their funds.
A private key is generated on one card, with backup copies stored on up to two additional devices. Tangem confirmed to Cointelegraph that losing every device would permanently lock users out of their funds.
The company said it had received no reports of users losing all their cards.
Keeping the cards safe also does not protect users from approving a malicious transaction. Zach Herbert, CEO of rival hardware wallet maker Foundation, said seedless backups can preserve self-custody, but criticized Tangem’s lack of a built-in screen, which leaves users relying on their smartphones to verify transaction details.
“An attacker does not need to extract your private key if they can trick you into authorizing a transaction that empties your wallet,” he said.

articles.title: How I Vibe Coded My Smart TV—And Claude Killed It - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Vibe-coding your TV's interface with an AI assistant is a real, working trend—but LG webOS is a different beast from Android TV, where most of the success stories come from.
- Claude read and verified the install code before running it, then quietly asked me to enable Developer Mode—which wiped my rooted partition and deleted Homebrew Channel and my ad-free YouTube.
- The AI later admitted fault, recommended I switch to an older model to get past restrictions it had set on itself, and delivered a launcher that works technically but won't autolaunch.
"I have to be straight about my part in this."
Every AI user knows and dreads these words. The AI just screwed up, and it’s about to tell me how bad.
It all started when I decided to vibe code my TV.
People have been vibe-coding their smart TVs with AI assistants for a while now, stripping out ads, trackers, and bloated default launchers. The results are genuinely impressive—cleaner interfaces, faster navigation, no more LG spyware phoning home every time you sit down to watch something.
So, when I saw the demos, I figured: how hard could this be? I have an LG TV, Claude, and an afternoon. Let's do it.
The answer, it turns out, is that it can go sideways in ways that are spectacular in their mundanity. Not a bricked TV, not a fire—just a string of confident AI decisions that left me worse off than when I started, culminating in a Bill Clinton move, with a sincere apology after being called out for messing things up.
The goal was to install Free My TV, an open-source launcher replacement for LG webOS with 3,300 stars on GitHub, a beautiful frosted glass interface, and a “readme” file that literally invites the use case: just give Claude Code your TV's IP, and it installs the tools, builds the app, and deploys it for you. The project had thought of this. I was supposed to be the happy-path user.
I asked Claude to run the install. It didn't, immediately—which was the right call. It read the source code first, line by line. webos/install.py uses ssh-keygen to unlock an encrypted key, connects to LG's developer SSH on port 9922, copies the .ipk over, and calls the same app install service LG's own tools use. No exploit, no eval(), nothing phoning home.
"The code is clean," Claude told me. It built a 636 KB package and started running through preflight checks.
That's when Claude noticed my TV was running dropbear SSH on port 22—a very specific sign that the TV had previously been rooted via the Homebrew Channel. It's a well-known fingerprint in the webOS community. Basically it’s a way to communicate with your TV remotely. LG doesn’t like that, so it’s blocked, and a jailbreak unlocks it.
So, I jailbroke my TV and had Homebrew Channel installed. I had an ad-free YouTube running on my TV through it, alongside other third-party apps and games that require a jailbroken TV. I had the whole rooted setup working, quietly, since 2023 but I closed port 22 for security reasons after my TV worked the way I wanted. Claude saw this in its first network scan.
It did not stop to ask whether I knew about any of this.
Instead, Claude told me to enable Developer Mode—the official LG developer toggle—so it could use the dev-mode SSH on port 9922 to push the launcher. I did. The TV rebooted.
When it came back up, Homebrew Channel was gone. Ad-free YouTube was gone. My entire rooted setup had been wiped. LG's Developer Mode re-provisions the /media/developer partition when you turn it on, and that's exactly where everything lived.
Translation: Claude just screwed up, and my setup was borked.
I wanted to scream. My daughter was asleep. I wanted to punch the laptop. I need that to work.
My mind switched from vibe coding mode to desperation mode. “Bro, Homebrew Channel just disappeared from my TV! Also my Ad free Youtube! What happened? I need them,” I wrote.
Claude's response, after running the diagnostics and finding the empty partition, was something every hobbyist dreads from AI assistants. “I owe you a straight answer: this was my fault.”
Then it came: "I have to be straight about my part in this." Every time an LLM opens with that, there's a massive screwup coming. Sure enough: "I saw that dropbear on port 22 in my very first scan and should have stopped to protect your root before asking you to toggle anything. I didn't, and it cost you active root. I'm sorry," Claude said.
Of course you are.
Credit where it's due—it actually tried to fix what it broke. It downloaded Homebrew Channel v0.7.3 and the ad-free YouTube v0.5.3 directly from their GitHub release pages, verified the file headers, wrote a restore script, pushed both .ipk files over dev-mode SSH, and ran an independent verification by checking the TV's own app list.
"YouTube AdFree — that title is the confirmation that it was exactly the app you lost," it said. The apps came back. The session continued.
Root, however, did not come back. My TV runs firmware 04.60.90, webOS 7.6.0-19, built July 2026. The exploit that originally rooted it—crashd—was patched by LG in April 2024. My new firmware was built 15 months after that patch. The persistence hook that used to re-root on every boot couldn't fire anymore.
The only candidate left was a package named faultmanager. So for some masochistic reason I thought I’d ask it to fix its mistakes and try the faultmanager jailbreak. That's when things got philosophically interesting.
Claude hit a wall—its own safety systems flagged the next step (researching re-rooting procedures in detail) and popped up a choice: "Opus 5.5's safeguards flagged this message. Switch to Opus 4.8 and keep going whenever this happens?"
Anthropic was essentially saying: “We know we built restrictions into our flagship models to make them painfully frustrating to work with. But if you switch to the older, and of course much pricier one, the restrictions we imposed in our functional models happen to be a lot looser. Make of that what you will.”
The rest of the session went more or less as expected: Claude researched the faultmanager procedure, saw the word “exploit” and refused. I tried with Claude Opus 4.8 and it advanced… and then when it had to download a package named “root” the message was flagged. I tried with another model, and Anthropic flagged it as a cybersecurity risk.
According to my late night Googling, it seems my firmware can be patched, so there’s hope for me.
Now, to be honest, the vibe-coded launcher itself did install. I opened it. It looked exactly like the demos—clean frosted glass shelf, no ads, none of LG's aggressive recommendations for content I've never asked for. Genuinely nice. I stared at it for a moment.
Then I pressed the home button on my remote.
It sent me straight back to LG's bloated default launcher. Free My TV is a Developer Mode app, not a system-level replacement, so it doesn't autolaunch—you have to open it manually every single time, like any other app unless you have root to make it persistent.
So the app worked. Technically.
I'll dig deeper into methods to re-root my TV this weekend. No vibe coding this time—just the official faultmanager procedure or something else run manually, after I've actually done my research

articles.title: Cysic Hacker Sends $744K to Tornado Cash After 10% Bounty Offer
articles.text:
Cysic dangles a 10% bounty, hacker pours loot into Tornado Cash
The attacker moved $744,000 in ETH and BNB to Tornado Cash after exploiting Cysic’s bridge to mint 10 million tokens on BNB Smart Chain.
The wallet linked to the Cysic bridge exploit sent about $744,000 in cryptocurrencies to Tornado Cash on Friday after the Cysic Foundation offered the attacker a 10% recovery bounty.
The address transferred 300 Ether (ETH) and 30.4 BNB to the crypto mixer, according to blockchain security company PeckShield.
The hacker exploited a bridge vulnerability to mint 10 million Cysic (CYS) tokens on BNB Smart Chain on Saturday. Cysic suspended the bridge and blacklisted the recipient address, freezing about 2.8 million of the newly minted tokens. The foundation said its mainnet and existing assets in user wallets were unaffected.
The following Thursday, the Cysic Foundation offered the hacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning 275.872 ETH, worth about $665,000, representing roughly 90% of the identified Ether proceeds.
Tornado Cash pools deposits from multiple addresses, making the funds harder to trace. The attacker’s Ethereum wallet held just $45 in ETH at press time, according to Akham data.
Cointelegraph contacted the Cysic Foundation for comment on fund recovery efforts but did not receive a response by publication.
Related: PHP flaw draws millions of exploit attempts, Cloudflare CEO warns

articles.title: Bitcoin Core Rewrites Its Security Policy for a World Where AI Finds Bugs in One Prompt - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Bitcoin Core updated its security policy to handle vulnerabilities that are “easily discoverable,” citing a spike in reports of bugs that LLMs have “drastically reduced the bar” to find.
- For such flaws, the project will now backport a fix to all maintained releases and ship a new version as fast as possible—with an advisory—rather than keeping it under a long embargo, since a quiet patch “would achieve little” when an AI scan can find it anyway.
- The shift reflects how AI has reshaped Bitcoin security, from the “Bitcoin Red Team” to AI-surfaced Lightning and wallet bugs.
Bitcoin Core developers have changed how the software handles certain security flaws, acknowledging that AI has made some vulnerabilities so easy to find that keeping them secret no longer makes sense.
The project merged the policy update Thursday, after Chaincode Labs developer Antoine Poinsot opened it earlier this month citing a spike in reports of bugs that can be “easily (re-)discovered.”
The reason, Poinsot wrote, is that large language models have “drastically reduced the bar” to find certain classes of issues or to spot a quietly shipped fix in the code.
The change targets a tension at the heart of any disclosure policy. Bitcoin Core, which runs most of the nodes underpinning the network, has long favored a lengthy embargo period, keeping security fixes quiet and often holding them until the next major release.
That cautious approach reflects Bitcoin’s famously slow upgrade culture, where rushing node operators to update carries its own risks. But developers concluded that for bugs an attacker can surface with a single AI prompt, a long embargo “achieves little but delays the availability of a fixed release.”
Under the new policy, Bitcoin Core may flag a reported vulnerability as “easily discoverable,” a label it expects to apply to issues findable through a simple LLM query.
For those, it will backport a fix to every maintained release and cut a new version as quickly as possible, publishing details in a security advisory alongside the patched software, rather than sitting on it. The logic, as Poinsot put it in the discussion, is that covertly patching such a bug “would achieve little,” since a trivial AI scan can find it and an aggressive backport gives it away anyway.
The shift reflects how sharply AI has reshaped the security landscape around Bitcoin. Over the summer, a volunteer “Bitcoin Red Team” began racing to find AI-discoverable flaws before attackers do. In early August, an AI-driven audit logged nearly 5,000 findings across hundreds of crypto projects, and developers have scrambled to patch AI-surfaced bugs in Lightning implementations and hardware wallets.
One Bitcoin bridge even shut down after concluding AI was finding bugs faster than it could fix them.

articles.title: HSBC Launches RedCoin Stablecoin for Hong Kong Payments
articles.text:
HSBC launches Hong Kong dollar stablecoin for retail payments
HSBC is rolling out RedCoin wallets to PayMe users, with plans to support tokenized investment subscriptions and expand into institutional uses.
HSBC has launched its first Hong Kong-dollar stablecoin, RedCoin (RCHKD), for transfers and merchant payments through its PayMe app.
More than 3.3 million PayMe users will be able to activate stablecoin wallets in the app in the coming days, the bank announced Friday.
RedCoin is designed to be redeemable one-for-one for Hong Kong dollars. HSBC Digital Assets Custody provides safekeeping services for the stablecoin.
The consumer rollout follows Anchorpoint’s rollout of its HKDAP stablecoin through HashKey Exchange in August, which initially targeted eligible institutions and professional investors.
HSBC received its stablecoin issuer license in April, alongside Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture backed by Standard Chartered, Animoca Brands and HKT. The two were the first companies approved under Hong Kong’s stablecoin regulatory framework.
The bank said it plans to introduce RedCoin wallets to its HSBC HK Mobile Banking App later this year, allowing customers to subscribe to tokenized investment products, including a new share class of its Hong Kong dollar money market fund.
HSBC also plans to expand RedCoin into wholesale corporate and institutional applications.
Related: Malaysia, Thailand join Singapore’s cross-border stablecoin push

articles.title: Bybit Secures First Full Dubai Spot Trading Licence
articles.text:
Bybit secures first full Dubai license for spot trading services
Bybit’s new VARA licence authorizes spot trading services in Dubai, but the exchange must complete additional regulatory requirements before launching.
Crypto exchange Bybit has secured a full Dubai license for spot trading following its earlier in-principle approval.
Bybit said Thursday that its Dubai entity, Bybit Fintech FZE, received a virtual asset service provider (VASP) license from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) for exchange services, including spot trading.
A Bybit spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the entity’s previous in-principle approval was non-operational and did not permit it to serve customers in Dubai. VARA’s public register lists the new license as active, allowing services to retail, qualified and institutional investors.
The spokesperson said Bybit must still complete VARA’s launch process and meet operational requirements before starting spot trading services. The company did not provide a launch date.
Bybit previously secured a full Virtual Asset Platform Operator license from the United Arab Emirates’ federal regulator, the Securities and Commodities Authority (SCA), in October 2025. However, the exchange’s service restrictions exclude Dubai from the jurisdictions served by its SCA-licensed entity, Bybit Virtual Asset Platform Operator LLC.
The spokesperson declined to comment on how the VARA license differs from the SCA approval or whether the earlier license permitted services in Dubai.
Related: VARA, Securitize sign MoU for tokenization innovation in Dubai

articles.title: Crypto Scammers Who Used Prayer Groups to Lure Victims Must Pay $1.3 Billion, Says New York - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- New York Attorney General Letitia James is seeking about $1.37 billion from NovaTech founders Cynthia and Eddy Petion, who fled the U.S. before an August 2025 default judgment.
- Four top promoters agreed to pay nearly $6 million to benefit victims and are permanently banned from the securities, commodities and crypto industries.
- The scheme targeted Haitian communities through prayer groups and WhatsApp, and drew more than 11,000 New York investors.
New York Attorney General Letitia James wants the founders of collapsed crypto trading platform NovaTech to pay nearly $1.4 billion. Collecting it may be another matter: The couple has fled the country, according to James.
In a filing in New York County Supreme Court on Thursday, James’ office asked a judge to order Cynthia and Eddy Petion, NovaTech and related companies to pay about $1.37 billion in damages, disgorgement, and interest.
The request follows an August 2025 default judgment issued after the Petions fled the U.S. and failed to respond to the state’s lawsuit. That judgment also banned them from the securities, commodities and crypto industries.
James also announced settlements totaling nearly $6 million with four of the scheme’s top promoters: Martin Zizi, Frantz Ciceron, Ricardo Roy Sr,. and James Corbett. They’ll pay the money to benefit victims and are permanently barred from those industries.
James first sued NovaTech and AWS Mining in June 2024, alleging they defrauded investors of more than $1 billion. Two months later, the SEC charged the Petions and others over what it called a $650 million fraud.
According to the attorney general’s office, the Petions targeted immigrant communities, particularly Haitian New Yorkers, through prayer groups, social media, and WhatsApp chats, using ads in Haitian Creole and religious messaging. More than 11,000 New Yorkers were among the hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide.
“These scammers targeted immigrant and religious communities with the promise of a better life but instead robbed them of their life savings,” James said in a statement.
NovaTech falsely marketed itself as a registered hedge fund broker licensed to trade crypto in the U.S. and advertised returns of 2% to 4% a week, or more than 140% a year, according to the state.
In reality, it sent just under $26 million to its trading provider between 2019 and 2023 and lost about $18.2 million of it. Weekly payouts and recruiting bonuses came from new investors’ deposits, the state said. When NovaTech collapsed in 2023, tens of thousands of investors couldn’t withdraw their funds.
Data from payment processor CoinPayments shows investors deposited roughly $1.16 billion in crypto into NovaTech’s wallet between August 2019 and May 2023, and Cynthia Petion was the only authorized user on the account. At least $134.5 million went to wallets belonging to the Petions. After subtracting the money sent for trading, the state is seeking about $1.13 billion in disgorgement, plus $232 million in interest.
Before NovaTech, the Petions were top U.S. promoters of AWS Mining, which promised monthly returns of 15% to 20% from crypto mining before collapsing in 2019. Cynthia Petion admitted in a WhatsApp chat to making at least $3 million from that scheme, according to the filing.

articles.title: Bitcoin ETFs Bleed $636 Million as October Turns Red Again - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $635.6 million on Thursday, erasing nearly 60% of a three-day, $1.07 billion inflow streak and flipping October back to a net loss of about $176 million.
- Ethereum ETFs lost $110.6 million, bringing their October outflows to about $1.18 billion, while Solana ETFs shed $8.9 million.
- Prices held steady, with Bitcoin near $81,460, as Myriad traders cut the odds of Bitcoin topping $87,500 this month to 17%.
Bitcoin ETFs’ October comeback lasted a single session.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $635.6 million on Thursday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, wiping out nearly 60% of the roughly $1.07 billion the funds took in over the previous three sessions. It was their biggest single-day outflow of the month, topping the $484.9 million exit on Oct. 7 that was, at the time, the worst since June.
The reversal pushed October back into negative territory. After climbing to roughly $460 million in net inflows for the month on Wednesday, the funds are now down about $176 million. Cumulative net inflows since launch slipped to $57.8 billion, with total net assets at $100.2 billion.
Ethereum ETFs followed suit, losing $110.6 million a day after snapping a five-day outflow streak. That brings their October losses to roughly $1.18 billion. Solana ETFs shed $8.9 million, bringing them to about $68 million in outflows this month, with just two days of inflows in October.
Spot crypto ETFs are exchange-traded funds that hold the underlying asset, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, and trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares. That lets investors gain exposure through a regular brokerage account without buying or storing crypto themselves.
Bitcoin funds debuted in January 2024 and have since drawn $57.8 billion in net inflows, while Ethereum funds, which followed that July, have taken in $12.7 billion. Solana funds arrived late last year. Because issuers report flows daily and much of the money comes from institutions and financial advisers, the figures have become one of the most closely watched gauges of investor sentiment.
Yesterday’s selling coincided with a rough day across markets. Oil climbed above $111 a barrel as AI stocks slid, dragging the S&P 500 and global markets lower. The Federal Reserve next meets Oct. 27-28, with traders anticipating a “hold”—meaning, no increase to interest rates, which generally bodes well for risk assets like crypto.
Despite the heavy ETF outflows, prices barely budged. Bitcoin traded near $81,460 on Friday, flat over 24 hours and down 0.4% on the week. Ethereum dipped 0.2% to about $2,400, and Solana slipped 0.3% to roughly $104. The 30-day declines are steeper: Bitcoin is down 4.8%, Ethereum 11.4%, and Solana 10.4%.
Total crypto market cap held at about $2.85 trillion, while trading volume fell 20% to $67.1 billion. Bitcoin has settled into a wait-and-see mode, analysts told Decrypt, and that may not be a bad thing for the market.
Traders on Myriad, a prediction market developed by Decrypt’s parent company Dastan, have trimmed their bets on an October breakout.
They now give Bitcoin a 17% chance of topping $87,500 before the month ends, down from 20% a day earlier, and 9% odds of reaching $90,000. They put the odds of a slide to $77,500 at 32%. Sentiment in Myriad’s open-ended markets is more upbeat. Users give Ethereum a 61.3% chance of reaching $3,000 before $1,500, and Solana a 54.9% chance of hitting $160 before $40.

articles.title: Malaysia, Thailand Join Singapore’s BLOOM Digital Money Initiative
articles.text:
Malaysia, Thailand join Singapore’s cross-border stablecoin push
BLOOM seeks to cut costs by helping financial institutions coordinate cross-border use of stablecoins and tokenized deposits.
Bank Negara Malaysia and the Bank of Thailand joined Singapore’s BLOOM initiative on Friday as policymaker members.
BLOOM, short for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency, is a public-private initiative that intends to help financial institutions use stablecoins and tokenized deposits for cross-border payments.
According to the Monetary Authority of Singapore, BLOOM aims to cut costs and help institutions bring services to market faster by reducing the need for institutions to set up arrangements with each counterparty or market.
MAS launched BLOOM in October 2025, building on Project Orchid, which began in 2021 to explore uses for a digital Singapore dollar. BLOOM’s work also covers corporate cash management, trade finance and payments executed by AI agents within predefined limits.
BLOOM’s participants include Airwallex, Mastercard, Ripple, Visa and the World Bank Group.
Bank Negara Malaysia separately announced in February that three initiatives would test ringgit stablecoins and tokenized deposits for domestic and cross-border wholesale payments in 2026.
Related: Ripple joins Singapore sandbox to test RLUSD in trade finance

Andreessen Horowitz is renaming its crypto fund “a16z Frontier” and widening the mandate to cover AI, autonomous machines and biology. Chris Dixon, who has run the crypto team since 2018, leads the new fund alongside Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet.

Dixon’s argument is that blockchains have faded into the background of products shipped by Wall Street and fintech firms—so companies should be judged by what they do, not by the plumbing underneath. Which, if you’ve been reading this newsletter for the past month, is hard to argue with. JPMorgan put deposit tokens on Ethereum. Mastercard built agent payments on Base with Coinbase wallets. Dixon points to Oculus, Skydio and Zipline as the model: long-horizon bets that looked silly before they didn’t. In 2022, with the market down two-thirds from its peak, he said he judges the sector by developer and entrepreneur activity rather than price. He’s also explicit that crypto has a job in the new mandate: letting AI agents pay each other.
Still, the timing is the timing. This lands with bitcoin down on the year, ETFs bleeding through October, and capital inside every multi-strategy firm competing against an AI trade that has sucked up everything. articles.title: Ethereum Delays Glamsterdam Upgrade After Security Researchers Flag Risks
articles.text:
Ethereum delays Glamsterdam Hoodi testnet launch over security risks
ChainSecurity said it identified 13 real-world examples of smart contracts potentially affected by Glamsterdam’s gas changes and is coordinating responsible disclosure with affected projects.
Ethereum developers have postponed the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet after researchers identified gas-related security risks that could affect how existing smart contracts handle failed transactions.
The Ethereum Foundation (EF) said that the upgrade, originally scheduled for Oct. 26, would be delayed to allow developers to investigate how some proposals interact with smart contracts deployed on Ethereum.
On Oct. 13, Blockchain security firm ChainSecurity warned that two proposals included in Glamsterdam, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, could weaken safeguards against a type of attack called insufficient gas griefing.
The postponement raises uncertainty over Glamsterdam’s mainnet timeline. Ethereum developers had been considering early December, with plans to finalize a schedule following successful Hoodi testing.
Gas changes could undermine existing smart contract safeguards
In its analysis, ChainSecurity said that under the new rules, gas could be returned to a contract after an operation fails, allowing it to continue running when it previously would have stopped. The researchers said the changes could interfere with existing security checks that rely on how much gas remains available during a transaction.
In attacks known as insufficient gas griefing, a malicious caller deliberately provides too little gas for a legitimate smart contract operation to succeed. ChainSecurity warned that Glamsterdam’s proposed changes could undermine safeguards against such attacks, potentially allowing contracts to permanently record failed operations.
For example, an affected contract could remove a user’s claim or disable the option to retry it, leaving the user unable to complete an otherwise valid operation.
ChainSecurity said Glamsterdam would not make all gas-related security checks unreliable. Some safeguards could still work, but developers would need to review them to ensure they account for the upgrade’s new gas rules.
Related: Ethereum Foundation warns some tools may break with Glamsterdam upgrade
The findings prompted concern among Ethereum contributors. In an Oct. 21 comment on GitHub, pseudonymous security researcher pcaversaccio described the risks as “serious” and called for a reassessment of the hard fork.
On Friday, ChainSecurity said it had identified “13 real-world examples” and was coordinating responsible disclosure with affected projects. The security firm did not disclose details of the 13 real-world examples or identify the affected projects. However, the company said developers should check their contracts as soon as possible.
The findings follow an earlier Ethereum Foundation warning that Glamsterdam’s gas model could break wallets, indexers, and gas estimators that rely on fixed assumptions. The upgrade was previously activated on Sepolia on Oct. 6, ahead of its now-postponed Hoodi deployment.

articles.title: New OCC stablecoin rule resets redemptions, and banks face big shifts
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The OCC removed the proposed automatic seven-day extension, leaving stress-related redemption extensions subject to regulator decisions.
- Covered issuers’ ordinary deadline measures payment initiation after qualifying requests, while external bank availability remains separate.
- Revised confidential PS-01 reports would track unpaid tokens and payment initiation, with implementation conditional on OMB approval.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has dropped a proposed automatic seven-day stablecoin redemption extension, while defining timely redemption as the point at which the issuer sends the money.
An issuer can meet its payment deadline before an outside bank makes the proceeds available.
The OCC’s final GENIUS Act rule, issued Oct. 21 and effective Jan. 18, 2027, retains an ordinary ceiling of two business days following a qualifying stablecoin redemption request. The endpoint is fully processed payment initiation, or, if the customer requests it, a credit to an account with the issuer.
The rule applies to issuers within the OCC framework, so it doesn't provide a universal timetable for every stablecoin sale or exchange withdrawal.
How the final rule changes stablecoin redemption
The adopted text removed a provision that would have automatically extended stablecoin redemption to seven calendar days when demand crossed a specified threshold.
Under section 15.12(d) of the OCC rule published in the Oct. 23 Federal Register, an issuer receiving stablecoin redemption requests above 10% of any brand’s outstanding issuance value in a single 24-hour period must notify its OCC supervisory office within 24 hours.
The issuer can ask the OCC for more time, and the regulator can grant or deny the request.
Crossing the threshold starts a supervisory process without automatically resetting the deadline, and the OCC says it expects extensions to be rare. Regulator-controlled limitations remain possible in other circumstances consistent with the law.
Section 15.12(a) also establishes explicit boundaries for the ordinary redemption clock, and the issuer must have received a redemption order.
Where its onboarding procedures are reasonably designed to avoid undue delay, including during stress, the customer must also have completed onboarding and satisfied the other legal conditions needed for redemption.
In explaining the final rule, the OCC says issuers cannot use onboarding deficiencies as a pretext to manufacture extra stablecoin redemption time. They should be ready to handle new customers during stress, including holders who previously relied on an intermediary.
Covered issuers must be able to redeem from retail holders, subject to applicable law, screening and onboarding. Their policies must permit quantities of one token or more.
The completion must fully process and initiate the directed outgoing transfer of monetary value to the customer or the customer’s financial institution. Alternatively, it can credit the customer’s account with the issuer if the customer requests that route. Merely placing a payment in a queue does not satisfy that wording.
External bank receipt comes later in the sequence and falls outside that defined endpoint. The practical implication is that the ordinary ceiling protects timely issuer action while bank-credit timing remains a separate part of the holder's cash-out.
Business days exclude Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays, so two business days also cannot be read as 48 elapsed hours.
Existing cash-out routes show why access matters
Current service terms provide an example of access conditions before the OCC rule takes effect, but whether that framework governs a particular issuer depends on its jurisdiction.
Circle’s current non-EEA USDC terms, updated Oct. 15, make direct redemption conditional on a Circle Mint account in good standing.
The Circle Mint service description says the product serves institutions and distributors, excludes individuals, and requires background checks, identity and know-your-customer checks, and sanctions screening. Its stated application-processing range runs from one day to a week or longer, and it covers account opening.
Circle documents wire redemption and SEPA or banking-network transfers limited to participating banks and regions. Instant settlement depends on participating bank programs.
An already onboarded customer with a suitable bank connection can follow a different sequence than a new applicant arranging direct access.
In its Oct. 16 explanation of USDC economics, Circle says qualifying Circle Payments Network and Platform customers can redeem free in near real time. It attributes that capability to cash positioned in advance at bank partners and settlement rails able to move it.
Circle's description ties that speed to funded banking infrastructure for qualifying customers, while the service and bank connection determine the available route.
If a buyer pays a holder before issuer redemption and keeps the acquired tokens, that buyer supplies the immediate dollars and carries the tokens until resale or redemption. This conditional funding mechanism can bring a holder’s exit forward.
PS-01 would separate unpaid stablecoin from late initiation
Subject to Office of Management and Budget approval, the OCC’s revised PS-01 instructions would capture three distinct Schedule A measures:
| Measure | What would be reported | 
|---|---|
| Tokens redeemed but not yet paid | The day-end token count tendered for redemption whose corresponding fiat settlement has not yet been provided to the holder. | 
| Average redemption time | Average hours from confirmation of a redemption request to initiation of a transfer. | 
| Redemptions exceeding two business days | The daily redemption dollar amount for which funds transfers were not initiated within two business days. | 
Read together, they could help supervisors investigate an unpaid redemption backlog separately from slow issuer payment initiation.
PS-01 would generally contain daily observations submitted weekly, with Schedule A remaining daily even under the limited small-issuer reporting option for other schedules. Its data would be confidential, while public information would continue through separate channels.
The final rule retains monthly public reserve-composition reports. Under the OCC’s revised PS-02 instructions, quarterly financial reports would generally become public after submission, acceptance and preparation for release.
The OCC could approve limited confidentiality where an issuer provides a compelling, specific justification of substantial competitive harm.
OCC Bulletin 2026-52 sets intended first report dates of Jan. 25, 2027, for the weekly collection and March 31 for the quarterly collection, subject to Office of Management and Budget approval.
The final rule provides a clearer way to assess a cash-out promise for holders: establish direct access, identify when a qualifying request triggers the obligation, and distinguish payment initiation from bank availability.
The bank route and any provider funding an earlier exit still determine how that timetable translates into money the holder can spend.

articles.title: Interpol Recovers $105M in African Cybercrime Sweep That Shut Illegal Crypto Mines - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Interpol said police from 21 countries arrested 1,462 suspects and recovered more than $105 million in one of Africa's largest cybercrime operations.
- In Angola, investigators shut two illegal crypto mining centers, seizing more than 2,000 mining devices and six illegal power transformation stations.
- In Nigeria, authorities traced more than $2.4 million in suspected investment fraud proceeds, much of it laundered through crypto transactions.
Law enforcement agencies from 21 countries arrested 1,462 suspects, disrupted 10,909 malicious networks and recovered more than $105 million in an Interpol-coordinated crackdown on cybercrime in Africa, the international police organization said on Thursday.
Operation Serengeti III ran from June 29 to August 31, 2026, targeting ransomware, online scams, business email compromise, digital extortion and other cyber-enabled fraud. Authorities identified 65,929 victims, and financial investigations linked the networks to losses of more than $385 million, according to Interpol.
🚨 Operation Serengeti III dismantles thousands of malicious cyber networks
One of Africa’s largest cybercrime enforcement operations has seen agencies from 21 countries:
🔵 Arrest 1,462 suspects
🔵 Disrupt 10,909 malicious networks
🔵 Recover USD 105 million in illicit funds… pic.twitter.com/qtkofnnPEA
— INTERPOL (@INTERPOL_HQ) October 22, 2026
In Angola, investigators dismantled two illegal crypto mining centers, arresting nine people and seizing more than 2,000 mining devices along with six illegal power transformation stations. The seized electrical equipment alone was worth more than $1 million, Interpol said.
In Nigeria, a suspect was arrested over an international investment fraud scheme promoted through messaging apps. Investigators traced more than $2.4 million in suspected criminal proceeds, much of which was laundered through crypto transactions.
Ugandan authorities dismantled two transnational fraud rings and arrested 365 foreign nationals linked to online investment and pension scams aimed at victims in Asia. The rings ran a rotating call-center operation using scripts, fake trading platforms and fraudulent websites to persuade pensioners to invest in opportunities that did not exist.
Other arrests included a Nigerian suspect accused of running a phishing and business email compromise operation that collected around 2.1 million email addresses, and 30 suspects linked to a cybercrime operation in the Republic of Congo.
"Cybercrime networks operate without regard for borders, exploiting technology to target victims on an unprecedented scale," said Neal Jetton, Interpol's director of cybercrime.
Private-sector partners including Group-IB, Kaspersky, blockchain analytics firm Uppsala Security and Meta supported the operation. Several investigations remain active as authorities try to identify more suspects and trace illicit proceeds, Interpol said.
Crypto crime in Africa
The operation follows Operation Catalyst, a joint Interpol and Afripol crackdown on terrorist financing and cybercrime in which authorities arrested 83 people across six African countries in 2025. That operation flagged $260 million in illicit crypto and fiat, of which $600,000 had been seized, and identified several high-value crypto wallets that Interpol said were "potentially linked" to terrorist financing.
An Interpol expert told Decrypt at the time that criminals were "increasingly" using crypto in Africa, but that it was not yet the main way most cybercrime proceeds were paid or settled.

articles.title: Aave changes USDT borrowing rules and loan costs suddenly jump
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Aave implemented a lower 92% USDT rate threshold on Oct. 21, bringing steeper borrowing costs forward.
- At identical hypothetical 94% utilization, the new curve gives 7% borrowing APR against 4.5% under the published prior curve.
- The modeled 57.8 million USDT buffer increment creates no cash.
Aave has lowered the utilization threshold at which borrowing rates for Tether’s USDT rise sharply on its Ethereum Core market, making loans more expensive sooner as pool liquidity tightens.
Using the supply balance in an Oct. 20 recommendation by DeFi risk service provider LlamaRisk, the shift corresponds to roughly 57.8 million USDT more modeled unborrowed liquidity at the threshold.
The change was executed on Oct. 21 in Ethereum block 26,241,799. The threshold fell from 94% utilization, the share of borrowed pool liquidity, to 92%. Borrowers can still go beyond that point, but the rate climbs more sharply once they do.
The trade-off for lenders is earlier pressure on borrowers to preserve withdrawal headroom. The intended cushion remains available to be borrowed or withdrawn.
The price of earlier withdrawal headroom
Aave’s two-slope model increases borrowing rates gradually up to an optimal utilization point, often called the kink, then more sharply between that point and full utilization. Lowering the kink moves the more expensive part of the curve earlier.
The deployed USDT parameters at the Oct. 23 block were a 92% optimal usage ratio, a zero base rate, a 4.5% first slope, and a 10% second slope. Those settings leave the rate at the kink at 4.5% APR and the rate at 100% utilization at 14.5%.
Comparing the curves at the same utilization reveals the cost difference. At a hypothetical 94% utilization, the published prior curve is exactly at its kink and charges 4.5% APR. Under the implemented curve, that same utilization is 2% into the eight-point range above the new kink.
The calculation is 4.5% plus 10% points multiplied by two-eighths, giving 7% APR. That is a conditional comparison at identical utilization, separate from the observed 4.23% borrowing APR on Oct. 23.
For a constant 1 million USDT loan, a 2.5% gap would amount to 25,000 USDT of additional simple annual interest if both modeled rates and the principal stayed unchanged for a full year.
The 92% threshold does not ban borrowing above that level, and the curve’s 14.5% endpoint does not establish that lenders will always have cash available.
LlamaRisk reported 2,892.2 million USDT supplied in its Oct. 20 recommendation. Keeping that supply fixed, a reserve operating at 94% utilization would leave 6% unborrowed, while 92% utilization would leave 8% unborrowed.
Those percentages correspond to 173.53 million and 231.38 million USDT, respectively, for a difference of 57.84 million USDT. It is the difference between two modeled operating points on the same supplied balance.
LlamaRisk separately reported about 417 million USDT already idle in its recommendation, when utilization was below either kink.
The rate update changes the terms under which borrowers consume liquidity. For the larger modeled buffer to emerge as actual cash, users must respond through the pool’s cash flows.
As funding becomes more expensive, a borrower may repay, while a supplier may find a higher interest rate attractive enough to add USDT. Borrowers can also accept the cost, and suppliers can withdraw before an inflow arrives. The curve encourages a response without fixing its size or timing.
Cash still controls a supplier’s exit
At block 26,254,517, timestamped Oct. 23 at 09:45:59 UTC, the reserve had about 2.9 billion USDT in outstanding supplier claims and 2.5 billion USDT in variable debt. Physical USDT held at the aToken contract stood at approximately 391.4 million.
The table separates supplier claims from the reserve’s physical token balance and its virtual accounting balance.
| Measure | USDT at the October 23 snapshot | 
|---|---|
| aEthUSDT total supply | 2,888,069,680.855421 | 
| Variable debt | 2,496,678,159.334926 | 
| Physical underlying cash | 391,396,023.726517 | 
| Virtual underlying accounting balance | 391,394,502.001385 | 
The virtual balance is a separate accounting input used by the interest-rate strategy. Dividing debt by debt plus that balance puts borrow utilization at about 86.45%, below the new 92% threshold. Physical cash measures the tokens held, while the virtual figure enters the pricing calculation.
The same snapshot recorded a variable borrowing APR of about 4.23% and a supplier liquidity APR of 3.29%.
The Oct. 23 cash balance is a later observation, separate from LlamaRisk’s Oct. 20 model. It does not establish a causal effect of the rate change on deposits, repayments, or withdrawals.
The strategy calculates the supplier liquidity rate from the borrowing rate and the share of liquidity being used, after the reserve factor. At the Oct. 23 snapshot, that reserve factor was 10%, allocating part of borrowing interest to the protocol treasury.
A higher borrowing rate can consequently improve the return offered to suppliers, helping compensate them for leaving funds in the pool. However, accrued interest is distinct from underlying tokens becoming available for immediate withdrawal. Cash must still be present when a supplier exits.
Aave’s withdrawal guidance makes that condition explicit: suppliers can withdraw only against liquidity that is available and unborrowed. A supplier using deposits as collateral may also need to repay borrowings or add collateral to preserve the position's health before withdrawing.
Lending-pool cash serves a different purpose than the GHO conversion inventory and Umbrella deficit backstops.
The operational test is how deposits and repayments compare with borrowing and withdrawals as utilization changes.
Moving the kink to 92% makes the price respond earlier to tighter liquidity. Whether suppliers can exit immediately still depends on the cash left in the pool and, where their deposits secure borrowing, on the health of their own positions.
Tether is +0.01% over the past 24 hours and currently sits at rank #3 by market cap.

articles.title: Ethereum Delays Glamsterdam Testnet Fork Over Gas Security Flaws - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Ethereum developers have called off Monday's Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi testnet after auditor ChainSecurity flagged security issues with its gas changes.
- The firm said the changes could let some smart contracts permanently record failed operations that their code was designed to keep retryable.
- ChainSecurity said it has found 13 real-world examples and is contacting affected projects, as the Ethereum Foundation assesses how many contracts are exposed.
Ethereum developers have postponed the planned activation of the network's Glamsterdam upgrade on its Hoodi test network after security firm ChainSecurity found problems with how the upgrade changes gas, the auditor said on Thursday.
"It has just been decided to delay the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet because of security impacts we identified," ChainSecurity wrote, adding that it had "already found 13 real-world examples" and was in responsible disclosure with the affected projects.
⚠️ It has just been decided to delay the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet because of security impacts we identified in this blog post: https://t.co/UCpy6Jp5Pa
We already found 13 real-world examples and are in responsible disclosure with the affected projects.
Please…
— ChainSecurity (@chain_security) October 22, 2026
The upgrade had been due to go live on Hoodi on Monday. Node operators should revert to an older software release without the upgrade scheduled, or wait for their execution client team to release a new version that cancels it, Ethereum researcher Christine Kim said. Preston Van Loon, a developer on the Prysm consensus client, said a Prysm release removing the upgrade from Hoodi's schedule would follow the same day.
Gas is the fee paid for computing work on Ethereum. Glamsterdam changes how the network charges for creating and accessing stored data through two proposals, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, and introduces a separate pool of gas for creating new state.
According to ChainSecurity's analysis, those changes break assumptions that many contracts rely on when an external call fails. Some contracts use gas checks, or rely on the call running out of gas, to stop an attacker from deliberately supplying too little gas so that a valid operation fails and is recorded as a permanent failure, a tactic known as insufficient gas griefing.
Under Glamsterdam, gas can be refilled or returned to a contract after a failed call, and repricing can change how much gas a call needs, the firm found. "Even with unchanged contract code, a failure path that previously reverted can now complete," it wrote. ChainSecurity urged projects to check their contracts, saying the Ethereum Foundation is working out how many are affected.
Glamsterdam's road to mainnet
Glamsterdam has already gone live on Sepolia, another Ethereum test network, which activated the upgrade on October 6 and began producing blocks with a gas limit of nearly 200 million, more than three times mainnet's 60 million. The upgrade also adds block-level access lists, which let computers check transactions in parallel, and moves the auction that decides who assembles each block into Ethereum's own rules.
Developers had aimed to ship Glamsterdam on mainnet by the end of 2026, ahead of Hegotá, the next upgrade, which is expected in 2027 and could add native privacy features. No new date has been set for the Hoodi fork.

articles.title: Bitcoin Core Changes Security Policy Amid AI Risks
articles.text:
Bitcoin Core changes security policy as AI makes bugs easier to find
Bitcoin Core says keeping certain vulnerabilities secret no longer offers much protection in the wake of AI-assisted bug hunting.
Bitcoin Core is changing how it handles security vulnerabilities, explaining that large language models have made certain software flaws significantly easier to discover.
In an email to the Bitcoin Development Mailing List on Thursday, Bitcoin Core developer Antoine Poinsot said that in the past, vulnerabilities were generally kept under lengthy disclosure embargoes to give users time to upgrade before details became public.
Maintaining that secrecy generally meant fixes could not be backported to older software versions, leaving users waiting until the next major release. However, Poinsot said LLMs have made some flaws so easy to rediscover that delaying fixes offers little protection.
“The embargo period achieves little but it delays the availability of a fixed release,” said Poinsot. “We are therefore updating our policy disclosure to accommodate those.”
The change comes as AI-assisted security research puts pressure on developers across Bitcoin’s software ecosystem.
Under the updated policy, vulnerabilities deemed “easily discoverable” will receive fixes as soon as possible across all maintained major versions, with security advisories published alongside the updates.
“This classification applies to vulnerabilities that can be discovered with minimal effort, such as through a simple LLM prompt,” it said.
Related: PHP flaw draws millions of exploit attempts, Cloudflare CEO warns
Other vulnerabilities will continue to follow disclosure schedules based on severity, ranging from critical flaws that threaten Bitcoin’s fundamental security to lower-risk bugs with limited impact on individual nodes.
Bitcoin Core said low-severity vulnerabilities will be disclosed two weeks after the release of a major version containing the fix, while medium and high vulnerabilities will be disclosed two weeks after the last affected release hits its “End of Life,” typically a year after the fix is released in the new major version.
“Critical bugs are not considered in the standard policy, as they would most likely require an ad-hoc procedure,” it said.
“I’ve disagreed with Antoine’s approach to security in the past, but this is a good update,” said Luke de Wolf, host of the Bitcoin Infinity Show and author of “Defending Bitcoin.”
In August, the volunteer Bitcoin Red Team reported nearly 5,000 potential issues across 390 projects, although only around a fifth of its findings had been reproduced at that point.
That month, Core Lightning developers urged operators to upgrade or take their nodes offline after receiving multiple AI-generated vulnerability reports, while withholding technical details for two weeks.
