articles.title: Lần đầu tiên NASA chụp được 3 vật thể từ “thế giới bên kia”
articles.text:
Chúng là 3 vật thể "trong truyền thuyết" sáng gấp 10 tỉ lần Mặt trời, làm bằng loại vật chất đối lập và có thể đã "tuyệt chủng" hàng tỉ năm trước khi gửi 4 bóng ma đến người Trái đất.
Từ lâu các nhà khoa học đã đưa ra 2 giả thuyết về thế hệ sao đầu tiên của vũ trụ mà chưa phương tiện nào quan sát nổi:
Một trong hai loại sao đó có thể vừa bị "quái vật" James Webb bắt được, theo Sci-News.
Chân dung cận cảnh một sao tối - (Ảnh: SCI-NEWS).
James Webb là siêu kính viễn vọng do NASA phát triển và điều hành chính, với sự hỗ trợ của ESA và CSA (các cơ quan vũ trụ của châu Âu và Canada), với tầm nhìn xa hàng tỉ năm ánh sáng.
Ánh sáng từ các vật thể đó cũng mất hàng tỉ năm để đến được "mắt thần" của kính viễn vọng, do đó công cụ này cũng cung cấp cái nhìn xuyên thời gian vào vũ trụ cổ đại.
Lần này, nó đã khám phá ra 3 vật thể kỳ lạ ở vùng không - thời gian chỉ 320-400 triệu năm sau vụ nổ Big Bang khai sinh vũ trụ, tức cách chúng ta trên dưới 13,4 tỉ năm ánh sáng.
Đó là JADES-GS-z13-0, JADES-GS-z12-0 và JADES-GS-z11-0, được phát hiện từ sứ mệnh Khảo sát thiên hà sâu nâng cao của James Webb (JADES).
JADES-GS-z13-0, JADES-GS-z12-0 và JADES-GS-z11-0, trong đó JADES-GS-z11-0 bị nhân bản làm hai do hiệu ứng thấu kính hấp dẫn tạo ra bởi các thiên hà gần hơn, đủ sức uốn cong không - thời gian - (Ảnh: NASA/ESA/CSA)
Tiến sĩ Kinda Freese, nhà vật lý thiên văn từ Trường Đại học Texas ở Austin (Mỹ), một trong những thành viên chủ chốt của nhóm JADES cho biết ban đầu chúng được xác định là các thiên hà sơ khai.
Tuy nhiên quá trình phân tích quang phổ chuyên sâu cho thấy không phải như vậy. Chúng chính là 3 sao tối "trong truyền thuyết".
Sao tối bị lầm lẫn là thiên hà bởi chúng có độ sáng gấp 10 tỉ lần Mặt trời, sáng như cả một thiên hà làm bằng sao bình thường. Gọi là sao tối vì chúng làm bằng vật chất tối - vô hình, nhưng có thể chiếm từ 25%-80% vũ trụ, theo một số nghiên cứu.
Các hạt vật chất tối không phát sáng, nhưng khi chúng va chạm bên trong ngôi sao và tự hủy, nhiệt năng sẽ truyền nhiệt vào các đám mây hydro đang co lại, tạo thành ánh sáng chói chang hơn hẳn các ngôi sao sáng bằng phản ứng nhiệt hạch.
Về lý thuyết, sao tối là loại "quái vật" đủ mạnh để biến thành lỗ đen siêu khối - còn gọi là lỗ đen quái vật - sau khi chết.
Vì vậy, các "bóng ma" từ quá khứ này sẽ giúp giải quyết thắc mắc bấy lâu về việc vì sao vũ trụ sơ khai có quá nhiều lỗ đen lớn khủng khiếp và quá nhiều thứ trông như thiên hà lớn.
Trước đây người ta cho rằng đó là điều vô lý bởi thiên hà lớn với lỗ đen siêu khối làm trung tâm như Ngân Hà của chúng ta sẽ cần rất nhiều thời gian để sáp nhập từ các thiên hà nhỏ với nhau.

articles.title: NASA reveals 16 stunning galaxies hiding cosmic chaos
articles.text:
NASA reveals 16 stunning galaxies hiding cosmic chaos
- Date:
- October 20, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA's stunning new gallery of 16 galaxies reveals colossal black hole jets, explosive star formation, and spectacular cosmic collisions through the combined power of Chandra, James Webb, Hubble, and other telescopes. These extraordinary images expose the hidden forces shaping galaxies across the universe and offer clues about the Milky Way's own past and future.
- Share:
Some galaxies glow with sweeping spiral arms, while others are shaped by violent collisions, powerful black holes, and explosive bursts of star formation. A newly released collection of 16 images from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory and other telescopes reveals the extraordinary diversity of these cosmic structures.
Like precious gemstones, galaxies come in many shapes and sizes, each with characteristics that tell a story about its history. Astronomers generally classify them into three major groups. Spiral galaxies, including our Milky Way, have winding arms extending from their centers. Elliptical galaxies typically contain older stars and are often thought to form through galactic mergers. Irregular galaxies have less orderly structures and can display a wide variety of cosmic activity.
Much as gemstones preserve clues about the geological processes that shaped Earth over billions of years, galaxies hold evidence of the forces that have shaped the universe. Studying these distant systems helps astronomers piece together the Milky Way's history and better understand what may await our galaxy in the distant future.
NASA Combines Chandra, Webb, and Hubble to Reveal Galactic Secrets
The new gallery features 16 images that bring together observations from some of the world's most powerful telescopes. Each includes X-ray measurements gathered by Chandra during its decades of operation in space.
These observations are combined with data from NASA's James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes, IXPE (Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, NuSTAR (Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array), and additional observatories operating on Earth and in space.
X-ray observations are especially valuable because they reveal extreme activity that other types of light can miss. Chandra can detect enormous clouds of gas heated to millions of degrees by powerful winds from massive stars, material expelled by supermassive black holes, and debris from stellar explosions. These processes also help spread chemical elements through space, including elements that ultimately become part of planets, the air we breathe, and our own bodies.
By combining X-rays with observations at other wavelengths, astronomers can see more of what is happening inside galaxies. The resulting images reveal how these vast systems form stars, interact with their surroundings, and change over billions of years.
Spiral Galaxies Reveal Explosive Star Formation
Several images highlight the remarkable activity taking place inside spiral galaxies. Messier 33 and NGC 3938 are viewed almost directly from above, allowing astronomers to examine their sweeping arms and identify regions containing energetic pairs of stars and the aftermath of stellar explosions.
Other galaxies reveal how their internal structures can help drive the birth of new stars. NGC 1672 and NGC 1385 are barred spiral galaxies, meaning they contain elongated central structures made of stars, gas, and dust. These bars can channel material toward the inner regions, providing fuel for intense episodes of star formation.
NGC 4725 demonstrates another way galaxies can produce new stars. Its observations reveal how an earlier encounter with another galaxy can disturb gas and stimulate star formation.
The collection also includes dramatic side views of NGC 4631 (the Whale Galaxy) and Messier 82 (the Cigar Galaxy). These galaxies feature enormous halos and powerful winds of gas heated to millions of degrees. Driven by intense stellar explosions, these outflows can carry material thousands of light-years into space, spreading important chemical elements into the regions between galaxies.
Supermassive Black Holes Blast Energy Across Galaxies
Some of the most dramatic features in the gallery come from the enormous black holes lurking at the centers of galaxies.
When these black holes actively consume surrounding material, their central regions become extremely energetic. Known as active galactic nuclei, these bright and powerful galactic cores can launch jets of particles and enormous outbursts that influence conditions across their host galaxies.
Centaurus A provides a striking example. Observations from Chandra and IXPE reveal a powerful stream of high-energy particles shooting tens of thousands of light-years into space from the galaxy's central region.
In Messier 106, jets launched from the central supermassive black hole interact with and heat surrounding gas. This activity produces unusual spiral structures that differ from the familiar arms normally associated with spiral galaxies.
The famous Sombrero Galaxy (Messier 104) offers another remarkable view. A supermassive black hole sits within its immense central concentration of stars, while Chandra's X-ray observations reveal a widespread halo of gas heated to millions of degrees and the hot remains of stars. These features surround the galaxy's prominent bands of dust, providing a deeper look at the energetic environment hidden within its elegant appearance.
Violent Galaxy Collisions Offer a Glimpse of the Milky Way's Future
Not every galaxy evolves peacefully. Some undergo enormous transformations as gravity pulls neighboring galaxies together, distorts their structures, or strips away the gas needed to create new stars.
Arp 143 captures the aftermath of a particularly dramatic encounter. A direct galactic collision produced an expanding ring, similar to ripples spreading outward after an impact. The disturbance also triggered waves of new star formation.
Other images show the chaotic consequences of galaxies merging. NGC 3256 and II Zw 096, the latter containing a powerful burst of star formation hidden behind thick dust, provide examples of the violent interactions that were especially common in the early universe.
These collisions also offer clues about the Milky Way's possible future. Our galaxy is expected to merge with the neighboring Andromeda galaxy billions of years from now, and observing other galactic mergers helps scientists understand how such an encounter could unfold.
The gallery includes several other unusual systems. NGC 1569 serves as a nearby example for investigating the intense episodes of star formation that occurred in young galaxies billions of years ago. NGC 660 displays a rare "polar ring" structure, with a ring of stars orbiting around the galaxy's poles rather than following its main plane.
Messier 90 illustrates a different kind of galactic transformation. As it travels through the Virgo Cluster, the galaxy is losing the gas it needs to form new stars. Its movement through the cluster strips away this material, potentially changing how the galaxy evolves.
Together, these 16 cosmic portraits show that galaxies are far from static collections of stars. They are constantly influenced by gravity, stellar explosions, black holes, and interactions with neighboring systems. By revealing these processes in remarkable detail, NASA's Chandra and its partner telescopes are helping astronomers understand the forces that shape galaxies, including our own.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
articles.text:
Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
- Date:
- October 20, 2026
- Source:
- Van Andel Research Institute
- Summary:
- A surprising clinical trial suggests that taking vitamin C daily could improve survival in people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers. Patients receiving the supplement had fewer adverse events and showed a promising survival advantage, raising hopes that a common vitamin could help protect against leukemia-related complications.
- Share:
Vitamin C plays an important role in keeping the immune system healthy, helping wounds heal, and protecting cells from damage. However, people with precancerous blood disorders and blood cancers often have persistently low vitamin C levels. Researchers have been investigating whether correcting this deficiency could improve their health and treatment outcomes.
New findings from the phase 2 EVITA clinical trial suggest that vitamin C supplementation may offer important benefits for people with precancerous blood conditions and early-stage blood cancers. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted by the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team.
The results, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER, revealed that patients who received 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C every day for one year experienced fewer adverse events during the study and its follow-up period. The supplement also changed the levels of certain immune signaling molecules, known as cytokines, in ways associated with more favorable outcomes. These changes suggest that vitamin C could influence inflammation-related processes involved in the growth and progression of abnormal blood cells.
Although vitamin C did not significantly affect the rate at which abnormal blood cells expanded, the researchers identified an encouraging result. An exploratory analysis showed that participants who received vitamin C were significantly more likely to be alive after approximately three years of follow-up than those who took a placebo. Scientists emphasize that this potential survival benefit must be verified in a larger phase 3 clinical trial.
Vitamin C Shows Promise for Patients at Risk of Leukemia
"We are tremendously excited and cautiously optimistic that our results could one day translate into a simple way to improve care and outcomes for people with pre-leukemia disorders," said Peter A. Jones, Ph.D., D.Sc. (hon), a distinguished professor at Van Andel Institute. Jones is also a co-corresponding author of the research and co-leader of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.
"Our approach reflects a growing emphasis on cancer interception -- intervening before cancer becomes established. We are working to build on the trial findings by exploring how exactly vitamin C interacts with pre-cancerous cells, including the idea that it may help restore normal epigenetic function in blood cells at risk of becoming leukemia."
The international research effort was led by Kirsten Grønbæk, M.D., Ph.D., a leading hematologist, professor at the University of Copenhagen, and member of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.
"These exciting preliminary findings lay the groundwork for a larger clinical trial to explore vitamin C as a possible way to improve patient outcomes," said Grønbæk. "It is too early to make definitive recommendations based on our results, but we are hopeful that a more expansive study will provide further insights."
First Clinical Trial Tests Daily Vitamin C for Precancerous Blood Disorders
The study enrolled 109 patients with either clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Both conditions can develop into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive form of blood cancer that is often difficult to treat. The likelihood of developing CCUS and related blood disorders rises with age, making these conditions particularly common among older adults.
Currently, no approved treatment can prevent CCUS from progressing to leukemia. Although stem cell transplantation is an option for treating MDS, many patients cannot undergo the procedure because of age or other medical conditions. None of the people enrolled in the trial were receiving cancer treatment when the study took place.
To determine whether vitamin C might offer benefits, researchers randomly divided participants into two groups. One received 1,000 mg of vitamin C by mouth each day for 12 months. The other received a placebo designed to be indistinguishable from the supplement in appearance, taste, and smell, but containing no vitamin C.
Neither the participants nor the clinical staff knew who was receiving vitamin C until the study concluded. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled approach is considered the gold standard in clinical research because it reduces potential bias and allows investigators to assess treatment effects more objectively.
The research was carried out at four hospitals: Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev, Aalborg University Hospital, and Keck Hospital of the University of Southern California.
What makes EVITA particularly notable is that it was the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to investigate oral vitamin C in patients with conditions that can precede leukemia or with lower-risk myeloid cancers. Earlier studies had primarily examined vitamin C administered intravenously and had focused on solid tumors rather than precancerous blood disorders or early-stage blood malignancies.
EVITA instead evaluated a daily oral dose comparable to that available in many over-the-counter vitamin C supplements.
More Than Half of Patients Had Low Vitamin C Levels
Blood samples collected throughout the study allowed researchers to track participants' vitamin C concentrations and determine whether supplementation corrected deficiencies.
At the beginning of the trial, more than half of the participants had insufficient vitamin C levels. Among those assigned to the supplementation group, blood concentrations returned to normal after they began taking vitamin C.
For patients living with conditions that could eventually develop into leukemia, the possibility of an accessible intervention is especially important. In many cases, physicians have little choice but to monitor the disease and watch for signs that it is progressing.
"The standard approach for patients with pre-cancer blood disorders is to monitor their blood cell counts over time. This is, understandably, very frustrating -- no one wants to hear that they have a condition that increases leukemia risk but there's nothing that can be done other than watch and wait," said Casey O'Connell, M.D., FACP, the Lawrence and Jane Kelly Chair in Hematology at the University of Southern California and lead clinician at USC's trial location.
"The EVITA trial took on this challenge by exploring vitamin C's potential to address the underlying factors that drive leukemia development."
How Vitamin C Could Influence Cancer Development
Scientists have investigated whether vitamin C could play a useful role in cancer treatment for more than seven decades. For much of that time, the evidence remained uncertain because studies produced inconsistent findings and employed different experimental methods.
During the past decade, however, improved research technologies have revealed that vitamin C has important functions beyond its familiar roles in nutrition and immunity. In particular, scientists have uncovered its involvement in controlling gene activity and guiding normal cell development.
One of the most important discoveries concerns TET2, an enzyme that helps prevent cancerous growth by controlling whether particular genes are switched "on" or "off." Vitamin C supports the activity of this enzyme, which helps maintain normal patterns of gene regulation.
Mutations affecting TET2 are frequently found in leukemia and related blood disorders. When the enzyme's normal function is disrupted, abnormal cells can gain an opportunity to multiply and potentially develop into cancer.
Experiments using cancer models have provided additional evidence of vitamin C's possible protective effects. These studies found that supplementation could interfere with cellular changes associated with cancer and slow the progression of leukemia. Notably, the strongest effects appeared when vitamin C was introduced before cancer had become established.
This research helped inspire the idea of using vitamin C as a form of early intervention, potentially targeting the biological changes that precede the development of leukemia.
Building Toward Larger Clinical Trials
Before launching EVITA, the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team conducted a pilot clinical study in 2016 to determine whether taking vitamin C orally could meaningfully raise its concentration in the blood.
The initial findings suggested that oral supplementation was a practical approach. Encouraged by those results, the researchers launched the phase 2 EVITA trial in 2017.
"This early work was critical because it offered a foundation from which to develop the present trial," said Stine Ulrik Mikkelsen, M.D., Ph.D., the study's first author and a clinician researcher in Grønbæk's laboratory.
"Vitamin C is important because it is involved in a range of biological functions, including the activity of enzymes that regulate normal cell function."
Researchers are continuing to examine the EVITA data to better understand the biological processes that might explain why patients receiving vitamin C showed improved survival.
Although the findings offer a promising direction for future research, additional clinical studies will be essential to determine whether vitamin C supplementation can reliably improve outcomes for people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers.
Other authors include Ali Al-Mousawi, M.D., Amalie Bach Puglisi, M.D., Anders Pommer Vallentin, M.D., Astrid Østergaard Mortensen, Heidi Naomi Ottesen, Linn Gillberg, M.Sc., Ph.D., Morten Tulstrup, M.D., M.Sc., Ph.D., Jakob Werner Hansen, M.D., Ph.D., and Mette Klarskov Andersen, M.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen and Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet; Zachary Madaj, M.S., Toshinori Hinoue, Ph.D., Stacey L. Thomas, Ph.D., Christine N. Isaguirre, Ryan D. Sheldon, Ph.D., Marie Adams, M.S., Ryan Burgos, and Peter W. Laird, Ph.D., of Van Andel Institute; Jakob Schmidt Jespersen, M.Sc., Ph.D., Niels Richard Hansen, M.Sc., and Jens Lykkesfeldt, Ph.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen; Stephen Baylin, M.D., of Johns Hopkins University and Van Andel Institute; Bo Kok Mortensen, M.D., Ph.D., of Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet and Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev; and Marianne Tang Severinsen, M.D., Ph.D., of Aalborg University Hospital.
Funding for the study was provided by Van Andel Institute through the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team, the Danish Cancer Society, and Greater Copenhagen Health Science Partners.

articles.title: Scientists reach the ultimate quantum limit on a surface
articles.text:
Scientists reach the ultimate quantum limit on a surface
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light
- Summary:
- Scientists have achieved a quantum breakthrough by creating an ultra-clean surface where individual molecules can maintain their delicate quantum properties at the fundamental limit. The discovery could unlock unprecedented control over molecules and help drive the next generation of quantum technologies.
- Share:
Scientists at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light (MPL) have achieved a breakthrough in quantum physics, developing a way to study individual molecules on a surface with extraordinary precision. For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that molecules attached to a surface can reach the ultimate quantum limit of optical coherence, overcoming a major obstacle that has long restricted molecular quantum research.
The findings, published in Science, could open new possibilities for investigating how molecules interact with surfaces and developing advanced quantum technologies.
Why Surfaces Have Been a Major Obstacle in Quantum Physics
Many emerging quantum technologies depend on extremely small objects, such as individual atoms and molecules, that interact with light. Known as quantum emitters, these tiny systems can produce single particles of light called photons, store quantum information, and help establish quantum connections between distant systems. These capabilities are important for future applications in quantum computing and secure quantum communication.
To study a single quantum emitter, scientists must keep it stable and confined to one location for extended periods. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by trapping atoms or molecules in a vacuum or embedding them inside solid materials.
Placing quantum emitters directly on a surface, however, offers an intriguing advantage. Scientists could potentially manipulate individual molecules by "touching them" with an extremely sharp probe. Techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) already use tips with atomic precision to investigate matter at incredibly small scales.
The difficulty is that surfaces are rarely as clean and stable as quantum experiments require. Contaminants from the surrounding environment can accumulate on them, creating disturbances that interfere with the delicate quantum behavior of nearby atoms and molecules. Until now, researchers had struggled to preserve the quantum optical properties of individual emitters attached to surfaces.
Scientists in MPL's Nano-Optics Division have now found a way around this problem.
A Clever Crystal Cleaning Method Solves the Problem
The research team, led by Prof. Vahid Sandoghdar, director at MPL and head of the "Nano-Optics" Division, developed an unusual cleaning method that takes advantage of a natural property of organic crystals.
At room temperature, the crystal material gradually evaporates through a process known as sublimation, in which a solid transforms directly into a gas without first becoming a liquid.
The researchers placed a small crystal inside a vacuum chamber equipped for extremely low temperatures, called a cryostat. As the crystal's uppermost layers slowly evaporated, they carried away unwanted contaminants, leaving behind a remarkably clean surface.
The team then cooled the crystal to just a few degrees Kelvin above absolute zero, the lowest theoretically possible temperature. This extreme cooling halted further sublimation and helped maintain the pristine surface.
Finally, the scientists used a tiny, specially fabricated oven to evaporate molecules onto the cold crystal, allowing them to settle on the clean surface.
Molecules Reach the Ultimate Quantum Limit
With this exceptionally stable environment in place, the researchers could investigate whether the molecules retained their fragile quantum properties.
Dr. Alexey Shkarin, a researcher in the Nano-Optics Division at MPL, explained: "The quality of quantum emitters can be evaluated by their coherence times, which indicate how long they keep their quantumness."
Coherence time describes how long a quantum system can maintain the properties needed for quantum behavior. The longer this coherence persists, the better the emitter can perform in applications that depend on precise interactions with light.
However, there is a fundamental physical restriction on how long coherence can last. Known as the Fourier limit, this boundary is determined by the time required for a quantum emitter to release its energy into its surroundings.
In an unstable or 'noisy' environment, disturbances can cause coherence to disappear hundreds or even thousands of times faster than this theoretical limit allows.
The scientists discovered that molecules deposited on their exceptionally clean crystal surface consistently reached the Fourier limit. This demonstrated that the surrounding environment was sufficiently quiet and stable to preserve the molecules' quantum coherence for the maximum physically permitted duration.
It is the first time researchers have achieved this fundamental limit with molecules attached to a surface.
New Possibilities for Controlling Individual Molecules
The breakthrough also allowed the team to investigate how a crystal surface influences the molecules resting on it.
Further experiments revealed that interactions with the surface can cause molecules to align in particular directions and alter their energy levels. The researchers also found indications that the surface might influence the molecules' shapes or the ways they vibrate.
These effects could provide valuable clues about how matter behaves at the molecular scale, while also offering new opportunities to control quantum systems.
"Our future work will focus on combining this method with AFM and STM to gain local nanometer control over individual quantum emitters," says Vahid Sandoghdar.
By combining their ultra-clean surface technique with powerful microscopy methods, the researchers hope to manipulate individual quantum emitters with precision measured in billionths of a meter.
Such capabilities could reveal previously inaccessible details about interactions between molecules and surfaces, while laying the groundwork for engineering new quantum states of matter and advancing future molecular quantum technologies.

articles.title: Christina Applegate misdiagnosis: Why can MS be difficult to diagnose?
articles.text:
Christina Applegate misdiagnosis: Why can MS be difficult to diagnose?
MS advocate Christina Applegate recently announced that her MS diagnosis was incorrect, based on new test results. Why can the disease be difficult to identify?
Actor Christina Applegate was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) over five years ago — but this week, she announced that a recent reevaluation found that she doesn't have the condition after all. In the wake of that revelation, she's been left without a diagnosis, and she said on a podcast that she felt she was "back at square one, where I don't know what's going on with me."
Applegate's case is not totally unique, although MS diagnosis has improved over the years. Studies offer different estimates of how frequently MS is misdiagnosed, with rates ranging from 5% to over 40%, depending on the patient population and clinical setting. There is also some degree of underdiagnosis — cases in which people with MS aren't flagged as having the disease.
So, how difficult is MS to identify, and what does that mean for patients? Live Science spoke with experts about the current state of MS diagnostics and the improvements that may be coming in the future.
"It's also really important that doctors and patients be aware that it's not inappropriate to revisit a diagnosis — to make sure it's right," Dr. Ari Green, chief of the Division of Neuroimmunology and Glial Biology at the University of California, San Francisco, told Live Science.
The importance of early diagnosis
MS is an autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system, meaning the brain and spinal cord. These attacks harm neurons directly and also take aim at myelin — a fatty, insulating substance that coats neurons' outgoing wires and helps them send signals efficiently.
This damage leads to distinctive scarring in nerve tissue and causes a range of symptoms, including vision problems, muscle weakness, tingling sensations, dizziness and bladder control issues. Patients with untreated and advanced MS can lose the ability to walk and stand or, in some cases, develop partial or complete paralysis.
These severe outcomes are becoming rarer as treatments have improved significantly, Green said. Current treatments keep immune attacks at bay and thus prevent further nerve damage.
"It's moved from people ending up with severe, profound disability at 10 or 20 years of disease, and now it's at like 30 or 40 years of disease, they have modest disability," Green told Live Science. The disease most often emerges between age 20 and 40, although it can occur in any age group. Importantly, Green said, "the earlier people initiate treatment who have MS, the better they do over the long term."
For that reason, it's important to reach an MS diagnosis efficiently, so that patients can start that critical treatment, said Dr. Yohance Allette, a neuroimmunologist and researcher at Penn State Health. "You're trying to be as proactive as possible with this."
"A diagnosis of exclusion"
However, there is no single, surefire test that can reliably show that a person has MS. "With MS, it comes down to the keyword 'criteria," Allette said.
MS experts have compiled a list of criteria, which are updated periodically, that reflect how the features of MS show up in lab tests; brain, optic nerve and spinal cord scans; and patients' symptoms. (Green was among the dozens of experts involved in the latest update, which was conducted in 2024 and published in 2025.)
So, what does diagnosis look like for a patient today? The first step is to recognize symptoms that might point to MS.
Those early symptoms — such as issues with balance, vision or bowel control — vary significantly from person to person and may not immediately raise red flags that the patient has a neurological problem, Green said. The way those symptoms emerge can be a clue, though; typically, MS symptoms worsen over the course of a day or a few days and then dissipate, he noted.
Once concerning symptoms are flagged, MRIs of the brain and spinal cord are taken. The scans may reveal evidence of myelin damage, and neurologists note the shape, size and location of those lesions. Damage often appears near blood vessels, since that's where immune cells access the brain, Green noted.
Other conditions — like migraine, uncontrolled diabetes or vascular disease — can also come with some myelin damage, so it's key to look for specific patterns related to MS. Neurologists who specialize in MS are practiced at this task, while doctors in other neurological specialties may not know how to distinguish MS-related myelin damage from that caused by other conditions, Allette and Green both noted.
MRIs of the optic nerves can also show MS-related damage, and these scans are emphasized in the latest diagnostic criteria, Allette noted. Electrophysiologic tests, which assess the function of nerves, are also "super important because they tell you something totally different than just seeing a lesion on MRI," Green said. Further signs of MS can be found via spinal taps, which sample the fluid around the brain and spinal cord that may carry proteins and inflammatory cells related to MS.
In addition to collecting these clues, doctors must rule out diseases that look similar to MS. These include neuromyelitis optica and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) — two other autoimmune conditions that affect the central nervous system. Both these diseases are associated with distinctive, rogue immune proteins, called autoantibodies, that latch onto various parts of the nervous system; those specific antibodies are not seen in MS.
Other conditions — such as the inflammatory disease lupus and neuromuscular disease myasthenia gravis — can sometimes look like MS at first glance, as well. Some of these "MS mimics" can be ruled out with data from spinal taps or antibody tests, while others require a more laborious battery of assessments.
"Ultimately, it's a diagnosis of exclusion," Allette said. "There are things that you can rule out quickly," while others take time to investigate thoroughly.
Conditions like MOGAD and neurosarcoidosis, an inflammatory condition sometimes mistaken for MS, can actually be worsened by MS medications, Green noted. So if a patient's MS flare-ups worsen after they start a treatment, that could hint that something else is the culprit, he said. But because there may be long gaps between flare-ups, doctors may need to track a patient for some time before their worsening becomes apparent.
Gaps to fill?
Given all the tools available, a patient can be reasonably confident in their MS diagnosis, Green said.
"In general, there's a fair amount of diagnostic confidence that comes with MS diagnosis today," he said. However, that confidence is highest when the tools are in the hands of a specialist who is following the most up-to-date criteria, he noted. The test results require interpretation, and that's one place where uncertainty can creep in.
Regarding Applegate's circumstances, "to speak bluntly, I think the case came as a bit of a shock because we always expect that part of society to have quick access [to high-quality medical care]," Allette said. For some patients, the road to accessing specialty MS care can be long, which can result in missteps, and even misdiagnoses, along the way. Applegate went five years with an incorrect diagnosis, but "would that have been seven or eight years for somebody who doesn't have that access?" Allette speculated.
Without knowing the details of Applegate's case, Allette and Green said it would be difficult to speculate on what resulted in her misdiagnosis. (Applegate mentioned that her brain scans had been reassessed with a "new technology," but didn't go into specifics.)
Looking toward the future of MS diagnostics, Green and Allette think emerging proteomic tests hold a lot of promise. Such tests generate a profile of the proteins and smaller fragments, called peptides, in a patient's blood or cerebrospinal fluid. They can be designed to look for proteins involved in driving the underlying immune attacks, as well as signs of nerve damage that MS wrecks, they explained.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 'The right diagnosis is unbelievably powerful': It can take years to diagnose rare diseases, and scientists are trying to fix that
- Why are dengue cases surging in Florida this year? An 'unlucky' combination of factors, experts say
- 'Zombie cells' may drive aging, and scientists are devising new ways to get rid of them
These in-depth, protein analyses could help paint a more comprehensive picture of MS, which could ultimately help scientists "look at that whole system in concert" to reach a strong diagnosis, Allette said.
No proteomics-based diagnostic tests for MS have been approved yet, Green clarified. And even with those upcoming advances, Green doubts there will ever be a simple, one-time test that can determine a patient has MS. "I think that's probably unlikely, that it would ever be that straightforward," he said.
He does think that, in time, scientists could pare down the number of tests required to reach a diagnosis, but he argued that the clinical evaluation conducted by a neurologist will likely remain crucial. "I'm doubtful that there's going to be a test that will fully replace that," he said, "at least in the foreseeable future."

She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

articles.title: Hiện tượng kinh ngạc trong không gian: Tại sao Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế lại rỉ sét?
articles.text:
Trạm Vũ trụ Quốc tế ở trong môi trường khắc nghiệt ngoài vũ trụ, thiếu không khí và độ ẩm, về lý thuyết thì không nên xảy ra hiện tượng rỉ sét. Vậy chính xác thì điều gì đã gây ra hiện tượng ăn mòn bí ẩn này trên Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế? Có những chất hóa học chưa được biết đến ở ngoài không gian hay có sự hiểu lầm trong hiểu biết của chúng ta về môi trường không gian?
Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế là nền tảng quan trọng để con người tiến hành nghiên cứu và thí nghiệm khoa học trong không gian, tuy nhiên trong những năm gần đây, một số vật liệu kim loại trên trạm vũ trụ đã bị rỉ sét. Hiện tượng này đã thu hút sự chú ý của mọi người, bởi vì trong môi trường khắc nghiệt, đặc biệt là trong không gian, vấn đề ăn mòn và rỉ sét của vật liệu kim loại sẽ trở nên rõ ràng hơn.
Trong không gian, vấn đề ăn mòn và rỉ sét sẽ rõ ràng hơn. (Ảnh minh họa: ESA).
Trong không gian, thành phần khí rất khác với môi trường khí quyển Trái đất. Không gian thiếu oxy và áp suất khí quyển, đồng thời có một lượng lớn các loại khí có trọng lượng phân tử thấp như hydro, nitơ và oxy. Những loại khí này có thể ăn mòn và làm rỉ sét vật liệu kim loại.
Trong quá trình phóng tàu vũ trụ, nó sẽ gặp phải những cú va chạm mạnh, nhiệt độ cao và rung lắc. Dưới tác dụng của các ngoại lực này, bề mặt vật liệu kim loại có thể bị hư hỏng, khiến kim loại tiếp xúc với môi trường bên ngoài dễ bị ăn mòn, rỉ sét.
Có rất nhiều thiên thạch cực nhỏ trôi nổi trong không gian, khi những thiên thạch này va vào bề mặt kim loại có thể gây ra những vết xước, móp nhỏ, thậm chí rất nhỏ. Đồng thời, tia cực tím và các hạt trong bức xạ Mặt trời cũng sẽ gây ra quá trình oxy hóa, ăn mòn vật liệu kim loại, đẩy nhanh quá trình rỉ sét của kim loại.
Trong không gian, thành phần khí rất khác với môi trường khí quyển Trái đất. (Ảnh minh họa: VOX).
Ăn mòn nhanh: Trong không gian, vật liệu kim loại sẽ bị ăn mòn nhanh hơn nhiều so với trên Trái đất. Điều này chủ yếu là do tác động ăn mòn mạnh hơn của các thành phần khí và bức xạ trong không gian lên kim loại. Đặc biệt, hydro và nitơ, trong không gian mỏng hơn bầu khí quyển Trái đất, nhưng tác động ăn mòn của chúng lại nghiêm trọng hơn. Vì vậy, vật liệu kim loại dễ bị rỉ sét trong không gian.
Thay đổi lớp bề mặt: Bức xạ và nhiệt độ cao trong không gian gây ra các phản ứng hóa học trên bề mặt kim loại tạo thành lớp oxit. Lớp oxit này không chỉ phá hủy bề ngoài của vật liệu kim loại mà còn ảnh hưởng đến tính chất cơ học và khả năng chống ăn mòn của nó. Ngoài ra, do môi trường chân không trong không gian nên phản ứng oxy hóa trên bề mặt kim loại có thể phức tạp hơn, càng làm trầm trọng thêm vấn đề ăn mòn, rỉ sét của vật liệu kim loại.
Suy thoái cấu trúc: Vật liệu kim loại dễ bị tổn thương trước tác động từ các thiên thạch nhỏ trong không gian và những tác động này có thể gây hư hỏng cấu trúc kim loại. Một khi độ bền và độ ổn định của kết cấu kim loại bị hư hỏng, nó sẽ ảnh hưởng xấu đến hoạt động bình thường của tàu vũ trụ.
Phi hành gia đi bộ ngoài không gian. (Ảnh minh họa: NASA).
Là một cột mốc quan trọng trong hành trình khám phá không gian của con người, Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế là một thành tựu tuyệt vời về thiết kế kỹ thuật hàng không vũ trụ. Tuy nhiên, vấn đề rỉ sét gần đây trên Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế đã mang lại sự quan tâm và suy nghĩ mới cho mọi người.
Vấn đề này cho thấy những thách thức lớn mà thiết kế kỹ thuật vũ trụ phải đối mặt, bao gồm các vấn đề như độ bền vật liệu, an toàn kết cấu, bảo trì và đổi mới trong các môi trường đặc biệt.
Thách thức về độ bền vật liệu: Trên Trái đất, các tòa nhà và cơ sở vật chất của chúng ta sẽ phải đối mặt với tác động của nhiều yếu tố thời tiết và môi trường bên ngoài khác nhau, như biến đổi khí hậu, bức xạ tia cực tím, v.v. Tuy nhiên, trong không gian, vật liệu còn phải đối mặt với những thách thức lớn hơn.
Tàu vũ trụ phải đối mặt với các điều kiện môi trường như nhiệt độ thay đổi khắc nghiệt, tia vũ trụ và tác động của thiên thạch vi mô… Những yếu tố này sẽ có tác động nhất định đến hiệu suất và độ bền của vật liệu. Vì vậy, thiết kế kỹ thuật không gian phải chọn những vật liệu đặc biệt thích ứng với những môi trường khắc nghiệt này để đảm bảo sự ổn định và an toàn lâu dài của kết cấu.
Tàu vũ trụ phải đối mặt với các điều kiện môi trường tác động nhất định đến hiệu suất và độ bền của vật liệu. (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu).
Những thách thức về an toàn kết cấu: An toàn kết cấu trong kỹ thuật vũ trụ là một vấn đề cực kỳ quan trọng. Trên Trái đất, độ bền kết cấu của các tòa nhà chủ yếu được quyết định bởi trọng lực, trong khi ở trong không gian, sự suy yếu của trọng lực khiến cho việc thiết kế và tính toán các kết cấu rất khác so với trên Trái đất.
Ngoài ra, trạm vũ trụ cần phải đối mặt với tác động của các lực bên ngoài như lực đẩy máy bay và chênh lệch áp suất không khí, những điều này có thể đặt ra thách thức đối với sự ổn định và độ bền của kết cấu. Vì vậy, trong thiết kế kỹ thuật không gian, các yếu tố này phải được xem xét hợp lý để đảm bảo kết cấu có thể chịu được nhiều ngoại lực khác nhau nhằm đảm bảo an toàn cho nhân sự.
Những thách thức về bảo trì và cập nhật: Là một cơ sở vũ trụ dài hạn, Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế yêu cầu bảo trì và cập nhật thường xuyên. Tuy nhiên, đặc thù của môi trường không gian khiến nhiệm vụ này trở nên vô cùng khó khăn.
Đi bộ ngoài không gian và mang theo thiết bị là một nhiệm vụ cực kỳ khó khăn đối với các phi hành gia, cộng với những hạn chế của bản thân tàu vũ trụ như áp suất không khí, thay đổi nhiệt độ, v.v., khiến việc bảo trì và cập nhật trở nên phức tạp hơn. Ngoài ra, việc ứng dụng và cập nhật công nghệ mới có thể gây ra những rủi ro và bất ổn mới, đòi hỏi phải có sự đánh giá và lập kế hoạch cẩn thận để đảm bảo sự ổn định và bảo mật của toàn bộ hệ thống.
Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế (ISS) là một công trình quan trọng. (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu).
Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế (ISS) là cột mốc quan trọng trong hành trình khám phá không gian của nhân loại, tuy nhiên, giống như bất kỳ vật thể nào trên Trái đất, ISS cũng phải đối mặt với sự xói mòn của thời gian và môi trường. Trong số đó, vấn đề rỉ sét của trạm vũ trụ luôn thu hút nhiều sự chú ý. Để giải quyết vấn đề này, các nhà khoa học đã giải quyết vấn đề rỉ sét bằng cách khám phá các phương pháp sơn phủ bảo vệ và tối ưu hóa vật liệu.
Lớp phủ bảo vệ là một trong những phương tiện quan trọng để giải quyết vấn đề rỉ sét của ISS. Đối với bất kỳ thiết bị cơ khí nào hoạt động trong môi trường không gian, chất lượng và độ tin cậy của lớp phủ bảo vệ là rất quan trọng. Để chống rỉ sét hiệu quả, các nhà khoa học tiếp tục nghiên cứu, cải tiến công thức, quy trình thi công lớp phủ bảo vệ. Trong số đó, một công nghệ tiên tiến được gọi là "lớp phủ hoạt động" được sử dụng.
Loại lớp phủ này có thể tạo thành một lớp sản phẩm phản ứng hóa học bảo vệ trên bề mặt lớp phủ dẫn điện để ngăn chặn sự hình thành các oxit sắt, do đó có vai trò chống oxy hóa và chống ăn mòn. Ngoài ra, các nhà khoa học cũng đã nghiên cứu công nghệ phủ micro-nano để cải thiện khả năng bịt kín và chống ăn mòn của lớp phủ bằng cách bổ sung các hạt nano vào vật liệu phủ. Những công nghệ phủ tiên tiến này mang lại sự bảo vệ đáng tin cậy cho hoạt động lâu dài của ISS.
(Ảnh minh họa: NASA).
Trong khi rỉ sét trên Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế gây ra một số lo ngại, các nhà khoa học và kỹ sư sẽ tiếp tục nỗ lực giải quyết vấn đề. Xét cho cùng, Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế là một cửa sổ quan trọng đối với nhân loại trong không gian, chúng ta nên cùng nhau bảo vệ nó và tiếp tục thúc đẩy quá trình khám phá không gian. Chỉ thông qua đổi mới và nghiên cứu liên tục, chúng ta mới có thể hiểu rõ hơn về môi trường không gian và có thể vượt qua những thách thức khác nhau và mở ra những khả năng rộng lớn hơn cho tương lai của nhân loại.

articles.title: NASA solves a strange mystery hidden inside asteroid Bennu’s boulders
articles.text:
NASA solves a strange mystery hidden inside asteroid Bennu’s boulders
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- University of Arizona
- Summary:
- NASA scientists have finally uncovered why asteroid Bennu loses heat so quickly despite being covered in massive boulders. Samples returned to Earth reveal that its rocks are filled with hidden cracks, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for years.
- Share:
NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission encountered an unexpected mystery when it arrived at asteroid Bennu in 2018. Instead of the relatively smooth terrain that earlier observations had suggested, the spacecraft found a rugged landscape dominated by enormous boulders, with very few areas suitable for collecting samples.
"When OSIRIS-REx got to Bennu in 2018, we were surprised by what we saw," said Andrew Ryan, a scientist at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory, who led the mission's working group responsible for analyzing the physical and thermal properties of its samples. "We expected some boulders, but we anticipated at least some large regions with smoother, finer regolith that would be easy to collect. Instead, it looked like it was all boulders, and we were scratching our heads for a while."
The discovery was especially confusing because of what astronomers had previously learned about Bennu's ability to retain heat. Measurements from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope in 2007 indicated that the asteroid's surface warmed and cooled rapidly as it rotated through sunlight and darkness.
Scientists describe this property as low thermal inertia. Materials with low thermal inertia, such as beach sand, quickly gain heat in sunlight and lose it once the Sun disappears. Large, solid rocks behave differently. Much like concrete, they typically hold on to warmth and release it gradually.
Bennu's boulder-covered surface appeared to contradict those earlier measurements, leaving researchers with a puzzling question: How could an asteroid covered in massive rocks cool so quickly?
Hidden Cracks Reveal the Secret of Bennu's Boulders
Observations collected by OSIRIS-REx while surveying Bennu offered an early clue. The asteroid's boulders might contain far more empty space than scientists had assumed, allowing them to lose heat faster than ordinary solid rocks.
When samples from Bennu were returned to Earth, researchers finally had an opportunity to examine that possibility directly.
Ryan and his colleagues used several laboratory techniques to investigate tiny rock fragments collected from the asteroid. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, confirmed that the rocks were indeed highly porous. However, porosity alone could not fully explain Bennu's unusually rapid heat loss.
The researchers discovered another important feature. Many of the rock particles contained extensive networks of cracks running through their interiors.
To investigate how these fractures influence the movement of heat, researchers at Nagoya University in Japan examined the samples using a technique called lock-in thermography. This method uses a laser to heat a tiny area of a sample while measuring how the heat spreads through the surrounding material, much like ripples expanding across the surface of a pond.
"That's when things became really interesting," Ryan said. "The thermal inertia measured in the lab samples turned out to be much higher than what the spacecraft's instruments had recorded, echoing similar findings obtained by the team of OSIRIS-REx's partner mission, JAXA's (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) Hayabusa-2."
The difference between laboratory measurements and spacecraft observations suggested that the size and internal structure of Bennu's rocks were essential to understanding their behavior.
Because the returned samples were much smaller than the enormous boulders covering Bennu, scientists needed a way to determine how heat would move through the material on a much larger scale.
NASA Uses 3D Scans to Look Inside Asteroid Rocks
At NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, researchers prepared the samples for detailed X-ray imaging while taking special precautions to prevent contamination.
Inside a glove box filled with protective nitrogen gas, team members sealed individual rock particles in airtight containers. They then transported the containers to a laboratory for X-ray computed tomography, or XCT scanning. After imaging, the particles were returned to the glove box without being exposed to Earth's environment.
"The sample goes into its own 'spacesuit,' gets a CT scan, and then comes back to its pristine environment, all without having any exposure to the terrestrial environment," said Nicole Lunning, lead OSIRIS-REx sample curator within the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science division at NASA Johnson and one of the study's co-authors. "We can image right through these airtight containers to visualize the shape and internal structure of the rock that's inside."
The scans gave scientists a detailed view of the samples' interiors, revealing structures that could not be examined simply by looking at their surfaces.
"X-ray computed tomography allows us to look at the inside of an object in three dimensions, without damaging it," said study co-author and NASA Johnson X-ray scientist Scott Eckley.
Each scan also produced a permanent three-dimensional digital record of the particle's exterior and internal features. These records were added to a publicly accessible database, allowing the samples to be studied without repeatedly handling the original material.
Ryan's team then incorporated the X-ray scan data into computer simulations designed to track how heat travels through asteroid rocks. By extending the calculations from individual particles to the much larger boulders found on Bennu, they were able to reproduce the low thermal inertia observed by the spacecraft.
A Discovery That Could Change How Scientists Study Asteroids
The results resolved a key mystery about Bennu's unusual surface. Scientists had previously considered whether the asteroid's boulders might be extremely porous, with a soft, fluffy, or even sponge-like internal structure.
Although the rocks do contain substantial pore space, the researchers found that their widespread internal fractures were equally important to understanding how they retain and release heat.
"It turns out that they're really cracked too, and that was the missing piece of the puzzle," Ryan said.
The discovery has implications beyond Bennu. Astronomers frequently rely on measurements of how an asteroid absorbs and releases heat to estimate the physical properties of its surface. Until now, interpreting those observations has been difficult without actual rock samples to examine.
Ron Ballouz, a scientist at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Maryland, and the study's second author, explained that the findings provide a valuable connection between measurements made remotely and the true internal structure of asteroid material.
"We can finally ground our understanding of telescope observations of the thermal properties of an asteroid through analyzing these samples from that very same asteroid," Ballouz said.

articles.title: Phát hiện "hóa thạch" 13 tỉ năm tuổi của vụ nổ Big Bang
articles.text:
Quả bong bóng khổng lồ được đặt tên là Ho’oleilana, có tâm nằm cách thiên hà Milky Way 820 triệu năm ánh sáng, có thể chính là tàn tích "hóa thạch" của sự kiện khai sinh vũ trụ.
Theo Sci-News, khối "hóa thạch" Ho’oleilana có đường kính khoảng 1 tỉ năm ánh sáng, được nhà thiên văn học Cullan Howett từ Đại học Queensland (Úc) mô tả là lấn át các cấu trúc vũ trụ lớn nhất từng được biết đến như "Vạn Lý Trường Thành" Sloan và siêu đám Bootes.
Ho’oleilana hiện ra đầy trêu ngươi trong dữ liệu của các cuộc khảo sát Comicflows-4 và Sloan Digital Sky.
Bong bóng khổng lồ Ho’oleilana, "hóa thạch" của vũ trụ buổi bình minh - (Ảnh đồ họa: Frédéric Durillon).
"Chúng tôi thậm chí còn không tìm kiếm nó. Quá trúc này quá lớn đến nỗi nó tràn ra tận rìa vùng bầu trời mà chúng tôi đang phân tích" - TS Howett nói.
Theo bài công bố vừa xuất bản trên tạp chí khoa học Astrophysical Journal, trong lý thuyết về Big Bang, trong 400.000 năm đầu tiên, vũ trụ là một vạc plasma nóng - giống như bên trong các ngôi sao ngày nay. Trong plasma, các electron được tách ra khỏi hạt nhân nguyên tử.
Trong thời kỳ "hỗn mang" này, những vùng có mật độ cao hơn một chút bắt đầu co lại dưới lực hấp dẫn, ngay cả khi lượng bức xạ cực mạnh đang cố đẩy vật chất ra xa nhau.
Cuộc đấu tranh giữa lực hấp dẫn và bức xạ này đã làm cho plasma dao động và gợn sóng hệt như những gì chúng ta thấy khi một hòn sỏi rơi xuống mặt nước.
Trong không gian 3 chiều, gợn sóng lan tỏa theo một hình cầu. Từ "hòn sỏi" trung tâm, các gợn plasma tỏa ra xa tận 500 triệu năm ánh sáng xung quanh, sau đó bị cố định khi vũ trụ nguội đi và không còn plasma.
Đó chính là quả cầu "hóa thạch" mà các nhà khoa học vừa nhìn thấy.
Nhưng đó không phải bong bóng duy nhất trong vũ trụ. Trong suốt hàng tỉ năm, các bong bóng như thế lần lượt ra đời và bên trong chúng, các thiên hà được hình thành với mật độ cực đại.
Thiên hà Miiky Way (Ngân Hà) mà hành tinh chúng ta đang trú ngụ cũng nằm trong một cấu trúc bong bóng giống như thế.
Vì vậy, việc nghiên cứu "sứ giả cổ xưa" của vụ nổ Big Bang, chiếc bong bóng vũ trụ lâu đời nhất từng được tìm thấy, có thể giúp các nhà khoa học vũ trụ lý giải những bí ẩn xung quanh việc hình thành và phân bố của các thiên hà, cũng như làm rõ hơn bức tranh về sự giãn nở của vũ trụ.

articles.title: Readers respond to our poll about flying cars — and most think it will take more than 5 years
articles.text:
'Most people can't handle driving in 2 dimensions let alone 3': Readers respond to our poll about flying cars
Tesla recently demonstrated its Rocket Roadster "flying car." We asked our readers whether they think flying cars will be widely available in the near future.
Last week, Tesla unveiled a new "flying" edition of its Roadster electric vehicle. While some experts remain skeptical that the new "Rocket" EV is feasible in the real world, the demonstration reignited a long-standing debate about whether flying cars could soon become a reality.
In response to this demonstration, Live Science polled its readers on whether they think flying cars will be available to consumers in the next five years.
Over 280 readers responded, with the largest voting group, 34% of readers, picking "No, we need more than five years for flying cars to take off." The next-highest voting bloc was even more skeptical with 23% of readers choosing "No, flying cars will never happen."
Several comments reflected this pessimistic view, with one commenter leaving this response: "No flying cars. In my almost 60 years of driving experience I find that most people can't handle driving in 2 dimensions let alone 3. Besides that we have face [sic] so many other problems: hunger, poverty, inadequate healthcare, the careless disregard for our planet. What are we leaving my grandchildren and great grandchildren??"
Related stories
Other commenters echoed this sentiment. "It will never happen as some cheap alternative to electric or petrol driven vehicles," one person responded. "Gravity is master on this planet so to rise above that and be floating or propelled around on some sort of air current, Nah! I cannot imagine the damage that will take place in any livable area, towns, suburbs, cities, parks, etc, etc., that list is endless. And imagine the protests should a general public be allowed to dive and fly above any or all livable areas."
Not everyone was as adverse, with another commenter remarking on how far Tesla's technological development has come. "The flying roadster is a statement of what Mr. Musk can do with technology more than anything else. In the same way he can make the Roadster fly, be sure that the technology designed into the Tesla Y, the Cybercab or the Starship are at the very frontier of science. Mr Musk has singlehanded revolutionized the car industry and space travel in less than 20 years (the first Tesla car was sold in 2008). No small feat."
Do you agree or disagree with our readers? Tell us your thoughts in the comments.
Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

articles.title: Why painful arthritis can return stronger after cancer treatment
articles.text:
Why painful arthritis can return stronger after cancer treatment
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- University of Texas M. D. Anderson Cancer Center
- Summary:
- Researchers discovered that recurring arthritis triggered by cancer immunotherapy may be driven by immune cells that remember previous attacks and return in a more aggressive state. The findings could pave the way for treatments that prevent painful flare-ups while preserving the immune system's ability to fight cancer.
- Share:
For some cancer patients, the effects of immunotherapy can linger in an unexpected place: their joints. Painful arthritis may return repeatedly, sometimes becoming more severe with each episode. Now, scientists have uncovered a possible explanation involving the immune system's ability to remember previous attacks.
Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have found evidence that arthritis triggered by certain cancer immunotherapies behaves like a disease driven by immune memory. Rather than launching an entirely new inflammatory response during each flare, the immune system appears to reactivate cells involved in earlier episodes.
The discovery could eventually help doctors identify patients at risk of recurring arthritis and develop treatments that control joint inflammation without interfering with the immune system's ability to fight cancer.
The study, published in Cancer Immunology Research, was led by scientists at UT MD Anderson and Yale University. The research team included Roza I. Nurieva, Ph.D., professor of Immunology; Synat Keam, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the Nurieva Laboratory; and Yuanteng Jeff Li, M.D., assistant professor of General Internal Medicine. Sang Taek Kim, M.D., Ph.D., an assistant professor at Yale University, also co-led the investigation.
"Cancer immunotherapy works by creating a lasting immune response against tumors, but that same persistence may also contribute to recurring inflammatory side effects that can be debilitating for patients," Nurieva said. "By identifying the immune cells that drive recurrent arthritis, we can inform treatment strategies that reduce the risk of future flares while preserving the therapy's effectiveness against cancer."
Why Cancer Immunotherapy Can Trigger Painful Arthritis
Immune checkpoint inhibitors are widely used cancer treatments that help the body's natural defenses recognize and attack tumor cells. These drugs are a form of immunotherapy that works by removing some of the molecular restraints that normally keep immune activity under control.
Although this approach can help the immune system destroy cancer cells, it can sometimes cause immune cells to attack healthy tissues as well. When the joints become targets, patients may develop inflammatory arthritis, a condition that causes pain, swelling, and inflammation.
For some patients, the problem does not disappear after the first episode. Approximately 20% to 50% of patients who develop this complication experience repeated arthritis flares, and symptoms can persist for months or even years after immunotherapy ends.
These recurring episodes are often more intense than the initial attack, raising an important question: Why does the immune system continue to produce inflammation, and why can its response become increasingly aggressive?
Scientists Discover Immune Cells That Remember Previous Attacks
To investigate, the researchers examined fluid taken from the joints of six patients during both their first arthritis episode and a later recurrence.
Their analysis revealed two distinct populations of immune cells that appeared during both flares. One consisted of inflammatory CD8 T cells, while the other was a specialized group of CD4 T cells expressing two markers known as PD-1 and CXCL13.
T cells are immune cells that help coordinate the body's defenses and respond to potential threats. Some can also persist after an initial immune response, allowing the immune system to react more quickly when it encounters a familiar target.
The presence of the same immune cell populations during separate arthritis attacks suggests that recurring inflammation may arise from cells already involved in the earlier episode. Instead of starting from scratch, the immune system appears to reactivate an established inflammatory response.
This immune memory mechanism could help explain why arthritis can repeatedly return even after cancer treatment has stopped.
Why Arthritis Flares May Become More Severe
The researchers also found that the recurring immune cells appeared more active during subsequent arthritis episodes. They produced increased amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, which immune cells use to communicate and influence one another.
Another finding was particularly unexpected. Regulatory T cells, which normally act as a braking system to prevent excessive immune activity, also began producing inflammatory molecules during recurring flares.
This suggests that some of the cells responsible for keeping inflammation under control may instead contribute to it, potentially weakening the body's ability to shut down the response.
The researchers also identified extensive communication networks connecting inflammatory cells within affected joints. These signaling networks became more pronounced during the second arthritis episode.
Together, the findings suggest that recurring flares involve a coordinated and increasingly active inflammatory environment, rather than just a handful of immune cells acting independently.
Could Immune Memory Help Predict Future Arthritis Flares?
Despite growing recognition of inflammatory arthritis as a complication of cancer immunotherapy, scientists still do not fully understand why it affects certain patients while others never develop the condition.
The newly identified immune cell populations could provide an important starting point. Future studies may determine whether these cells can serve as biomarkers, meaning measurable biological indicators that help doctors recognize patients who are more likely to experience recurring arthritis.
Understanding which immune cells sustain the inflammation could also guide the development of more precise treatments. Ideally, such therapies would prevent or reduce painful arthritis flares while leaving the beneficial cancer-fighting effects of immunotherapy intact.
Because the investigation examined samples from only six patients, additional research will be needed to confirm the findings and establish whether the identified immune cells can reliably predict future episodes.
Still, the results offer a promising explanation for a difficult complication of cancer treatment: an immune system trained to remember and fight tumors may also retain inflammatory responses that continue to harm the joints.

Immune Hallmarks of Recurrent Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor–Mediated Inflammatory Arthritis. Cancer Immunology Research, 2026; 14 (10): 1653 DOI: 10.1158/2326-6066.CIR-25-1639

articles.title: Scientists can now 'watermark' AI-generated proteins to deter bioweapon creation. But will it really work?
articles.text:
Scientists can now 'watermark' AI-generated proteins to deter bioweapon creation. But will it really work?
A new technology encodes an invisible mark into the structure of AI-generated proteins, but experts said the system's guardrails can still be bypassed.
With artificial intelligence (AI), scientists have a powerful new tool for creating never-before-seen proteins, which can be used to make either groundbreaking new medicines or devastating bioweapons.
To help guard against nefarious uses of these proteins, scientists have recently figured out a way to "watermark" them without compromising their function. A team from Google DeepMind developed this technique to better track the provenance of AI-designed proteins.
"This has the potential to reduce biosecurity threats, such as unauthorized toxin creation, and may help with database curation, preventing artificial designs from cluttering the standard databases," said Roy Sleator, a biology professor at Munster Technological University in Ireland, who was not involved in the research.
"In practice, it could help trace a design's origin, flag engineered proteins for extra biosecurity checks, and reduce misleading claims about how a protein was made," Sleator told Live Science in an email.
However, in its current form, the same AI technologies that add watermarks can also strip them away, other experts warned.
New ways to hide watermarks
The unveiling of the AI program AlphaFold in 2020 was a milestone in protein engineering. The tool, which won Demis Hassabis, John Jumper and David Baker the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024, can reveal the 3D structure of a protein from the sequence of its building blocks, called amino acids. Proteins fold like origami, adopting 3D shapes that dictate their function.
However, AlphaFold's technology also opened the door to generating brand-new proteins that could be used to create biothreats, including viral proteins that can evade our immune systems and existing vaccines.
"Anything that can be used for good can be used for bad," said George Rose, professor emeritus of biophysics at Johns Hopkins University.
Current screening tools identify novel dangerous or restricted molecules by seeing how similar their amino acid sequences are to those of recognized threats. But the problem is that AI could come up with proteins that don't look like anything we've ever seen. That's what the new watermarking technique aims to solve.
The DeepMind team has framed the watermarking effort as a "family" of related techniques they call SynthIDBio. The first member of this family is SynthIDBio-sequence, which encodes watermarks into the amino acid sequences of proteins created by a program called ProteinMPNN.
When users tell ProteinMPNN the desired 3D shape for their protein, it chooses amino acid options that ultimately fold into that shape. SynthIDBio-sequence subtly influences how the program chooses each amino acid according to a secret watermarking "key." Once the sequence is generated, anyone who knows the hidden code can assess how likely the sequence is to have been created under the key's bias. In their recent study, the DeepMind team showed that proteins built with this watermark could still bind to their targets as well as non-watermarked proteins.
A sister technique, called SynthIDBio-structure, instead embeds a watermark directly into the protein's structure. It does this by altering the function of AlphaFold 3, DeepMind's flagship protein prediction algorithm.
When AlphaFold predicts a structure, SynthIDBio-structure gives it a side mission: The AI must make minuscule tweaks to how the atoms in the protein are arranged. These tweaks can be picked up by a detector later, and they're small enough that they don't look like obvious distortion.
In a test, these two systems created hidden watermarks that could be detected with incredible accuracy, flagging more than 99% of watermarked proteins and correctly ignoring 99.9% of non-watermarked proteins.
How to bypass a protein watermark
Live Science spoke to several experts who agreed that SynthIDBio was an impressive technical feat. However, they said it wasn't ready for widespread implementation yet.
The two techniques are "effective but brittle," Bruce Wittmann, a principal applied scientist at Microsoft, told Live Science in an email. That's because, as the DeepMind team also notes in their paper, the watermarks can be easily removed.
"For sequences, watermarks can be removed by 'resequencing' — effectively, altering the protein amino acid sequence such that the watermark is no longer detectable," Wittmann said. "For structures, watermarks can be removed by adding noise to or otherwise modifying the spatial coordinates of the structure." Screening tools wouldn't be able to detect if a watermark had been removed from a protein.
Experts are also skeptical that watermarking would provide a long-term solution for biosecurity.
An indelible watermark could identify who originally made a nefarious protein, or identify when a user was accessing a protein generation software without permission. This might deter some criminals, but terrorists looking to create a novel protein for a biological weapon would be less likely to care about being identified after a successful attack, said Max Brackmann, a chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear arms expert at the Spiez Laboratory in Switzerland.
Additionally, the vast majority of software for protein prediction and generation is open-source, meaning much of the code is freely available to use and modify. That makes it far harder to bake watermarking into these programs. Wittmann warned that the field would have to shift toward closed-source models before watermarks could become an industry standard.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
He added that watermarking could act as one layer of a biosecurity defense shield, rather than offering standalone protection. Top-down regulation would be challenging to enforce. "I imagine it would be very difficult to ensure the regulations were being followed," he said.
Rose was even blunter about regulating the use of generative proteins.
"I'm convinced it won't work," he said. "Once there's a sweet technology that does something, government regulation to keep it under wraps has never been really successful."
Stutz, D., Cowen-Rivers, A.I., Ortiz-Jimenez, G., et al. (2026) Function-preserving watermarking of AI-generated proteins. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10965-y
Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.
RJ Mackenzie is an award-nominated science and health journalist. He has degrees in neuroscience from the University of Edinburgh and the University of Cambridge. He became a writer after deciding that the best way of contributing to science would be from behind a keyboard rather than a lab bench. He has reported on everything from brain-interface technology to shape-shifting materials science, and from the rise of predatory conferencing to the importance of newborn-screening programs. He is a former staff writer of Technology Networks.
