articles.title: Trà sữa từ 7.000 đồng xuất hiện dày đặc trên nhiều tuyến phố Hà Nội
articles.text:
Trên phố Khâm Thiên (Hà Nội), nhiều cửa hàng trà sữa, hồng trà và trà trái cây bình dân xuất hiện san sát nhau. Các thương hiệu Hồng Trà Ngô Gia, Tam Hảo, Thanh Trà, Olong Gia Gia... đồng loạt mở điểm bán với giá khởi điểm từ 7.000 đồng/ly.
Đặc điểm của các cửa hàng này là diện tích nhỏ, ít chỗ ngồi và chủ yếu bán mang đi. Một số điểm bán sử dụng quầy pha chế sát mặt đường hoặc mô hình cửa sổ nhận đồ. Người mua có thể dừng xe, gọi món và lấy đồ uống mà không cần vào cửa hàng. Khách hàng chủ yếu là học sinh, sinh viên và người trẻ có nhu cầu mua đồ uống với chi phí thấp.
Mức giá khởi điểm 7.000 đồng thấp hơn đáng kể so với nhiều món trà sữa tại các chuỗi có thương hiệu, nơi giá bán có thể lên tới 35.000-60.000 đồng/ly. Thậm chí, mức giá này còn thấp hơn nhiều sản phẩm tại Mixue hay Bingxue, những chuỗi đồ uống bình dân từng phát triển mạnh tại Việt Nam.
Các cửa hàng trà sữa giá rẻ còn xuất hiện trên nhiều tuyến phố đông học sinh, sinh viên như Trương Định, Chùa Láng, Cầu Giấy, Nguyễn Trãi...
Trà sữa giá rẻ phát triển mạnh tại TPHCM từ vài năm trước, sau đó mới xuất hiện tại Hà Nội từ cuối năm 2025. Mô hình này có nét tương đồng với làn sóng đồ uống bình dân tại Trung Quốc, nơi nhiều chuỗi trà sữa và kem phát triển nhờ giá bán thấp và quy trình vận hành đơn giản.
Cuộc cạnh tranh giá rẻ
Theo chia sẻ từ một thương hiệu, mức giá 7.000 đồng/ly được xây dựng dựa trên 4 yếu tố chính: bao bì đơn giản, quy trình vận hành tinh gọn, nhập nguyên liệu với số lượng lớn và tập trung vào trải nghiệm khách hàng thay vì quảng cáo.
Theo đại diện thương hiệu, chi phí nguyên liệu và bao bì cho một ly trà sữa giá 7.000 đồng vào khoảng 5.000 đồng. Tuy nhiên, mức lợi nhuận thực tế còn phụ thuộc vào chi phí nhân công, mặt bằng, điện nước và các khoản vận hành khác.
Thực tế, một ly trà sữa thường có giá cao hơn mức này. Giá 7.000 đồng thường áp dụng cho sản phẩm cơ bản, chưa bao gồm các loại topping hoặc lựa chọn nâng cấp.
Khi khách gọi thêm trân châu, thạch, pudding hoặc chọn cốc lớn hơn, tổng số tiền phải trả sẽ tăng lên. Hóa đơn thực tế có thể lên mức 15.000-20.000 đồng, tùy món và lựa chọn của khách. Đây vẫn là mức giá cạnh tranh so với nhiều thương hiệu trà sữa truyền thống.
Trà sữa giá rẻ thu hút đông đảo người tiêu dùng trẻ. Mai Anh, sinh viên tại Đống Đa, cho biết với mức giá khoảng 20.000 đồng/ly, học sinh, sinh viên có thể uống thường xuyên mà không tốn quá nhiều tiền. Tuy nhiên, giá rẻ không phải yếu tố duy nhất quyết định việc quay lại quán. Hương vị, chất lượng đồ uống và vệ sinh vẫn là những tiêu chí quan trọng.
Ông Trần Khánh Minh Sơn, chuyên gia F&B, cho rằng sự xuất hiện của nhiều thương hiệu trà sữa giá rẻ cho thấy cuộc cạnh tranh trong lĩnh vực đồ uống ngày càng gay gắt.
Trà sữa từng bùng nổ tại Hà Nội vào khoảng năm 2017, khi hàng loạt thương hiệu như Ding Tea, Gong Cha, Royal Tea và TocoToco mở rộng hoạt động. Trào lưu này dần hạ nhiệt. Một số cửa hàng đóng cửa hoặc chuyển sang kinh doanh các loại đồ uống khác.
Thị trường sau đó chứng kiến sự phát triển của các chuỗi đồ uống bình dân như Mixue và Bingxue. Mixue gia nhập thị trường Việt Nam năm 2018, sau đó mở rộng hệ thống cửa hàng nhượng quyền và trở thành một trong những thương hiệu nổi bật ở phân khúc kem, đồ uống bình dân.
Nếu Mixue và Bingxue góp phần phổ biến mô hình trà và kem giá thấp, sự xuất hiện của nhiều cửa hàng trà sữa giá rẻ cho thấy cạnh tranh về giá đang trở thành một hướng đi đáng chú ý trong phân khúc đồ uống bình dân. Mô hình này hướng tới nhóm khách hàng nhạy cảm với giá, trong đó có học sinh, sinh viên và người trẻ.
Để duy trì mức giá thấp, các cửa hàng phải kiểm soát chặt chi phí nguyên liệu và vận hành. Bao bì cũng được lựa chọn theo hướng tiết kiệm. Nhiều cửa hàng dùng cốc nhựa thông thường và màng ép nắp. Không gian phục vụ được thu gọn để ưu tiên khu vực pha chế và nhận đơn.
Theo ông Sơn, mô hình giá rẻ đòi hỏi các cửa hàng kiểm soát chặt chi phí nhưng vẫn phải bảo đảm chất lượng nguyên liệu và an toàn thực phẩm. Mức giá thấp tự nó không đồng nghĩa với chất lượng thấp; người tiêu dùng cần quan tâm đến nguồn gốc nguyên liệu, điều kiện chế biến và vệ sinh tại điểm bán.

articles.title: Fi’s GPS-equipped dog trackers are on sale for 30 percent off
articles.text:
If your dog or cat is prone to getting lost, or you frequently go on adventures together, you can save 30 percent on Fi pet trackers through October 25th when you enter coupon code SCARY at checkout. The sale includes several satellite-connected trackers, including the Fi Ultra GPS we previously tested, which is down to $209.30 after the discount. That effectively brings it down to its original launch price.
Fi’s GPS-equipped dog trackers are on sale for 30 percent off
We also spotted discounts on Kirby Air Riders for the Nintendo Switch 2, a JLab microphone, and Lego’s Grogu set.
The IP68-rated Fi Ultra is fully waterproof, even in saltwater, and lasts up to five days, depending on how active your dog is. The accessory — which conveniently attaches to your dog’s collar or harness — uses a combination of LTE, GPS, and Starlink satellite coverage to track your dog’s current location and recent history, even in cellular dead zones; it can also send noise and vibration alerts to catch your canine’s attention.
Fi Ultra dog tracker
The Fi Ultra is the first dog tracker to combine T-Satellite with Starlink, GPS, and LTE connectivity to help you find your lost dog anywhere.
We spent time with the Fi Ultra earlier this year, testing it in a remote location in South Carolina. While the tracking was precise, the two- or three-minute update interval could be problematic for fast dogs, and it drained the battery quickly in Lost Mode (we barely got two days on a full charge). It’s also fairly sizable, making it a better fit for larger pups.
Unsurprisingly, you’ll need an active subscription to use the Fi Ultra’s tracking features, though you’ll get a discount on your first term, with six-month, one-year, and two-year plans available that offer lower overall monthly rates. For example, a one-year plan is $99 for the first year, and $189 each year after. However, the plans only work in the United States and offer no satellite coverage in Alaska.
Other deals to consider
- You can currently grab a physical copy of Kirby Air Riders for the Nintendo Switch 2 at Amazon for $48.99, a decent discount from its usual list price of $69.99. The colorful, fast-paced racing game offers surprising depth in terms of character and kart customization, with both cosmetic and functional upgrades to purchase and deploy over time. Read more.
- The JLab JBuds Talk USB-C microphone is on sale at Amazon for $24.99, where it usually fluctuates between $50 and $100, the full MSRP. A dedicated microphone can make a huge difference in audio quality over headphones or your laptop’s built-in mic. The Talk features four directional modes for different situations and a 96KHz/24-bit sample rate for high-quality recordings and voice clarity.
- Amazon is selling Lego’s Star Wars Grogu set for a discounted price of $103.99 ($26 off), which matches its lowest price to date. The 1,200-piece kit features Grogu in his beskar armor, with a satchel to carry his equipment (or snacks). You can also reattach his arms and facial features for different expressions, and a built-in lever lets you turn his head.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
articles.text:
Last week, Starshield — the version of SpaceX’s Starlink used by the Ukrainian military — was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds from accessing the service. The Ukrainian army’s interceptors, which counter Russian drones carrying bombs, suddenly stopped working at high speeds, making it easier for Russia to attack the country’s energy infrastructure and leading to a reported two deaths and at least 17 injuries.
Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
As SpaceX throttles Ukraine’s Starshield, experts warn that Elon Musk’s de facto monopoly over launch and satellite tech poses a major threat to global security.
Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
As SpaceX throttles Ukraine’s Starshield, experts warn that Elon Musk’s de facto monopoly over launch and satellite tech poses a major threat to global security.
The Ukrainian military reported receiving no advance warning about the Starshield speed restriction. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was a direct message from the US amid rising tensions between himself and President Donald Trump. The abrupt nature of the cutoff and its potentially dangerous military and humanitarian ramifications led to widespread public outcry focused both on Trump for pulling the rug out from under Ukraine and on SpaceX CEO Elon Musk for enabling him.
Since then Musk and Trump have traded denials back and forth. Musk first said that SpaceX has no control over Starshield and decisions are made by the US military, while the White House denied taking action. Then reports emerged that Musk was the one who suggested the slowdown tactic to Trump, who then accepted it, followed by a further report that Musk himself unilaterally ordered the restrictions.
The finger-pointing is of little interest to Ukrainians, who are focused on trying to defend their country from a brutal ongoing Russian invasion. Zelenskyy is well aware that he is being used as a scapegoat as Trump flails around attempting to blame Ukraine for the rising oil prices caused by his unpopular war with Iran.
But Ukraine needs to play nice to some extent, given how dependent it is on US technologies like Starlink/Starshield that enable it to mount a defense against Russian attacks. Starlink access has been deliberately restricted there before, including in 2022, when coverage was not extended to cover a counterattack operation in Crimea. If Musk decided to pull the plug completely, the effect on Ukraine could be devastating.
This amount of geopolitical power being wielded by an unelected tech oligarch is the direct result of consolidating so much of the space industry into just one company, and one man’s hands. And the scope of Musk’s control goes well beyond Ukraine. From the defense of nations to the ability of NASA to launch its astronauts into space, SpaceX has been irreplaceable — and that means Musk has the space industry in his grip.
A de facto monopoly
SpaceX’s recent IPO positions it as one of the most valuable companies in the world. And while the company has generated most of its recent revenue from its Starlink service, it made its name as a company that launches rockets into space.
SpaceX’s Falcon 9 is the most successful rocket in history, and its “rideshare” program, which lets small satellite operators share space on a rocket, has dropped the price of launches to historic lows. This has helped organizations from small startups to university research departments launch their own satellites and has been hailed as a democratizing force in the space industry.
However, that success has come at a cost, which is that SpaceX now holds all the cards when it comes to access to space.
“For all intents and purposes, SpaceX has a monopoly on launch right now,” said Wendy Whitman Cobb of the School of Advanced Air and Space Studies at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama. “There are competitors out there,” she said, such as United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, and Rocket Lab, “but nobody comes even close to SpaceX in terms of frequency, mass, scale, cost. I mean, they’ve got everything in the bag.”
Space economist Oğuz Karasu of the Oxford Space Initiative concurred. SpaceX doesn’t have a monopoly on launch in the legal sense, he said, but in practical terms it does. And that gives the company tremendous pull over the industry as a whole.
“The rocket launch industry is around 8 percent of the entire [space] industry,” Karasu said, “but without that 8 percent, you can’t have the rest of it.”
The gatekeeper for space
SpaceX, which didn’t respond to a request for comment, has a tremendous advantage in providing space-based services like satellite internet. The company has been able to build out its network of over 10,000 Starlink satellites currently in low Earth orbit by launching them cheaply and efficiently using its Falcon 9 rockets.
“This is almost like an antitrust issue,” said defense expert Andrew Reddie of the University of California, Berkeley. “The issue is that SpaceX launches support Starlink constellations that are owned by SpaceX. There is no incentive for a SpaceX launch to be used to provide constellations for other countries that would compete.”
Interestingly, SpaceX has previously launched Amazon Kuiper (now Leo) satellites on a handful of missions — arguably as a preemptive defense against antitrust complaints. Or perhaps SpaceX is simply so confident in its position that it can afford to be magnanimous (or to flex a little on its rival) by launching a few competitor satellites.
The downside of a monopoly, at least for the customer, is that eventually prices rise.
SpaceX doesn’t share prices for its launches publicly, but both Whitman Cobb and Karasu say they’ve heard complaints that Falcon 9 launches are getting more expensive, particularly for low Earth orbit deployments. And the Starlink service has seen considerable increases in price since its beta launch in 2020.
Of course, there are plenty of reasons for a company to increase its prices, from inflation to rising costs, but when a company has enormous market dominance (and now shareholders to please) there isn’t much incentive against raising prices to increase profits.
If this business model sounds familiar, it’s because it’s one of Silicon Valley’s favorite and most destructive tactics. Uber perfected the art of predatory pricing, whereby investor cash is used to artificially lower prices so that a company can corner a market and push out competition. Then, with the monopoly safely in place, the company can jack up its prices and lower the quality of its product or service, secure in the knowledge that customers no longer have any other viable alternatives.
The unseen power of space
This might sound like an obscure problem, something that might make life more difficult for a few high-tech operations but has little relevance to the day-to-day lives of most people. But space infrastructure is now embedded in the mechanisms of our most essential technologies, in the form of satellite communications and GPS data.
“If GPS goes down, you’re not going to be able to get gas at the gas pump, you’re not going to be able to get money out of the ATM,” said Whitman Cobb, “let alone not be able to do financial transactions or get an ambulance to the right place on time.”
It’s not that space experts are realistically worried that Elon Musk is going to lose his mind and cut off Starlink access worldwide, or cause a collision that could take down GPS. It’s that the space industry is woven, unseen, into so many parts of our everyday lives that allowing one company or one person to control access to space hands them enormous power.
“All of our current economic activities are based on space technologies right now,” said Karasu. “Giving this much control, or this much power, to one person is not good for society’s future.”
Even huge agencies like NASA and the Space Force face risks from being too dependent on SpaceX. With the company deciding to retire its workhorse and extremely reliable Falcon 9 rocket, reportedly not taking any new missions from 2028, the Space Force is struggling to find launch options for its military satellites, and NASA now faces a potential future in which it doesn’t have access to the Crew Dragon capsule for carrying its astronauts to and from the International Space Station.
History has shown the dangers of having only one launch option. After the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003, which cost the lives of seven astronauts, the entire program was canceled and no humans were launched into space from the US from 2011 until 2020.
That’s why NASA is continuing to support beleaguered Boeing in its slow and troubled development of the Starliner capsule, because dependence on a single launch provider means putting all of your very expensive and delicate eggs into one precarious basket. That was demonstrated in February this year, when issues with the usually rock-solid reliability of the Falcon 9 temporarily grounded it, leading to concerns that NASA’s launch of the Crew-12 mission to the space station could be delayed.
This was a timely reminder that even the most impressive and reliable of technologies — and, to be clear, the Falcon 9 is both an incredible feat of engineering and outstandingly successful — can have failures or outages. NASA continues to contract with smaller companies like Rocket Lab and Blue Origin, and has repeatedly stressed its desire to have multiple commercial providers for services like transporting astronauts to the space station.
“Even NASA is realizing, okay, we are putting all our bets on a single player,” said space business expert Michele Scataglini of the Oxford Space Initiative and University of Oxford. “The market needs to have more competition, otherwise it’s not a market.”
Whether any of these companies will be able to catch up and provide a meaningful, affordable alternative to SpaceX remains to be seen. It will be hard for any company to keep pace with SpaceX’s sister companies developing complementary technologies as well.
“The complementarity of the assets that SpaceX has built — artificial intelligence, the batteries, the launch capabilities — these are all self-reinforcing capabilities for the firm, that I would say none of the other players alone possesses,” said Scataglini.
Too much power in too few hands
For now, with Starlink access restored in Ukraine, the country will continue to walk the tightrope of trying to defend itself using technology it does not ultimately control. Unlike previous restrictions of Starlink usage there, which were arguably more about limiting offensive capabilities, “what seems to have been impacted in this most recent episode is Ukrainian defensive capability,” said Reddie, the defense expert. “And then you end up with all the harrowing images of apartment blocks on fire and people getting pulled out of the buildings.
“And so that’s the major security challenge, that you’ve effectively got a non-state actor making decisions as if they’re a government.”
Scataglini concurred, describing the events in Ukraine as a global wake-up call. “There’s a single entrepreneur that has more power than governments in deciding how strategic defense capabilities can be used,” he said.
In times of stress and uncertainty — and between ever-climbing costs of living, a decimated social safety net, fears about AI coming for our jobs, and rising global populism and extremism, there’s plenty to be stressed and uncertain about — it is tempting to turn our gazes inward, to look out for our own interests and prioritize the needs of our own nations.
But space does not respect national boundaries, and what happens in orbit around our planet affects us all. The risk, Scataglini said, is that “we are moving into one firm dominating the launch market and deciding who goes up, and who doesn’t. Which country has access to space, and which one does not, because not all nations around the world, especially if you think about the Global South, will have easy access to these capabilities.”
Looking to the future, experts hoped that out of the brutal events in Ukraine could come more public awareness of the dangers of too much power held in too few hands.
“I’m cautiously optimistic that, at least in this case in particular, it is highlighting the dangers of being reliant on a single company, a single individual,” said Whitman Cobb. “It took something bad happening — people dying — for people to realize, oh, wait, maybe there’s a problem here.”

articles.title: Tính giá điện theo giờ: Người dân khó tránh khung giờ đắt đỏ
articles.text:
Dự thảo Luật sửa đổi, bổ sung một số điều của Luật Điện lực có một nội dung đáng chú ý là đề xuất bổ sung cơ chế giá bán lẻ điện theo thời gian sử dụng, gồm giờ cao điểm, thấp điểm và bình thường, trong đó có khách hàng sinh hoạt khi đáp ứng điều kiện kỹ thuật.
Trao đổi với VietNamNet, TS Nguyễn Huy Hoạch, Hội đồng Khoa học Tạp chí Năng lượng Việt Nam, cho rằng giá điện theo thời gian sử dụng có thể tạo động lực tiết kiệm điện. Ngoài việc giảm tổng lượng điện tiêu thụ, người dân có thể chủ động chuyển một số hoạt động sang khung giờ có giá thấp hơn.
Tuy nhiên, hiệu quả của cơ chế này phụ thuộc lớn vào cách thiết kế biểu giá và khả năng thay đổi thời điểm sử dụng điện của từng hộ gia đình.
Giá điện giờ cao điểm quá cao sẽ tăng gánh nặng cho người dân
Theo TS Nguyễn Huy Hoạch, với cơ chế giá điện bậc thang hiện hành, đơn giá tăng theo tổng lượng điện tiêu thụ trong tháng. Trong khi đó, giá điện theo khung giờ cao điểm, thấp điểm và bình thường sẽ tạo động lực để khách hàng dịch chuyển một phần nhu cầu sang giờ thấp điểm.
Những gia đình có thiết bị dễ điều chỉnh thời gian vận hành như máy giặt, bình nước nóng có bảo ôn hoặc thiết bị sạc xe điện có thể chủ động thay đổi thời điểm sử dụng. Đây là nhóm có khả năng phản ứng với tín hiệu giá và tận dụng mức giá thấp hơn để giảm chi phí tiền điện.
Ngược lại, phần lớn nhu cầu thiết yếu của các gia đình thường tập trung vào buổi tối, khi người lớn đi làm về, trẻ em đi học về và các thành viên chuẩn bị bữa ăn, tắm giặt, học tập, nghỉ ngơi. Những hoạt động này gắn với lịch làm việc, học tập và nhịp sống xã hội nên khó thay đổi chỉ vì giá điện.
Nếu giá điện giờ cao điểm được đặt quá cao, hóa đơn tiền điện của nhiều hộ gia đình có thể tăng, trong khi họ không có nhiều khả năng thay đổi thời gian sử dụng điện. Khi đó, gánh nặng chi phí tăng thêm chưa chắc tương xứng với hiệu quả điều tiết phụ tải.
Vì vậy, ông Hoạch cho rằng cần phân biệt giữa nhu cầu thiết yếu khó thay đổi và những hoạt động có thể chủ động điều chỉnh thời điểm sử dụng điện. Chính sách nên tập trung khuyến khích nhóm thứ hai, thay vì đặt kỳ vọng các gia đình thay đổi những sinh hoạt cơ bản.
Theo ông, mức chênh lệch giữa giá điện giờ cao điểm và thấp điểm phải đủ tạo tín hiệu kinh tế, nhưng không nên quá lớn ngay từ đầu. Nếu chênh lệch quá nhỏ, người dân ít có động lực thay đổi. Trường hợp giá giờ cao điểm quá cao trong khi khả năng dịch chuyển phụ tải còn hạn chế, chính sách có thể chủ yếu làm tăng chi phí sinh hoạt thay vì giảm được nhu cầu điện vào thời điểm hệ thống chịu áp lực.
Mức chênh lệch giá cũng không nên được lựa chọn theo cảm tính hoặc chỉ dựa trên kinh nghiệm áp dụng với khách hàng sản xuất, kinh doanh. Cơ quan quản lý cần căn cứ vào biểu đồ phụ tải của toàn hệ thống và hộ gia đình, khả năng điều chỉnh thời gian sử dụng điện cũng như tác động đến hóa đơn của từng nhóm khách hàng.
Cần đánh giá rõ tác động trước khi áp dụng
Theo chuyên gia năng lượng Nguyễn Huy Hoạch, hóa đơn tiền điện tăng hay giảm không chỉ phụ thuộc vào chênh lệch giá giữa giờ cao điểm và thấp điểm. Kết quả còn liên quan đến mức giá điện bình quân, tỷ trọng điện tiêu thụ ở từng khung giờ và cách kết hợp biểu giá theo giờ với cơ chế bậc thang hiện hành.
Giá điện bậc thang và giá điện theo thời gian sử dụng phục vụ những mục tiêu khác nhau. Cơ chế bậc thang khuyến khích tiết kiệm tổng lượng điện, trong khi giá theo giờ hướng đến dịch chuyển thời điểm tiêu thụ. Nếu áp dụng đồng thời, cơ quan quản lý cần làm rõ cách tính để người dân dễ hiểu, dễ dự đoán hóa đơn.
Chuyên gia đề xuất trước khi triển khai trên diện rộng, cần mô phỏng hóa đơn theo nhiều phương án giá và các nhóm hộ có mức tiêu thụ, điều kiện sinh hoạt khác nhau. Việc so sánh trực tiếp hóa đơn theo cơ chế mới với cách tính hiện hành sẽ giúp đánh giá nhóm nào được hưởng lợi, nhóm nào có nguy cơ tăng chi phí.
Bên cạnh đó, cơ quan quản lý có thể nghiên cứu lộ trình áp dụng từng bước, kết hợp hướng dẫn sử dụng điện hiệu quả và khuyến khích người dân tự nguyện điều chỉnh phụ tải. Những hộ có trẻ nhỏ, người cao tuổi hoặc điều kiện sinh hoạt đặc thù cũng cần được tính đến khi đánh giá tác động khi áp khung giờ cao điểm, thấp điểm.
Cũng theo ông Hoạch, nên thí điểm trước khi áp dụng rộng rãi. Việc thí điểm cần thực hiện ở những khu vực có đặc điểm phụ tải và điều kiện sử dụng điện khác nhau, đồng thời xác định rõ các tiêu chí đánh giá như mức giảm phụ tải giờ cao điểm, lượng điện chuyển sang giờ thấp điểm, biến động hóa đơn và chi phí đầu tư hệ thống đo đếm.
Kết quả thí điểm cần được công khai để làm căn cứ điều chỉnh biểu giá và khung giờ. Nếu phụ tải giờ cao điểm giảm không đáng kể nhưng hóa đơn của nhiều hộ tăng, phương án cần được xem xét lại trước khi mở rộng. Ngược lại, nếu hiệu quả điều tiết phụ tải được chứng minh và tác động đến người dân nằm trong giới hạn chấp nhận được, chính sách có thể từng bước nhân rộng.
Chuyên gia cũng lưu ý, có công tơ đáp ứng yêu cầu đo đếm theo giờ chưa đồng nghĩa với việc đã đủ điều kiện áp dụng ngay cho mọi hộ gia đình. Chính sách còn cần dữ liệu phụ tải đáng tin cậy, cơ chế tính giá minh bạch, hệ thống giải đáp khiếu nại và phương án hạn chế những tác động bất lợi đối với nhóm khách hàng khó thay đổi giờ sử dụng điện.
Giá điện tính theo khung giờ có thể là một công cụ quản lý nhu cầu điện, nhưng không phải giải pháp duy nhất để giảm áp lực phụ tải giờ cao điểm. Theo ông, chính sách giá cần được triển khai trong tổng thể các giải pháp về nguồn điện, truyền tải, lưu trữ năng lượng và quản lý nhu cầu, với mục tiêu vừa nâng cao hiệu quả vận hành hệ thống, vừa giữ chi phí điện sinh hoạt ở mức hợp lý cho người dân.

articles.title: Bose CEO says Skullcandy reaches buyers Bose is ‘largely missing’
articles.text:
Bose bought Skullcandy on Wednesday, the company said in a statement. The seller was a fund managed by Mill Road Capital Management, a private investment firm in Connecticut. Skullcandy joins McIntosh and Sonus faber in Bose’s group of audio brands.
Skullcandy will sit inside Bose’s Premium Consumer Audio business. It keeps its base in Park City, Utah, where it started on a chairlift in 2003. Bose said it plans to give the brand more access to its technology, resources and global distribution.
“As a privately held company, we have the freedom to make bold, long-term investments in opportunities we believe in, and Skullcandy is a great example of that,” Bose chief executive Lila Snyder said in the statement.
“We believe this is a win for Skullcandy and our fans,” Skullcandy chief executive Brian Garofalow said.
Partners first
The two companies already worked together. Skullcandy designs the headphones and Bose handles the audio, Harry Rabinowitz reported for Wired. Bose licenses that audio under the Sound by Bose name.
The partnership began with the Method 360 ANC earbuds in 2025. The Crusher 1080 ANC noise-cancelling headphones followed in July. TechRadar saw a newer pair, the Noise Master Buds Open, at IFA in Berlin last month, Tom Bedford wrote.
The customers Bose wants
Bose said Skullcandy’s roots in boardsports open new ways to reach consumers “where it has less presence today.” Skullcandy also has a following in music, gaming and fitness, Bose said.
“Skullcandy gives us access to a customer base that we think we’re largely missing with the Bose brand,” Snyder told Wired.
Snyder told Wired that Park City is the centre of board sports culture, which is why Skullcandy is staying there. Skullcandy’s products also cost less than those of Bose and its other brands, Wired reported. Snyder also discussed younger buyers, wired headphones and AI with Romaine Bostick on Bloomberg.
Engadget’s Ian Carlos Campbell compared the deal to Apple’s 2014 purchase of Beats. Dr Dre and Jimmy Iovine co-founded Beats, and Apple sells it beside its own AirPods. Campbell wrote that Skullcandy could be “the Beats to Bose’s Apple.”
Bose’s third deal this year
Skullcandy is Bose’s third acquisition of 2026. In June it bought StreamUnlimited Engineering, a Vienna company that makes streaming software and modules for connected audio products. On 1 October it bought Firelight Technologies, the Melbourne maker of the FMOD audio software for games.
Bose’s president of premium audio, Raza Haider, spoke to Becky Scarrott of TechRadar weeks before the deal. He said Bose wants its technology in as many places as possible.
“One brand can’t cover every single passion point, otherwise it becomes a plain vanilla tech giant,” Haider said.

articles.title: The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
articles.text:
We gave the iPhone Duo a 7 /10. But that wasn’t always the score we planned, and it might not be the right score forever. Such are the challenges of reviewing — and assessing — a big, new idea about the most popular smartphone in history.
The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
On The Vergecast: Notes on an iPhone Duo review, a PHP scandal, Brendan Carr, and more.
On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate whether the Duo deserved the score it got, and try to work through how this device might change over time. Is the outer screen, as Daring Fireball’s John Gruber suggested, the worst iPhone ever? Would it be a better product if it started as an iPad rather than an iPhone? Would we feel differently about this thing if it were simply called the iPad Duo? It’s easy to see how the Duo will improve over time, but will it ever be the phone for everyone?
After that, the hosts talk about the huge PHP cybersecurity flaw that rocked the web this week and what it means for the future of the web, AI, and everything. It was a strange week for the web in general, as the ongoing increase in AI shopping has forced retailers everywhere to figure out how they want to interact with customers — and by customers, we mean Muse agents. Then it’s time for Brendan Carr Is a Dummy, an impending reboot inside of Netflix, and some very confusing Gemini news.

articles.title: Unitree’s founder says AI will ‘undoubtedly surpass humans’
articles.text:
Unitree Robotics is building a system that lets its humanoid robots improve themselves, founder Wang Xingxing said on Thursday. He calls it Unitree Rehearsal. He named it the company’s most important project of the year, Minxiao Chang reported for the South China Morning Post. Wang spoke at a physical AI conference that Unitree hosted in Hangzhou.
Under the plan, AI would search research papers, write code and test it in simulation before trials on real robots, according to the SCMP. Unitree already uses AI this way and then collects feedback from real tests to adjust its models, Bloomberg reported.
A breakthrough as soon as 2028
Wang also moved his timeline forward. He now expects humanoids to complete 80% of tasks set by voice as soon as 2028, Bloomberg reported. That covers work in factories or homes, according to a transcript Unitree shared with Bloomberg. Wang calls that point the “aha” moment for practical robots. TNW has not seen the transcript.
In August, at the World Robot Conference in Beijing, Wang said robots were nearing a “ChatGPT moment”. At the same event he said mass use in factories and homes could take 10 years, according to Bloomberg.
“If you take a humanoid home now and ask it to clean the room, honestly I don’t think it can complete that task,” Wang said in the transcript.
He said recent advances in AI models such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 changed his mind.
“I had some skepticism about AI model developers last year,” he said.
This year, he said, the most advanced developers have begun letting their models improve themselves.
“As long as you give a frontier model data and time, it will undoubtedly surpass humans in many areas,” he said.
This week, Recursive released a coding model that was largely built by AI.
Wang said Unitree’s humanoids running GPT-6 can now paint, changing colours and rinsing the palette, and play Go. Unitree plans to expand production to meet possible demand for tens of millions of robots. It makes tens of thousands a year today, Bloomberg reported. Wang said Unitree is building its own models while working with AI labs in China and abroad.
A robot bodyguard
On Wednesday, Unitree posted a one-minute video of the H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian. In it, the humanoid punches and knees cars in a scrapyard. It also confronts an intruder holding a knife and lifts a car to free a trapped person.
The robot runs for approximately eight hours, Unitree said in its post on X. It can jump from a four-metre platform, according to Mark Wilson at TechRadar. Unitree has given no price or release date. It builds on the H2, which costs $29,900. TechRadar wrote that the H2-X would struggle to pass the safety certification needed to sell as a personal bodyguard.
The video labels the scenes “extreme testing” and warns against imitating them, Mike Pearl reported for Gizmodo. Unitree’s post asks people to use the robot “safely and in a friendly manner.”
Shares and funding
Unitree’s shares rose five-fold on their Shanghai debut in August and are now about a quarter below their August peak, Bloomberg reported. Chinese venture and state funds have put more than 100bn yuan ($15bn) into robotics startups this year, according to the tracker ITjuzi. China has also reportedly slowed humanoid IPOs since then. For now, humanoids sell mainly to researchers and enthusiasts, Bloomberg noted.

articles.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.text:
Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority, adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”
Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.
That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.
Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.
This is what the policy says:
“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”
“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”
If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

articles.title: OpenClaw’s Peter Steinberger spent about $10M on tokens in a month
articles.text:
Peter Steinberger created the open-source AI agent OpenClaw and now works at OpenAI. He estimates he spent about $10M on AI tokens last month. He said so on stage at Cloudflare’s Connect conference in San Francisco on Wednesday, Thomas Claburn reported for The Register. Tokens are the units AI companies use to charge for the text a model reads and writes.
Steinberger was in a session on AI agents with Cloudflare’s chief technology officer, Dane Knecht. Knecht noted that Steinberger has said he has an almost unlimited budget for tokens.
“A virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have,” Knecht said.
The audience reacted with surprise, according to The Register.
“What people don’t always understand is not all of that is useful,” Steinberger said.
Accenture caps its staff’s Claude spending at $29 a month. OpenAI, meanwhile, is reportedly racing to close a $30bn funding round before Anthropic’s IPO.
Agents in the cloud, agents checking agents
Steinberger said the main problem for many people is that infrastructure has not caught up yet.
“Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn’t this all be in the cloud?” he said.
Nvidia’s new RTX Spark laptops, launched last week, are built to run AI agents locally.
Knecht asked how people should decide what data to give an agent. Steinberger said it depends partly on the model itself. Much of a model’s behaviour does not come from the code that wraps it, he said. Even with risks such as prompt injection reduced, he would not give an agent every permission.
“You want to have another agent that can give it permissions or not and then this agent has to negotiate with another agent,” he said.
He said the agents often back down or find a simpler route within the guardrails. Together, the two systems make him far more willing to let the agent work alone.
A token bill he has talked about before
Steinberger joined OpenAI in February. In a blog post at the time, he wrote that OpenClaw would move to a foundation and stay open source. He has spoken about his token use since.
“Last year I was constrained by token. Now I fixed that by joining OpenAI,” he told an agentic engineering meetup in San Francisco in June.
At Y Combinator’s Startup School in August, he was asked when AI agents will run all the time and work on their own. He said the limit is cost, because few people are willing to spend that many tokens.
“That’s not so much a tech problem. It’s more a token problem,” he said.
Open source and the future
Knecht raised the frustration of open-source maintainers who have stopped accepting AI-written code. Steinberger said the process should change, because contributors rarely explain how they reached their code.
“If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher,” he said.
He also doubts that everyone will run hundreds of agents in a few years. He expects each person to have one intelligence that helps them through the day and may even predict what they need. Meta has said its Muse agent looks like OpenClaw because it was built that way.

articles.title: The first broken iPhone Duos are here
articles.text:
The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale today, but a few units already have broken screens. According to posts on Reddit about the affected units, the issue appears to be happening at a similar spot on all of them: Some kind of problem shows up on the inner screen along the hinge and a strange bright line (or lines) across the right side of the display.
The first broken iPhone Duos are here
Now that the first folding iPhone has launched, we’ll find out quickly what can go wrong.
Here’s how one user in Australia described what happened to their phone:
Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.
I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.
As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.
There were no marks or damage on the inner screen’s surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user said that the Apple Store replaced their phone with “a brand-new one on the spot.”
A post showing an image of another broken screen includes a video in a comment demonstrating yet another.
And a separate Reddit thread collected other pictures of affected Duos.
Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

articles.title: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields
articles.text:
Moody's opted to maintain its credit rating on France as the country contended with a week of civil unrest and rising political risk.
The agency kept France's credit rating at Aa3, a level Moody's still deems "high grade," but it also maintained its negative outlook on the nation.
"The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report.
Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow the deficit.
Investors were anticipating Moody's rating decision as France, the second-largest economy in the euro zone, grappled with protests and a sharp surge in bond yields.
"This political instability, also visible in the current social tensions, risks hampering the French government's ability to address key policy challenges such as an elevated fiscal deficit, rising debt burden, and durable increase in borrowing costs, thus leading to a more rapid weakening in the sovereign's key credit metrics than we currently expect," Moody's said in its report Friday.
This week, the nation's 10-year bond yield surpassed 5% for the first time since 2002. The spread against German bunds is also at a 15-year peak.
Currently, France's deficit-to-GDP ratio is at roughly 5.5% of its GDP, sharply above the 3% limit for member nations in the European Union. The country faces more than $1 trillion of debt that will mature by 2030. Just a month ago, the French finance ministry warned that the nation's debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to hit 121.7% in 2027.
At the same time, France has been rocked by protests. Last weekend, more than 500,000 people marched to express their frustration against declining public services and high costs of living.
S&P Global and Fitch cut their ratings on France in 2025.

articles.title: Turmoil hits AI build-out as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
articles.text:
Neoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared. Meta turned cash flow negative. And SK Hynix's Solidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.
It's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade.
The Nasdaq followed Thursday's beating with an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer was Alphabet, shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.
While the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence build-out is showing signs of strain.
Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN all fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack, has seen spreads on its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.
Meanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15%.
"What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday.
Fears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider, dropped 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast.
AI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.
Analysts at research and advisory firm Gartner predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, perhaps the leading AI evangelist remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that "demand for the neoclouds is off the charts."
"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal. "That's going to get solved."
Withdrawn IPO
Wall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giant SK Hynix, one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it's pulling an IPO for its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK Hynix purchased Solidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, from Intel in 2021.
"While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends," SK Hynix said in a release.
Despite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.
Meta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter of over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.
Spreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS on Nvidia and Oracle also touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. Oracle's stock has lost over one-third of its value this year, and now the company faces risks of a credit rating downgrade.
John Williams, who leads the derivatives practice at law firm Milbank LLP, says investors are seeking numerous ways beyond buying CDS to hedge their bets with respect to the AI trade.
"There's so much investment going into it that it's just very appropriate to look for risk management tools, completely regardless of whether you're bullish or bearish," Williams said. "It would be crazy for people not to be looking for appropriate risk management tools for it."
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told CNBC's "SquawkBox Asia" last week that it's "all kind of tied together," referring to AI's impact on the whole market.
"Can you drop a bowling ball in one part of the pool and not get any waves downstream to the rest of the Nasdaq?" he said. "I don't know. I have some concern about that."
— CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this report

articles.title: Scalpers offer Apple iPhone Duo buyers hundreds extra outside Beijing launch
articles.text:
The iPhone Duo has an eye-popping price tag, but initial interest in Apple's first foldable phone in China appears solid.
On the day of the global launch on Friday, scalpers like Alex Wang stood outside the flagship store in Beijing's popular shopping area, Sanlitun, offering to pay customers an extra 3,000 Chinese yuan ($448) to buy their newly purchased phones on the spot.
"I feel the Duo can be sold with a higher price for half a month," he told CNBC while watching the lines of Duo customers who had pre-booked their phones. "The main reason is the tight supply."
Though foldables are still a niche product globally, China's market is the single largest, according to Counterpoint Research.
Apple fan Mary Tong, who was first in a line of about 100 people at the Sanlitun store, showed up at 6 a.m. to pick up her foldable device.
"Apple has been the laggard," she said. "I think many Chinese do prefer foldable phones."
Huawei is promoting its own AI assistant XiaoYi to boost the Chinese smartphone maker's competitiveness against Apple and other homegrown rivals. Huawei, which already has a broad lineup of foldable phones, launched a new trifold called the Mate XT2 that is priced at about $3,000 on Sept. 7, two days before Apple's Duo announcement.
China's Xiaomi unveiled its own pricey foldable, the 18 Fold, around the same time.
Even before the Beijing Apple store's regular opening hours, customers without a reservation showed up to test their luck to get their hands on the new phone. Apple had said the Duo would not be available for walk-in purchase on launch day in mainland China and would be "limited" in other countries. Each online purchase was restricted to two phones.
Zhang Zheng said he had tried to order one on the site but was discouraged by the delivery timeline, which stretched to January 2027. He said he still wants to buy one.
"I think it will be useful for work and it's cool to look at," he said.
While there was buzz about the device itself, expectations for Apple Intelligence were negligible. The company said a version of the AI system is set for beta testing this month for the mainland China market and will include features like live translation, Clean Up in photos, and writing tools.
On Oct. 14, Beijing approved Alibaba AI models for use in Duo and other Apple devices as part of the U.S. tech giant's pending AI rollout in the country. Apple received Chinese regulatory clearance over the summer.
Chinese official media cited ex-CEO Tim Cook on a recent China trip as saying Apple's revamped Siri AI would not be available in the country yet.
Duo customer John Zhao said he had tried Apple Intelligence while working overseas, and it was "nice but not beyond imagination." He expects the Chinese version to be less exciting.

articles.title: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
articles.text:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that aims to reduce mortgage costs as rising interest rates and inflation make homeownership less affordable.
The order, titled "Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People," directs federal agencies to proactively cancel mortgage insurance on eligible future loans and expand a program to make refinancing cheaper, among other actions.
In an X post on Thursday, Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte said "millions of Americans will save thousands and thousands of dollars."
But it's difficult to know the future consumer impact without more details, according to Keith Gumbinger, vice president of mortgage website HSH.
Trump's executive order comes less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with rising costs and housing affordability a major concern among voters. It builds on previous orders to restrict Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes, among other actions.
Homeownership has become less affordable in recent years. In 2025, the monthly payment for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage on a median-priced home was roughly 33% of the median family's income, up from 26% in 2022, according to the Federal Reserve's latest Survey of Consumer Finances published in early October.
Whether you're a current homeowner or future buyer, here are some of the key things to know about the new executive order.
Mortgage insurance changes
Conventional loans — mortgages not insured or backed by U.S. government programs — typically require private mortgage insurance, or PMI, when a down payment is less than 20% of the home's purchase price. By contrast, Federal Housing Administration mortgages require mortgage insurance on all loans.
Trump's executive order directs the FHFA to create a pilot program that cancels eligible borrowers' mortgage insurance "proactively" once their home equity reaches a certain threshold, according to the White House. This would apply to mortgages originated after the pilot program launches.
Currently, conventional loan borrowers can generally remove PMI once their loan balance is below 80% of the purchase price or once they have reached 20% equity, according to Fannie Mae. Once your balance reaches 80% of the original value, you can ask your loan servicer if you're eligible to remove PMI, or they may remove it automatically when your balance reaches 78% of the original value.
In a statement Thursday, Seth Appleton, president of U.S. mortgage insurers, an industry trade organization, said: "We commend the President's focus on lowering costs for future homeowners, and the private mortgage insurance industry is proud to already be delivering on that goal."
Typically, the cost of PMI can be 0.2% to 2% of the loan annually, but varies based on your down payment size, credit score, amount borrowed and other factors, according to Fannie Mae.
For example, if you purchased a $600,000 home with a 10% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 7.3%, your monthly mortgage insurance could be $351, according to a private mortgage calculator from Freddie Mac.
"Most mortgages ... are carrying PMI at this point in time, especially with the way home prices have been and down payments being as small as they've been in recent years," Gumbinger said.
During the second quarter of 2026, the median home down payment was 13.7% of the home's purchase price, or $27,100, according to a September report from Realtor.com.
Mortgage refinancing costs
Trump's executive order also aims to reduce mortgage refinancing costs by making permanent the FHFA's pilot program that waives the lender's title insurance policy and allows "cost-friendly alternatives," according to the White House.
"I don't know that it's necessarily a game-changer in terms of the cost of housing, which is dictated by home price and mortgage rates at the moment," Gumbinger said. "But you know, every little bit certainly helps."
As of Oct. 23, mortgage interest rates for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages were 7.32%, according to Freddie Mac, and refinance demand was down 59% in mid-October, compared with the same week the previous year.
Originally planned through November 2027, the FHFA pilot was "limited in scope," for refinances with a loan-to-value ratio below 80%, in a handful of states, former FHFA director Sandra Thompson said during a congressional hearing in April 2024.
Thompson estimated that consumers could save $500 to $1,500 in closing costs for loans sold under the pilot program.
Making the program permanent could save borrowers because the lender's title insurance policy, which is usually required for new loans and refinances, "has always been fairly pricey," Gumbinger said.
The lender's fees related to title and title insurance generally make up the largest share of mortgage closing costs, according to a 2025 Urban Institute report.

articles.title: Meta shares are down 9% this week. Here's why Mike Khouw is buying now
articles.text:
Size is a relative matter. The standard Manhattan apartment would seem almost claustrophobic compared to the vast expanses offered by suburban living. A similar dynamic is playing out in the market.
Mega-cap companies are generally defined as those with market capitalizations exceeding $200 billion. Of course, the largest companies are another order of magnitude larger than that. For example, Meta, which reported stellar earnings this week, has a current market capitalization of $1.65 trillion.
But concerns about its AI buildout expenses wiped $135 billion from its market cap in just four sessions, or put another way, roughly the value on and entire Uber. Market cap is one way to understand how big these companies are, but another is by examining the size of their operations, and their opportunities.
Consider Muse.
Meta's personal AI agent is designed to be more of an active digital assistant than a conventional conversational chatbot. Muse can open browsers, fill out forms, send emails, schedule appointments, book travel, and (potentially) even make purchases.
To understand how large an economic opportunity this represents for the company, consider what something like that might be worth. $5 per month per user? (Not in subscription fees necessarily, mind you, just monetizable economic value). That seems a bit low for something so powerful. $10/month? Quite realistically. Then consider the size of Meta's ecosystem's daily active user base across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. That number is truly "mega": 3.6 billion, supposedly counting each person only once. If we assume that each of those individuals has and uses a global phone - 5.86 billion unique people on the planet do - that means Meta interacts at least once with 61.4% of them each day.
If Muse is worth $120/year and reaches just 1% of Meta's Daily Active People, that's $4.3 billion/year. If it's worth half that amount, but reaches 20% of their daily actives, that's $43.2 billion/year. The first number seems absurdly low as a back-of-the-napkin figure, but the $135 billion valuation loss in less than a week is offset by $20 billion in revenue (the company trades at just under 7x revenue). If Muse can generate $30 billion in revenues, it is a megacap company in its own right!
So why has the company sold off if everything is so rosy? A massive $25 billion lawsuit in New Mexico, a potential PR headache related to a deal struck between the company and its founder to resolve potential tax liabilities associated with a possible billionaire's tax in California that preserves his voting rights, and, of course, concerns about debt, on the balance sheet and off, to finance the enormous investment that the company is making (and expanding) in AI, and AI jitters generally. But at 20x FY earnings, and less than 17x FY2027 estimated earnings, the company is now pricing a lot of that in. Those headaches create headwinds, but the underlying story provides support.
The trade
I like selling December strangles here, specifically the 580/745 strangle, for which one would collect about $21.30/share as of today's closing prices. The trade makes profits virtually anywhere between the 1-year highs and lows - and it's pretty much right in the middle of that range now.

articles.title: Apple is set to take back the market-cap crown from Nvidia. Upcoming earnings may push it over the top
articles.text: Apple is set to leapfrog Nvidia and reclaim its title as the world's largest company as tech investors embrace consumer hardware again. Apple's upcoming strong earnings may be the catalyst that pushes it over the top. Apple on Friday was trading at a market value of $5.05 trillion, compared to $5.10 trillion for Nvidia. Apple shares are having a great October — up 4% — as concerns about the AI financing environment drag Nvidia down 7% for the month. Apple's market value briefly surpassed Nvidia in July, before falling back below. The new iPhone Duo hits stores Friday , with customers lining up to get their hands on it. Enthusiasm around that event has helped push the shares to an all-time high this week as the rest of the tech sector suffers. Apple is currently one of the top five holdings in our Essential 40 ETF . The iPhone Duo is a premium product, starting at $1,999 and climbing above $3,000 for the highest-storage model. That's a much different story from Apple's recent focus on lower-priced models in international markets. Demand has been strong. Preorders sold out almost immediately after opening Oct. 16, with some delivery estimates stretching into January. Apple has reportedly even raised its production targets. That's a sign that Apple's hardware business is coming back to life, particularly at the high end of the market. Earnings ahead As exciting as the Duo launch is, I'm curious to see what happens when Apple reports earnings on Nov. 2. Revenue expectations are around $113 billion, following Apple's earlier guidance for 9% to 11% year-over-year growth. I'll be watching what management says about iPhone demand, but Apple's services business could be the catalyst that keeps the wind in its sails. Services generated about $109 billion in revenue in fiscal 2025, accounting for only about a quarter of Apple's business. Yet it carries gross margins of approximately 75%, compared with roughly 37% for hardware. That means services contribute more than 40% of Apple's total gross profit despite making up a much smaller share of revenue. Could Apple lead the market again? For a while, Apple has been viewed more as a defensive, quality-growth investment while Nvidia and other AI stocks captured investors' attention. Now with Apple leading the Magnificent Seven and closing in on Nvidia's valuation, I think the market may be starting to recognize the strength of its broader business. The question is whether Apple can reclaim its old role as the stock that sets the tone for the entire market. With hardware demand picking up and earnings just around the corner, I wouldn't be surprised if Apple once again becomes the company everyone is watching. Jeff Kilburg is the founder and CEO of KKM Financial. articles.title: Next week brings major risks for the stock market, just as the AI trade keeps faltering
articles.text: Next week will bring major risks for a stock market that's trying to find its footing as the AI trade continues to stumble, with several megacap earnings, a Federal Reserve meeting and a key inflation report in store. Wall Street is heading into the thick of earnings season, with 163 S & P 500 companies set to report results next week. Chief among them are financial updates from Alphabet , Amazon and Microsoft , the next hyperscalers to release earnings after Meta Platforms and Tesla found a surprisingly poor reception this past week, dragging down the broader market in their wake. "The fact that the market has skepticism around potential good news in the technology space, particularly, that's worth watching," said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at the investment management group at Nationwide. "That's why I'm really curious to see how next week goes." Meta's results unnerved investors who worried about the sustainability of the social media giant's AI spending plans. The stock slumped more than 9% this week, after reporting negative free cash flow for the first time ever going back to its public debut. On Thursday, the spread on Meta's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs, adding further to fears. Tesla eventually ended the week higher, up about 5%, after initially falling after its results showed enormous investments into emerging technology verticals. Questioning AI sustainability That has added to fear that the hyperscalers reporting next week will also disclose news of heightened capital spending, perhaps by as much as $100 billion, according to Mark Mahaney, who heads Evercore's Internet research team. Alphabet and Microsoft report next Wednesday, and Amazon posts results Thursday. But the latest slide in stocks could also mean that investors have already priced bad news into those companies, Mahaney said. Alphabet shares are down by more than 5% this week. Amazon and Microsoft are each down by about 1%. "The market fear is now in the stock," Mahaney said. If the two companies were to announce they did not need to raise capital, or announce just a modest equity or debt deal, the stocks could actually rise, he added. Those results could determine just where the tech trade ends October. On Friday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was set to close out the month down by more than 3%, with the S & P 500 also lower. The Dow Jones Industrial Average alone is set to end the month higher, by nearly 3%. There's also just greater division among the tech stocks. Semiconductors have been crushed, down more than 15% this month. Memory stocks plunged more than 20%. The Magnificent Seven companies are down more than 2%. But software stocks, and cybersecurity names in particular, are set to end the month with gains. Fed credibility, PCE Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh will have to strike a delicate balance next Wednesday when he takes the podium at the press conference following the Fed's next policy meeting, according to Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon. If the central bank holds rates steady at their current 3.75% to 4.00%, as is widely expected , Warsh will have to explain the pause to a room full of reporters. The Fed had signaled at the September meeting that it was unanimous in taking inflation seriously. In the weeks since, the economic data has shown that inflation is moving still further away from the Fed's 2% target, as surging gas and diesel prices pile on pressure. But a weak September jobs report , and a succession of Fed officials signaling a patient view of higher interest rates, have curbed expectations of a rate hike at the Oct. 27-28 meeting. Those skeptical officials who have expressed little need for urgency include Fed Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams. That heightens the stakes for chairman Warsh, who has expressed a preference for fewer words at a time when investors may prefer clearer communication. "I think there is growing pressure on the Fed to deliver upon its words. It's not sufficient to be talking a tough game on the inflation front and reiterating your commitment to price stability," Daco said. "If you don't deliver upon those commitments, then markets will start to question your credibility." The Fed meeting on Wednesday will be followed the next day by the release of the central bank's preferred inflation gauge. The September reading for the personal consumption expenditure price index is projected to have risen 0.5%, slower than the prior month's reading of 0.9%. But core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, is expected to have risen 3.1% over the past year, up from 3.0% previously. Split between tech and everything else On the surface, the third quarter earnings season is bearing out as expected. Of the S & P 500 companies that have reported thus far, 82% have beaten expectations. When results are over, the broad market index is set to have posted earnings growth of roughly 30% versus the third quarter a year ago. It's the latest continuation of a historic earnings boom that is virtually unprecedented considering that companies are not coming out of the throes of some economic calamity, but instead building on AI momentum. And, it continues to suggest the market can continue to do well, especially as it heads into the best six months on the calendar, from November through April. The recent increase in bearish sentiment may also suggest equities are due for a near-term pop. Still, the weakness in tech bears watching, as any further cracks in the AI trade could mean a tech-fueled selloff. Nationwide's Hackett expects that technology will continue to underperform, having already absorbed the bulk of the gains from AI. But he also said the rest of the market remains in "good shape," and he plans to stick with stocks that may have been overly punished and could start outperforming. "We're in a coiled spring moment right now, where the outcome is very likely to be positive," Hackett said. Week ahead calendar All times ET. articles.title: CrowdStrike CEO's alarming prediction — plus, the sell-off spreads beyond tech
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks are lower as this week's selling goes beyond tech. The Dow is the big loser Friday, down more than 1% as defensive stocks join what has largely been a weaker AI trade this week. There are some bright spots in technology, like cybersecurity and chip stocks, keeping the sector modestly in the green on the day but not enough to keep the S & P 500 and Nasdaq out of the red. Club names Micron and Intel are higher. The only other positive sector is energy, which is having a strong session. That's because oil prices are surging on rising tensions in the Middle East. The U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude is above $103 per barrel. International Brent topped $116 for a six-month high. These elevated oil levels and recently hotter government price data are keeping inflation fears front and center ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting. According to the CME FedWatch tool, the odds are pretty low, just over 10%, for an interest rate hike Wednesday afternoon following the central bank's two-day gathering. The market puts the chances of a December rate increase at nearly 78%. If that happens, it would be the Fed's second rate hike in 2026 following the one in September, which was the first in three years. For the week, the Dow is modestly higher, while the S & P 500 and Nasdaq are modestly lower. Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are our winners Friday and for the week. The reason? Researchers discovered that AI could exploit security flaws in PHP, a programming language used on nearly 70% of websites, among the most widely used server-side languages. The vulnerabilities had been known for years, but exploiting them was considered too difficult and time-consuming for hackers. AI changed that, figuring out how to break into vulnerable servers, potentially steal sensitive information, and take control of websites. The discovery prompted urgent government warnings and a rush to install security fixes after details of the vulnerabilities leaked ahead of schedule. "This affects tens of millions of internet-facing servers," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz told CNBC on Friday. Although patches were released Wednesday, many outdated versions of PHP are still in use, and the patch almost certainly didn't fix all of PHP's problems. "You're going to see a lot of breaches happening in the coming months from this," Kurtz warned. The bigger takeaway is that AI is making sophisticated cyberattacks easier and cheaper to carry out, increasing the need for advanced cybersecurity defenses. Kurtz said AI-powered attacks observed by CrowdStrike doubled each month from July through September. "It almost becomes unsustainable unless you're using defensive AI to be able to combat what the offense is doing, and that's what CrowdStrike is focused on," he said. That growing threat reinforces our conviction in cybersecurity as a long-term AI winner. Our decision Friday to trim CrowdStrike after a strong rally was strictly about right-sizing our position, not a change in confidence in the business. CrowdStrike's weighting in our portfolio had swelled to nearly 5%. The trim brought it back down to 4.25% and secured a gain of roughly 187% on stock purchased in late 2024. Next week is the busiest of earnings season . About a third of the S & P 500 is scheduled to report quarterly results, including 11 companies in the portfolio. articles.title: In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
articles.text:
After SpaceX restricted use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect and drop out of the sky, Kyiv is looking for alternatives.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said on Thursday that it has signed a letter of intent to develop new defense and satellite communication capabilities in partnership with Finnish tech companies Nokia and ICEYE, which makes satellites.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."
Zelenskyy also announced a partnership with Norway this week to jointly develop air defense and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield.
Chad Anderson, founder and CEO of venture capital firm Space Capital, said such an alternative could be "two to three years away" and that "matching Starlink's scale is a longer road."
SpaceX has around around 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan McDowell.
Anderson said Starshield may be an even tougher service to replace. "The Pentagon's own contracting documents say SpaceX is the only provider that can meet some of its needs through 2026. Capital isn't the constraint any more. Launch is."
Even Starlink competitors have relied on SpaceX launches to put their satellites in orbit.
As of Friday, Ukraine officials said the country is still experiencing restrictions on Starlink, which cut connectivity for drones or other aircraft traveling at speeds over 100 mph.
Both the Trump administration and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have shirked responsibility for the unannounced Starlink service changes that Ukraine reported more than a week ago. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he would call on Musk to lift the restrictions.
SpaceX executives didn't respond to a request for comment.
Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties are calling for a formal probe of Musk and SpaceX regarding the alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.
Jay Shambaugh, a senior fellow at Brookings and professor of economics and international affairs at George Washington University, told CNBC in an email that the sudden Starlink changes are "part of a pattern since Trump came back into office of the United States acting as an unreliable ally."
Shambaugh cautioned that, "over time, that can reduce U.S. exports to the EU if those countries don't want to be dependent on something where the U.S. can cut them off."
Rivals to Starlink are on the horizon, including Amazon's Leo, France's Eutelsat and a forthcoming service from Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin called TeraWave, which has yet to deploy its first satellites.
Beyond Ukraine, several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS², a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but its first launches aren't expected until 2029.
Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, venture and private equity investors have poured about $8 billion into Starlink and Starshield alternatives, according to research by Anderson, whose firm tracks industry deals. About $3.9 billion of that funding has gone to potential Starlink competitors, mostly Spacesail and China SatNet.
Virginia Burger, senior defense policy analyst with the Project on Government Oversight, told CNBC in an interview that the problem today is there's no drop-in replacement for Starlink, and combat is moving more into "unmanned systems, drone warfare and other systems that require high-speed internet."
— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed reporting.
