articles.title: Trump dropping some Canada tariffs but 'replacing' them with other products
articles.text:
The White House on Friday said it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods, but replace them with other products from the major U.S. trade partner.
The move was revealed after Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, took credit for pushing the Trump administration to issue tariff exemptions on several categories of Canadian imports she says are "crucial" for her state's industries.
But Collins' announcement, which The Wall Street Journal first reported, did not mention that while tariffs would be removed for some Canadian products, new ones would be added to the list of goods subject to steep U.S. duties. The White House announced the new tariffs less than an hour after Collins touted the new exemptions to the tariffs, which are unpopular in the state where she's fighting for reelection.
President Donald Trump earlier Friday signed a proclamation "removing certain products" from the list of items that he slapped 50% tariffs on over the summer using a 96-year-old trade law.
But he is "replacing those products with certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others," according to a White House fact sheet detailing the proclamation.
The changes are being made to "further refine the scope of the tariffs on certain Canadian products," according to the fact sheet, which does not mention Maine.
The new additions and removals from the list of goods covered by the "Section 338" tariffs will take effect Oct. 30, four days before the Nov. 3 U.S. election, the fact sheet said.
Asked what Collins had agreed to in her conversations pushing Trump administration officials for lower tariffs on products affecting her state, her spokeswoman Phoebe Keller told CNBC that the senator "requested exemptions for products that are important to Maine and will continue to do so."
Before the fact sheet was made public, Collins' office sent a press release crediting the senator with securing the new tariff exemptions on "nine categories of products crucial for Maine's agricultural industries."
That announcement came as voters have already started casting ballots in the pivotal Maine Senate race, where Trump's unpopular tariffs have been a top issue.
Collins' Democratic opponent, fifth-generation Maine logger Troy Jackson, quickly pushed back, insisting Collins deserves blame for enabling Trump's tariff policies.
"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire," Jackson said in a statement.
Trump has slapped heavy tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods during his second term as president as he has escalated a trade war against the top U.S. economic partner. Many of those tariffs have put considerable strain on businesses in Maine, which imports far more products from Canada than from any other country.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement Friday afternoon that Trump's latest tariff proclamation is part of his efforts to "address Canada's discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce."
"The President is taking action in response to Canada's continued discrimination against and additional retaliation targeting U.S. commerce, with the goal of protecting American farmers, manufacturers, and workers," said Middleton. "This administration will continue to use every available tool to restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships and safeguard the economic prosperity and national security of the American people."
Collins has previously touted her efforts to push back on the president's protectionist trade policies. In the first televised debate between Collins and Jackson on Oct. 6, the GOP incumbent took credit for removing some items from Trump's list of tariffs on Canadian goods, including road salt.
Jackson fired back, "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt."
In her press release Friday, Collins said she has asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "for tariff relief" for the Maine-centric products, stressing the "burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families."
"I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner," she said.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Mexico is the largest U.S. trading partner.
The products being exempted from the Section 338 tariffs include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and packing bags, refrigeration equipment, multiple forms of machinery and seaweed and algae products, according to Collins.

articles.title: Kinder Morgan, Energy Transfer and Williams could benefit from cheap natural gas
articles.text: U.S. natural gas prices are down about 24% this year while the amount in storage sits slightly above the five-year average. Midstream operators can benefit from higher throughput because much of their revenue comes from fees tied to transporting and processing gas. Kinder Morgan, Energy Transfer and Williams are the three pipeline operators highlighted for their scale, networks and exposure to natural gas demand. Cheap natural gas is pressuring drillers, but the pipeline operators that process and transport the gas are making a killing. When natural gas prices are depressed and supply is overflowing, the physical volume of gas moving through the country's pipelines will respond to satisfy the surging power demands of industrial hubs and, increasingly, artificial intelligence data centers. This puts midstream infrastructure giants like Kinder Morgan , Energy Transfer LP and Williams Companies in a sweet spot. Natural gas prices have collapsed almost 28% year-to-date, with about 15% decline this week alone. The November contract was down 5.2% Friday, to $2.65 per million British thermal units. For most commodities, one would suspect that lower prices would result in less production. But about 37% of the U.S. gas pulled from the ground in 2024 was an unavoidable byproduct of rigs drilling in the nation's five major oil producing regions, according to the Energy Information Administration . As this year's higher crude oil prices made drilling more lucrative, the associated volumes of gas coming to market have also risen, regardless of the commodity's price or demand. Unseasonably mild weather has added to the glut and pushed natural gas stockpiles above the historical five-year average of 3,609 billion cubic feet, the EIA said Thursday. Natural gas in storage rose by 77 Bcf in the week ended Oct. 16 from the prior week, to 3,644 Bcf. Yet, the glut is moving through a largely fixed network. Interstate pipeline construction has been effectively choked off by aggressive regulatory litigation and environmental gridlock, which means existing infrastructure operates as a collection of high-barrier, government-sanctioned monopolies over the nation's energy flows. The supply and demand mismatch allows midstream operators to translate super-high throughput into secure, fee-based cash flow and dividend distributions. Kinder Morgan The premier beneficiary of this dynamic is Kinder Morgan, which physically moves about 40% of all natural gas consumed in the United States. Kinder Morgan operates a dominant, interconnected web of steel pipelines that links oversupplied shale basins directly to major demand centers and Gulf Coast export complexes. On Wednesday, Kinder Morgan reported record third-quarter adjusted earnings of 35 cents per share, up 21% year over year. For all of 2026, Kinder Morgan said it expects adjusted EPS of $1.36. Kinder also said it would invest $4.7 billion in two natural gas pipeline projects, bringing its backlog to $14.4 billion, with the vast majority — a record $13.2 billion — targeted to natural gas projects. "We continue to see significant, incremental project opportunities across our natural gas pipeline network driven primarily by power and LNG, and we will continue to pursue them aggressively," Dax Sanders, Kinder's president, said on the earnings conference call Wednesday. Through Thursday's close, Kinder Morgan stock is ahead more than 23% year to date. Several Wall Street firms increased price targets on the stock in the wake of the results. KMI 3M mountain Kinder Morgan stock over the last three months Energy Transfer Operating right alongside Kinder Morgan is Energy Transfer , which leverages 140,000 miles of gas, oil, and product pipelines that connect major U.S. production basins to key domestic utilities and international transport hubs, generating cash flows that are insulated from commodity fluctuations. Its stock is up more than 20% year to date. Energy Transfer offers a uniquely attractive total return profile by combining a market leading 6.5% distribution yield with an aggressive consolidation strategy. Ninety percent of the company's business is entirely fee based . Energy Transfer trades at a substantial discount to its peers due to higher leverage and its complex structure. As a master limited partnership, Energy Transfer has the liquidity of a regular stock and the tax benefits of a private partnership. An MLP pays no corporate income tax. Instead, the majority of its cash flow is distributed to investors, who are responsible for the tax. ET'E 3M mountain Energy Transfer stock over the last three months Williams Cos. Rounding out this elite tier is Williams, whose irreplaceable Transco pipeline system serves as the primary artery feeding the booming, high-demand data center alleys in Virginia and the southeastern U.S. As tech giants build out gas-fired generation to power their massive AI clusters, they are heavily dependent on the Transco. Williams stock is up more than 17% year to date. By capturing predictable fees on a massive, permanent baseline of cheap American energy, these three midstream powerhouses represent a high-quality structural play for investors. articles.title: Investors are starting to find opportunities in the battered bond market
articles.text:
Even after another bond market rout Friday, investors are turning their attention toward Treasurys, anticipating that yields may be topping out.
The benchmark 10-year note spent the day flirting with the psychologically important 5% level as oil prices surged and a fresh consumer survey showed that inflation expectations remain a good distance above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal.
Still, some market participants see reason for hope in a market bludgeoned this year over worries about rising prices, tensions in the Middle East and stiff competition from artificial intelligence hyperscalers flooding the market with debt.
Bank of America's Michael Hartnett in a client note declared "The Price is Right" on the battered Treasury market, which he noted has seen its worst long-run return in the past 100 years.
The investment strategist noted in his weekly money-flow summary that the "secular contrarian [trade] would be adding bonds," drawing a parallel to similar long-run negative returns for stocks and commodities that later proved to be good entry points
Despite the negative returns and soaring yields this year, investors are putting money into fixed income and government debt in particular.
Treasurys saw $5.4 billion in inflows over the past week, part of $12.1 billion overall into the bond market, according to data compiled by BofA. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, a $47.3 billion fund that offers exposure to long-dated government debt, has seen $1.14 billion in fresh investor cash over the past month.
One reason for investor enthusiasm is the simple belief that the Treasury sell-off has exhausted itself, with the market pricing in the various risks to the market and now at least ready to stabilize.
Thursday's trading saw the 10-year yield crater a massive 19 basis points, or 0.19 percentage point.
Nicholas Colas, co-founder of DataTrek Research, calculated the gain as a "3 standard deviation move," or well outside the expected trading range for the flagship Treasury security for the day. Given current conditions, including another sanguine reading on unemployment claims Thursday, Colas wrote in his daily market note that the trade "catalyst was not a sudden change in the market's view on the U.S. economy."
"Our read is that the Treasury market is taking the equity and corporate debt market's collective angst about AI-related CapEx funding as a sign incremental issuance will slow," he added. "With less of this paper coming to market, Treasuries face less competition for capital."
Historically, stocks and bonds generally move opposite each other. As risk appetite grows, investors generally eschew the safety of bonds, and vice versa.
That hasn't been the trend lately, as Friday's slide in the stock market coincided with an aggressive sell-off in bonds, a trade largely driven by fears of escalating oil prices hitting both asset classes.
However, Colas said history suggests the correlation again will return, making a stocks/bonds mix still "a reasonable approach, recent painful history notwithstanding."
Moreover, he called the Thursday plunge in yields "an important signal."
"The fever of higher rates may not have entirely broken," he said, "but [Thursday] was a solid step in the right direction."

articles.title: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets
articles.text:
Before the Iran war, Qatar was one of the biggest natural gas exporters in the world. After only eight months, the Gulf state is now buying supplies from its principal competitor — the United States.
QatarEnergy struck a deal Thursday with U.S. exporter Cheniere Energy to buy 4 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, annually through 2054. The purchase price is indexed to the U.S. Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are expected to begin in the 2030s.
"We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century," Cheniere CEO Jack Fusco said in a statement.
The gas that Doha will buy is less than 1% of the global LNG trade of more than 400 million metric tons. But "in terms of an individual deal, this is about as big as you see in the U.S," said Alex Munton, director of global gas and LNG at Rapidan Energy in Houston.
The deal signals how the Iran war is reshaping global energy markets to the benefit of U.S. companies, cementing the dominance of American LNG exporters. Shares of Cheniere and Venture Global, the other independent U.S. player, have gained 26% and 40%, respectively, since the start of the war.
Qatar knocked out
Qatar was second only to the U.S. in LNG exports before the war. But shipments have since collapsed in the eight months since Iran bombed its key production facility at Ras Laffan. The attack badly damaged two production lines, taking out about 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.
It will take about three years to repair the damage at Ras Laffan, Qatar's energy minister, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, has said. The Persian Gulf state has declared force majeure — citing unexpected, uncontrollable events preventing contracts from being honored — every month since the March attack.
"It did give us a big blow, if you will, for our production capability for the next few years," Al-Kaabi said in an interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in September. Qatar is exporting "very little" LNG right now because "we can't export through the Hormuz Strait," he said.
"Very sparingly, some ships are crossing the straits but a very small amount, it's not something that would even be measurable in a percentage point," the energy minister said. 
Freedom of navigation
And it is far from clear what security conditions in Hormuz will look like when the repairs are done at Ras Laffan. The decades-long contract with Cheniere indicates that Qatar sees a risk that freedom of navigation will never return to Hormuz as Iran keeps attacking tankers, Munton said.
It is harder to find ways to get around Hormuz in the case of LNG because it is fundamentally a waterborne product, the analyst said.
"It's liquefied so it can be put on a ship and that requires access to seaborne routes," Munton said. "They've got to access the Strait of Hormuz. There's no other way of getting LNG to market. They're just stuck."
With its production badly damaged and Hormuz blocked off, QatarEnergy is expanding its LNG trading business through the Cheniere deal, Munton said.
It secured a $3 billion loan earlier this month from Chinese banks that could allow it to secure more U.S. LNG to honor its international delivery commitments, said Manav Gupta, a UBS analyst, in a note to clients Thursday.
Bullish Wall Street
Venture Global, for example, is in advanced talks with QatarEnergy to supply 3 million metric tons annually, unnamed sources told Reuters.
With the Qatar deal, Cheniere is disproving the bears' case that it will struggle to secure incremental sales which would in turn constrain capacity expansion, Gupta said. UBS has a stock price target of $340 on Cheniere, implying 18% upside from Thursday's close.
Wall Street is broadly bullish on both Cheniere and Venture Global. Nearly 90% of equity analysts who cover Cheniere rate it a buy, with an average price target of $314, implying about 9% upside from Thursday's close.
Nearly 60% of analysts recommend Venture Global as a buy with the rest rating it a hold. The average price target of $17 would amount to some 35% upside from Thursday's close.
"The U.S. once again is being called on by buyers to diversify supply," Munton said. "So much is under construction in the U.S. that you get to the point where now the U.S. is becoming disproportionately big in terms of global [LNG] market share."

articles.title: Musk's SpaceX is still restricting Starlink in Ukraine and the toll is rising
articles.text:
SpaceX's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday.
"Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S., in a Friday post on X.
"Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait."
Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said.
Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.
"They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on."
"Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are."
Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel.
"While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google.
Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear.
Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine."
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back."
But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored.
"I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him."
Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service.
Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."
On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."
-- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story.

articles.title: The S&P 500 is forming a bearish chart pattern. Can it snap out of it?
articles.text: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.) The S & P 500 has struggled to break decisively above 7,800 since first reaching that area in late July. Along the way, it has repeatedly tested its rising 50-day moving average while developing a negative momentum divergence, with the 14-day RSI making lower highs since peaking in May. Negative divergences alone don't necessarily lead to immediate declines. However, what's particularly interesting is how similar technical conditions developed ahead of the market's two largest corrections over the past year and a half. The first occurred from late 2024 into early 2025. Following an extended advance, the S & P 500 began testing its rising 50-day moving average as negative RSI divergences developed. Subsequent breakout attempts failed, preceding the sharp decline associated with the tariff tantrum. A similar sequence unfolded in late 2025. Momentum deteriorated as the S & P 500 tested its rising 50-day moving average and struggled to break above 7,000. Those failed rallies eventually gave way to a correction of approximately 10%, accompanied by the Iran conflict. Today, we're seeing a familiar combination: repeated tests of the rising 50-day moving average, difficulty sustaining a breakout above 7,800, and persistent negative momentum divergences. The similarities don't guarantee another significant decline, but they deserve attention. Importantly, the catalyst matters less than the market's reaction. Repeated failures of bullish patterns can eventually give way to a successful topping formation, potentially leading to a more meaningful decline. Right now, a potential bearish formation has taken shape, and additional downside follow-through would complete the pattern. That's concerning, but we've seen this before. In fact, the uptrend since the March lows has been characterized by multiple bearish patterns that ultimately failed. Buyers have consistently stepped in just when the technical picture looked its worst. Here are four of them. Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis , an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. We exited Broadcom . Rising bond yields and West Texas Intermediate crude up over $103 per barrel, due to fears of renewed tensions between the U.S. and Iran, are not helping stocks. Portfolio director Jeff Marks pointed out that despite yesterday's broader weakness, it wasn't all bad news for our Club names, with Eli Lilly , Johnson & Johnson , and Kimberly-Clark seeing notable gains. While all three are down Friday, Jeff said the moves are a reminder of why it is "always good to have some of these in a portfolio to be diversified for months like this." All three still have nice gains week to date. 2. Meta Platforms shares fell again Friday, extending Thursday's nearly 7% decline. It's one of our worst performers for the week. Jeff said that Meta is at the center of a growing concern among investors — "how is the AI buildout going to get funded?" Wall Street is increasingly worried about how the social media giant will finance its AI ambitions, which include expansion of its hit new AI agent Muse, as free cash flow turned negative for the first time since the company's 2012 initial public offering. Meta raised the low end of its full-year capital expenditure outlook. In an SEC filing, the company mentioned needing to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars over a period of several years beginning as early as fall 2026." As for the Club, we're sticking with Meta given its strong fundamentals and promising Muse roadmap, which were on display during the just-reported quarter. However, the bright spots have been overshadowed by all this other stuff. 3. We picked up a few shares of GE Vernova during yesterday's sell-off. Jim Cramer felt that it was a good time to make the move after watching and waiting. "Why don't we pick up a little bit, play for a little bit of a bounce, because remember the data center demand story is still quite strong," he said. When GE Vernova reports earnings next week, Jeff said we want to hear about continued strong orders for the company's heavy-duty gas turbines and strong pricing. We will also want to see that their electrical business is doing well, too. Looking ahead, 10 other Club names are on next week's earnings docket: Boeing , Alphabet , Microsoft , Linde , Eli Lilly , Starbucks , Amazon , Intel , FedEx , and FedEx Freight . articles.title: College campuses have (largely) gone silent. Can practicing small talk and phone-free spaces change that?
articles.text:
Charlie Harker had high hopes for college.
Before starting her freshman year in 2023, the Lebanon, Ohio, resident had planned to meet people through clubs or at the dorms. She'd expected there would be an open, vibrant atmosphere ripe for making friends. She'd quickly find her people.
"And then I got to school," says the 21-year-old senior at the University of Cincinnati. "I didn't know anyone on my floor. No one had their door open. No one would really talk to you." That fun and peer-filled campus life she'd been promised by both family and pop culture turned out to be, at least to some extent, a relic of the past.
Harker's college experience is fairly common these days. From 2003 to 2025, 20-to 24-year-olds' socializing and communicating in the U.S dropped 52%, from an average of 64 minutes per day in their leisure time to an average of just over 30 minutes per day. Over the same period, 15-to 19-year-olds' leisure time socializing dropped 32% to 38 minutes, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Students these days view school as more "transactional" than in the past, says Steven Rogelberg, Chancellor's professor of organizational science, management and psychology at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. "You go there, you take your classes, and then you leave."
That's a problem for a variety of reasons. If they're not meeting in class or stopping each other in the hallways, young people may be missing out on developing both friendships and social skills, which are critical for long-term life and career success. Making small talk, for instance, can help forge both personal and professional relationships down the line, says Kristie Patten, dean of NYU's Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development.
Also essential: building confidence, which can come both from successfully navigating social situations and making painful mistakes. Without that practice, both campus and life can become more insular and sterile.
"Parents and school systems, and maybe even legislators, are going to have to deal with this if we want a future where we have kids and adults who understand how to be social with one another," says Lance Garrison, dean of the College of Professional Psychology at The Chicago School.
"The trajectory we are on right now is one toward increasing isolation, increasing loneliness, increasing anxiety."
Some students and schools are tackling their campus antisocial problems head-on. CNBC Make It spoke with 15 students, educators and mental health experts to see how we got here — and where we might be going.
'I think a lot of people just got used to not hanging out'
Today's college students were already at a disadvantage, socially speaking, well before stepping foot on campus.
Not only were they forced to isolate during middle school or high school because of the pandemic, many are also finding fewer spaces to meet in real life, as malls and movie theaters — traditional meeting grounds for young people — have shuttered in recent years. "A lot of them never had to build those muscles of how do you socialize in person," says Chicago-based therapist Andrew Fishman.
For some teenagers, that inability to connect meant new norms. "I think a lot of people just got used to not hanging out with people after school," says Harker about high school.
For others, it's made approaching people that much scarier. The less you have a chance to talk to someone new, says Garrison, "the more anxious you are going to be about engaging in those types of activities."
On campus, that could also mean high rates of loneliness. When asked how often they feel or felt lonely in college in a CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll conducted in August 2026, a quarter of 18-to 34-year-olds said "always" or "often," versus just 14% of 35-to 64-year-olds. The modeled error estimate for this survey was plus or minus 3.0 percentage points.
The dining hall is 'people with AirPods and watching YouTube sitting alone'
When they finally reach the hallowed halls of their universities, many students are constantly connected to a device. Often, they are heads down in screens or engrossed in whatever's happening in their headphones.
Before class, 19-year-old Karla Berrueto, a junior in standing at the University of Houston, reports: "No one really talks to each other." Twenty-one-year-old Jean Antoine, a senior at Loyola Marymount University, offers a similar appraisal. At the dining hall, it's "more of people with AirPods and watching YouTube sitting alone" than talking, he says.
Even when people go out of their way to connect offline, they're frequently stymied. Franco Geldart, a 20-year-old sophomore at Northeastern University, joined a cooking club his freshman year. He found striking up conversations with people a bit awkward. Often, "I was sitting [there] for an hour and I didn't speak with a single person," he says.
Most of the students CNBC Make It spoke with attended up to a handful of parties per year. Some described them as events you attend with friends and leave, rather than fluid opportunities to engage with new people.
The trajectory we are on right now is one toward increasing isolation, increasing loneliness, increasing anxiety.Lance GarrisonDean, College of Professional Psychology at the Chicago School
Asked how often they initiate or initiated conversations with people at school they didn't know, 31% of Gen Z said "rarely" or "never," according to the CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll, versus 26% of Millennials and 22% of Gen X.
Another new element of today's campus is the plethora of online platforms on which one can be called out for doing … anything, really, making even the most mundane decisions terrifying.
Yik Yak and Fizz are anonymous digital message boards. Fizz alone is live at more than 800 U.S. college campuses, according to its website. Many schools also have dedicated Barstool Sports Instagram pages, often affiliated with the popular sports blog but unaffiliated with the schools. All three may contain posts making fun of individual students' behavior.
Harker remembers going to a football game her freshman year and losing the friend she came with. She felt paralyzed, scared of trying to befriend people who'd reject her and even more terrified of getting photographed sitting at the game by herself.
"If I just sat there alone," she says she thought, "would I get on the Barstool page?" What would the social repercussions of that be?
Yik Yak, Fizz and Barstool Sports did not respond to CNBC Make It's request for comment.
'We're going to bring back house parties'
To be clear, young people are still forging connections on campus. They are figuring it out. Some are even experiencing similar levels of social fluidity as prior generations.
And some see what's been happening on campus and taking action.
Geldart is working on an application for a new club at Northeastern this year called Wildcard. It would partner with existing clubs and do one-off drop-ins in which members from each club would be randomly paired up for a project.
"It's just to get people talking," he says.
At New York University, students have spearheaded a campus-wide initiative called NYU IRL, centered on connecting in the age of technology. With the help of a coalition of deans, faculty, staff and grad students, NYU IRL projects include phone-free spaces, a phone breakup challenge with Catherine Price, author of "How to Break Up With Your Phone," and a video series about how to make small talk. More than 1,000 students have signed up for the phone breakup challenge alone.
For her part, Harker found someone she knew at the football game where she'd lost her friend and the two became each other's go-to game date. She joined a sorority and now lives in a house with a number of her friends.
Harker's working on creating more opportunities for people to meet. She remembers attending one house party her freshman year, for example. "It was the best experience I ever had," she says. It was an easy, casual way to get to know people. Harker and her roommates are now trying to replicate that experience.
"We have this thing," she says, "we're going to bring back house parties."

articles.title: We're exiting our position in this chipmaker and right-sizing another winner
articles.text: We're making two trades in Friday's tough broader market. We're exiting our position in Broadcom , selling our remaining 120 shares at roughly $326 each. Jim Cramer's Charitable will no longer own a position in AVGO. We're selling 85 shares of CrowdStrike at roughly $251. The Trust will own 665 shares of CRWD, reducing its weighting in the portfolio to from 4.25% from 4.8%. We're taking advantage of Friday's small bounce in Broadcom shares to sell our remaining stake, capturing an average gain of roughly 128% on stock we purchased in 2023 and 2024. We sold some shares on Tuesday to take the position size down to 1% from 1.36%. Still, with the data center theme struggling due to funding concerns, Jim wants to take a more defensive approach to the portfolio and hold fewer names until we see how the pending Anthropic IPO, expected as soon as mid-November, plays out and gain more clarity on Meta Platforms ' future equity raises. "The collapse of the data center requires us to circle the wagons," Jim said. "We can't have too much of the ones we have. We can pick as we did with GEV but nothing aggressive. And all tag ends should go like Broadcom." He continued: "Circling means we want to be bigger in the better ones." For example, he expressed the difficulty of selling Micron at these levels and would rather be a buyer of the memory maker at some point. AVGO YTD mountain Broadcom YTD We may be selling Broadcom after a brutal decline from its June highs; we took a chunk off the top in the $480s, but we've cut this position over the past few months at higher prices. We understand there may be frustration around selling an AI beneficiary with a strong revenue outlook and reasonable valuation after a big drawdown. But these sales are about protecting our big gains and limiting our exposure to a group that has come under fire. This line of thinking served us well in Arm Holdings when we exited our position around $300 in early July, and in our Corning exit in the mid-$140s last month. CRWD YTD mountain CrowdStrike YTD We will also sell some CrowdStrike into this week's roughly 9% rebound. This decision doesn't reflect anything negative about the cybersecurity company's fundamentals. Rather, it's a portfolio management move to right-size the position (once again) following a big move that pushed its weighting toward the top of the portfolio. From this sale, we will realize a gain of roughly 187% on stock purchased in late 2024. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long AVGO. See here for a full list of the stocks.) articles.title: Giá vàng miếng, vàng nhẫn sáng 24/10 tại SJC, PNJ, DOJI, Bảo Tín Minh Châu và Bảo Tín Mạnh Hải
articles.text:
Giá vàng miếng, vàng nhẫn sáng 24/10 tại SJC, PNJ, DOJI, Bảo Tín Minh Châu và Bảo Tín Mạnh Hải
Giá vàng trên thị trường quốc tế chịu áp lực trước triển vọng lạm phát. Theo đó giá vàng giao ngay rơi xuống dưới 4.000 USD/ounce.
Theo khảo sát đầu giờ sáng 24/10, giá vàng miếng tại Công ty SJC được niêm yết ở mức 139 – 142 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào – bán ra). PNJ, DOJI và Bảo Tín Mạnh Hải cũng niêm yết cùng mức giá này.
Tại Bảo Tín Minh Châu, giá vàng miếng được niêm yết ở mức 137,4 – 142 triệu đồng/lượng. Trong khi đó, Phú Quý giao dịch ở mức 138 – 142 triệu đồng/lượng. Như vậy, giá bán vàng miếng tại cả 6 thương hiệu được khảo sát đều ở mức 142 triệu đồng/lượng, song giá mua vào chênh lệch tới 1,6 triệu đồng/lượng.
Đối với vàng nhẫn 9999, Công ty SJC niêm yết giá ở mức 135 – 139 triệu đồng/lượng. Đây là mức giá bán thấp nhất trong nhóm thương hiệu được khảo sát.
Tại PNJ, giá vàng nhẫn được niêm yết ở mức 138 – 141 triệu đồng/lượng. DOJI giao dịch ở mức 137,5 – 141,5 triệu đồng/lượng, là thương hiệu có giá bán cao nhất trong nhóm khảo sát.
Trong khi đó, Bảo Tín Minh Châu niêm yết giá vàng nhẫn ở mức 137,4 – 141,4 triệu đồng/lượng. Phú Quý giao dịch ở mức 138 – 141 triệu đồng/lượng. Tại Bảo Tín Mạnh Hải, giá mua vào vàng nhẫn được ghi nhận ở mức 136,4 triệu đồng/lượng.
Như vậy, giá bán vàng nhẫn tại các thương hiệu có đủ dữ liệu niêm yết dao động từ 139 đến 141,5 triệu đồng/lượng, chênh lệch 2,5 triệu đồng/lượng giữa nơi cao nhất và thấp nhất.
Trên thị trường quốc tế, giá vàng giảm khá mạnh và tuột mốc 4.000 USD/ounce, hiện giao động quanh 3.980 - 4.000 USD/ounce.
Kim loại quý chịu áp lực trước ngưỡng hỗ trợ quan trọng 4.000 USD/ounce khi dữ liệu mới công bố cho thấy tâm lý người tiêu dùng Mỹ gần như không thay đổi, trong khi kỳ vọng lạm phát tiếp tục gia tăng.
Theo báo cáo được Đại học Michigan công bố ngày thứ Sáu (23/10), chỉ số niềm tin tiêu dùng Mỹ tháng 10 đạt 48 điểm, cao hơn mức 46,3 điểm mà các nhà kinh tế dự báo. Con số này cũng cao hơn kết quả khảo sát sơ bộ 46,3 điểm và chỉ thấp hơn đôi chút so với mức 48,1 điểm ghi nhận trong tháng 9.
Bà Joanne Hsu, Giám đốc Khảo sát Người tiêu dùng của Đại học Michigan, cho biết tâm lý người tiêu dùng nhìn chung ổn định trong tháng này, với mức giảm chỉ 0,1 điểm so với tháng trước.
Theo bà, sự cải thiện niềm tin trong nhóm cử tri ủng hộ đảng Cộng hòa và đảng Dân chủ đã được bù trừ bởi mức suy giảm trong nhóm cử tri độc lập. Mặc dù đánh giá của người tiêu dùng về triển vọng kinh doanh trong 12 tháng tới cải thiện khoảng 14%, chỉ số này vẫn thấp hơn 16% so với tháng 10 năm ngoái.
Đáng chú ý, sự suy giảm của chỉ số đánh giá điều kiện kinh tế hiện tại trong tháng 10 hoàn toàn xuất phát từ tâm lý thận trọng đối với việc mua sắm hàng hóa lâu bền.
Theo bà Hsu, chỉ số đánh giá điều kiện mua sắm các mặt hàng này giảm mạnh 18%, chủ yếu do lãi suất cao và những lo ngại ngày càng lớn về khả năng chi trả của người tiêu dùng.
Đối với thị trường vàng, sự gia tăng kỳ vọng lạm phát có thể tạo ra những tác động trái chiều. Một mặt, lo ngại về sức mua suy giảm có thể thúc đẩy nhu cầu nắm giữ vàng như một tài sản bảo toàn giá trị. Mặt khác, kỳ vọng lạm phát duy trì ở mức cao có thể khiến Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) tiếp tục giữ chính sách tiền tệ thắt chặt, qua đó gây sức ép lên kim loại quý.
Trong bối cảnh giá vàng đang giao dịch sát ngưỡng hỗ trợ tâm lý 4.000 USD/ounce, diễn biến kỳ vọng lạm phát và triển vọng lãi suất Mỹ sẽ tiếp tục là những yếu tố quan trọng được thị trường theo dõi.
